title: Asian Pear and Cucumber Salad
times: Prep: 15 minutes · Cook: 0 minutes · Total: 15 minutes, serve within the hour · Serves 4 as banchan

schema.name: Asian Pear and Cucumber Salad
schema.description: **Stream: heritage — the palate cleanser that grows on trees.
recipeIngredient: 1 large Asian pear (about 400 g), cored, cut into matchsticks (skin on — the skin is the texture)
A pinch of coarse salt (about 2 g), over the cucumber only, 5 minutes

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2

blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the palate cleanser that grows on trees. Asian pear — the crisp, watery, honeyed fruit that marinates meat in this cuisine's other records — takes the leading role here: matchsticked with cucumber and dressed in a light sweet-soy-sesame with a gochugaru thread. It is the fresh bowl for the heaviest grill meals, the one that resets a palate loaded with gochujang (#M13) and lacquer (#M03), and the only bowl on the fresh list that belongs to dessert's register while staying firmly at dinner.

title: Baechu Geotjeori Fresh Kimchi
times: Prep: 20 minutes · Cook: 0 minutes · Total: 20 minutes, best within 3 hours · Serves 6–8 as banchan

schema.name: Baechu Geotjeori Fresh Kimchi
recipeIngredient: 1/2 large head napa cabbage (about 1 kg), cut into 4 cm lengths
1 tbsp coarse salt (about 15 g), plus more to taste
1 tbsp fish sauce (15 ml) — or 1 tbsp soy sauce for the vegan table
2 scallions (about 30 g), sliced; 1/2 Asian pear (about 100 g), in fine matchsticks; 1 tsp sesame seeds (about 4 g)

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Gochugaru, fish sauce, garlic, ginger, and sugar worked to a paste, loosened with a tablespoon of the cabbage's rinse water; pear matchsticks and scallion folded through. Checkpoint: the paste tastes complete and slightly over-strong (sweet-savory-hot with a raw gochugaru edge) — the cabbage's water rounds it within the hour.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: The squeezed cabbage and the dressing tossed together by hand, massaged for a full minute so every leaf's surface takes the paste, sesame oil and seeds last. Checkpoint: the bowl test, ten minutes after mixing: crisp, wet-crunchy leaves, the dressing clinging rather than pooling, the flavor fully arrived — bright, sweet-hot, green. No sourness, and none expected: geotjeori's identity is the absence of the ferment.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the unfermented same-day kimchi. Geotjeori is kimchi's answer to right now: napa cabbage salted just enough to soften, dressed in the full kimchi paste, and on the table within the hour — no ferment, no jar, no waiting. It is sweeter and greener than the fermented bowl (#B01), built for the day the jar runs empty or the grill was decided this morning. This is also the record for the first-time kimchi maker: every flavor of the tradition, none of the calendar.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• A short salt, not a brine. Toss the cut cabbage with the salt, rest 20 minutes, and it weeps enough to wilt the leaves a half-step while staying crisp — geotjeori's whole texture.   • Build the dressing while the cabbage sits.

title: Baechu Kimchi
metadata: Korean · Medium · Makes 1 large jar (about 2 kg, a month's table)
times: Prep: 2 hours, hands-on · Cook: 0 minutes · Total: 2 hours, then 1–3 days fermenting at 15–20 °C, then the fridge · Makes 1 large jar (about 2 kg, a month's table)

schema.name: Baechu Kimchi
schema.description: **Stream: heritage — the table's anchor.** Every grill table on this site leans on the same bowl: napa cabbage kimchi, the fermented national dish, sour and crunchy and alive, cutting every rich thing the fire produces.
schema.recipeYield: Makes 1 large jar (about 2 kg, a month's table)
recipeIngredient: 2 large heads napa cabbage (about 3 kg total)
1 cup coarse sea salt (about 200 g) for the brine
150 g Korean radish (mu) or daikon, cut into fine matchsticks
4 scallions (about 60 g), cut into 4 cm lengths
1/2 Asian pear or 1 small apple (about 100 g), grated
8 cloves garlic (about 32 g), grated or blitzed
2 tbsp salted shrimp (saeujeot, about 30 g), minced — the traditional depth, optional if unfindable
1 cup gochugaru (about 100 g) — mild for the default batch
1/2 cup water (120 ml), or the saved brine
1 large glass jar or onggi (ceramic crock), clean and dry

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Dress the quarters, leaf by leaf, by hand. Hold a drained cabbage quarter over the paste bowl and work the paste up under each leaf with your gloved or very red bare hands — stem bases get the most, green tops a smear. Do not shred the cabbage: the quarters stay whole, stuffed from the outside in. This hand work is the recipe's heart; a machine has never made this dish. Checkpoint: every leaf's stem carries a visible coat of paste and flecks of radish; the quarter, pressed gently, holds together as one piece.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Pack the jar tight, in layers. Fold each dressed quarter over itself (fold the tip toward the core), press it into the jar, and push down hard to squeeze out air pockets — oxygen is the spoilage path, brine is the preservation path. Leave 5 cm of headspace at the top: the ferment expands. Press a clean weight (a small jar, a boiled stone) on top and lid it loosely — never sealed, the ferment needs to breathe or it will bubble over. Checkpoint: after a day, brine rises over the cabbage on its own. If it has not, top up with a little salted water (1 tsp salt per cup) — the vegetables must ferment under liquid, that is the entire safety architecture.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Ferment warm, then hold cold. 1–3 days at cool room temperature (15–20 °C — the Korean autumn kitchen's window; warmer runs faster and sharper) until the jar smells sour-sweet and lively and the brine fizzes faintly at a stir, then into the refrigerator, where the ferment slows to a crawl and the flavor deepens for weeks. Checkpoint: the taste at jar-opening day: cabbage still crunchy, paste savory-hot, a clean sourness arriving on the finish — young kimchi, mild and bright. A week in the fridge it rounds; two weeks it sharpens; a month it is the sour, complex elder that stews (#M13's fried-rice day-after) are built for. You are not choosing one kimchi; you are choosing this week's chapter of it.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the table's anchor. Every grill table on this site leans on the same bowl: napa cabbage kimchi, the fermented national dish, sour and crunchy and alive, cutting every rich thing the fire produces. This record is the whole-cabbage, cut-at-the-jar method — a proper batch, two hours of honest work and a few days of patience — because the kimchi that answers samgyeopsal (#M10) and dwaeji bulgogi (#M13) should be the real one, not the shriveled retail jar's sad cousin. The process has three crafts in it: the salt that softens the cabbage, the paste that becomes the flavor, and the ferment that turns both into kimchi.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Salt the cabbage the traditional way, in quarters. Cut each head lengthwise into quarters through the core (leave the core attached — it holds the quarters together), then salt between every leaf: a pinch of coarse salt at the thick white stem base of each leaf, lighter toward the green tops. Sit the salted quarters in a tub or sink, weighted, 2 hours, turning every 30 minutes. The cabbage weeps, softens, and bends without breaking — that bend is the brine's finish line. Rinse twice in cold water and drain 30 minutes in a colander. Checkpoint — a stem folded gently between your fingers bends like a thick noodle, without snapping. Snappy cabbage was under-salted or under-time — salt it longer, there is no other fix.
  • Build the paste while the cabbage drains. Gochugaru, water (or saved brine), grated pear, garlic, ginger, fish sauce, salted shrimp, sugar — stirred into a thick rust-red slurry. Then the radish matchsticks and scallions folded through: they carry the paste between the leaves and become the batch's best bites.

Trust the jar's signals, keep everything under brine, and the ferment will teach you its calendar faster than any recipe can.

blocks.html:
Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The brine: cabbage bends without snapping, rinsed and drained 30 minutes.
  • The dressing: paste on every stem base, quarters whole, hand-worked.
  • The pack: air pressed out, 5 cm headspace, weight on top, lid loose.
  • The ferment: sour-sweet smell and faint fizz at 1–3 days at 15–20 °C, then refrigerated.

blocks.name: finish-plate
blocks.html:
Finish & Plate

Cut a dressed quarter crosswise into bite lengths over the jar (the brine catches the drips), pile into the small bowl with tongs, and set it beside the grill's richest plate. The jar goes back to the fridge the moment the meal ends — the batch's clock never stops, it only slows.

title: Chadolbaegi with Scallion-Soy Dipping Sauce
times: Prep: 10 minutes · Cook: 6 minutes · Total: About 20 minutes at the table · Serves 4

schema.name: Chadolbaegi with Scallion-Soy Dipping Sauce
schema.description: **Stream: restaurant.** Chadolbaegi — paper-thin frozen beef brisket shavings — is the tabletop grill's speed round.
recipeIngredient: 700 g beef brisket, frozen hard and machine-sliced paper-thin (order "chadolbaegi" at a Korean market; freeze your own block 3–4 hours and have it sliced or shave it yourself on a mandoline)
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), kimchi (#B01), sangchu geotjeori (#F03), soju's presence is traditional and optional

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Lay the frozen shavings flat, one layer, as many as fit without touching. They cook in 8–12 seconds a side — the grill boss stands over them with tongs the entire time. The edge will crisp and frill while the center barely sets; that is the dish. Checkpoint: the color change runs pink-frost to gray-brown at the edges with the fat turning translucent. Pull the slice the moment it no longer looks raw; a fully cooked-through chadolbaegi slice is a ruined one.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Dip while hot, straight from tongs to bowl to mouth. Rice between rounds; the fat is rich in a way that wants starch and acid beside it. Checkpoint: eating test: crisp edge, melting center, the dip's vinegar and scallion cutting the fattiness. If it tastes purely of fat, the dip is too gentle — more vinegar and gochugaru.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Repeat in small batches. The shavings come off the freezer pack a handful at a time; any that thaw on the platter go on the grill immediately at a slightly cooler spot, or into the next round of fried rice instead. Checkpoint: by the last batch the dip bowl should be reduced and cloudy from repeated dunking — the traditional end state, and the sign of a full table.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: restaurant. Chadolbaegi — paper-thin frozen beef brisket shavings — is the tabletop grill's speed round. The slices are cut while frozen hard, dropped on the grate still frost-cold, and cooked in seconds per side; the whole pleasure is the contrast of a crisp lacy edge against a melting, barely-set center, dunked in a sharp scallion-soy dip. It is the cheapest cut on the K-BBQ menu and routinely the favorite order, because chadolbaegi's ratio of drama to effort has no rival. Ten seconds of patience at the fire, and the fat does everything else.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Keep the meat frozen until the moment it grills. This is the one record where "straight from the freezer" is the technique: thawed chadolbaegi welds to the grate and loses the shavings' shape. Work from the freezer in batches.
  • Mix the dip in a bowl the whole table can reach: everything whisked, scallions last. It should taste sharp and a little hot — the meat is rich and needs a dip that fights back.
  • Set the grill to its hottest sustainable setting; chadolbaegi wants the same fire you'd sear a steak on, about 230 °C at the grate if you can measure.

blocks.name: storage-variations
blocks.html:
Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • The frozen block keeps 2 months sealed; thawed slices should be cooked the same day. The dip keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves overnight.
  • Variations: the dip builds toward cho-gochujang (#SA03) for a hotter table; leftover shavings into kimchi fried rice; the same dip on grilled mushrooms (#SF02's lane) carries the vegan table.

title: Cho-Gochujang Sweet-Tangy Chili Sauce
times: Prep: 10 minutes · Cook: 0 minutes · Total: 10 minutes · Makes about 200 g

schema.name: Cho-Gochujang Sweet-Tangy Chili Sauce
recipeIngredient: 1.5 tbsp honey or corn syrup (about 30 g)
1 tbsp water (15 ml), plus more to loosen
1/2 tsp gochugaru (about 1.5 g), optional heat edge
1/2 cucumber, deseeded and small-diced (about 75 g) — the cold-noodle classic's version
Thin slivers of Asian pear (about 40 g) for the raw-seafood lane

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Vinegar, honey, and water whisked clear; gochujang in, worked to one even red-orange with no dark streaks. Checkpoint: a spoon dragged through leaves a slowly-closing trail — the thickness of thick honey for the noodle build.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Garlic, sesame oil, sesame seeds; the build-ins to the bowl's job; a final taste — the vinegar should be present on the finish of a dipped finger, a clean snap after the sweet. Checkpoint: the eating test on a piece of plain cucumber: snap, sweet, heat hum, acid line. If the cucumber tastes pickled in ten seconds of sitting, the vinegar ran a splash heavy; if it reads as plain gochujang, the vinegar is shy.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — vinegar's bowl. Cho-gochujang — "vinegar gochujang" — is the bright member of the dip family: gochujang loosened and sharpened with vinegar and sweetener into a spooning-and-dunking sauce that runs where ssamjang (#SA01) sits. It is the classic partner for raw and chilled things — cold noodles, cucumber, hwe-style seafood — and at the grill table it is the bowl for anything that wants sweetness cut with a real acid line: the shrimp records, the squid (#SF04), skewers (#M18). One bowl, ten minutes, and the vinegar does the transforming.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• The order: dissolve the sweet in the sour before the paste joins. Vinegar and honey whisked until clear, then the gochujang worked in — this direction dissolves the paste smoothly; the reverse direction chases lumps.
  • Loosen to the target use: a spooning sauce for noodles and cucumber runs thicker (barely falling from the spoon); a dunking bowl for grilled pieces runs looser (another tablespoon of water). Decide the bowl's job before the last splash.
  • Taste after the sesame oil, before the build-ins: it should read sweet-and-sour first, fermented-warm second — like a Korean sweet-chili sauce that went to school. Sharper or sweeter is a teaspoon of vinegar or honey away.

If the cucumber tastes pickled in ten seconds of sitting, the vinegar ran a splash heavy; if it reads as plain gochujang, the vinegar is shy. title: Classic Korean Pear Beef Bulgogi
times: Prep: 20 minutes, plus 2–8 hours marinating · Cook: 10 minutes · Total: About 30 minutes at the table (marinate ahead) · Serves 4

schema.name: Classic Korean Pear Beef Bulgogi
recipeIngredient: 700 g beef sirloin or chuck eye, sliced 1–2 mm against the grain (ask the butcher for bulgogi-slice, or freeze 40 minutes and slice yourself)
1 small onion (about 150 g), half grated, half sliced into rings
1/2 Asian pear (about 150 g), grated with its juice — do not substitute apple juice
2 tbsp rice wine or mirin (30 ml)
2 tbsp honey or brown sugar (about 40 g)
2 scallions (about 30 g), sliced; 1 tsp toasted sesame seeds (about 4 g)
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), baechu kimchi (#B01), pajeori scallion salad (#F02), lettuce leaves for ssam, ssamjang (#SA01)
Optional moat vegetables: 100 g king oyster mushroom slices, 1/2 carrot (about 60 g), ribboned

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Build the slurry. Combine grated pear, the grated half-onion, garlic, ginger, soy, rice wine, honey, sesame oil, and pepper in a bowl large enough for the beef. Stir until the honey dissolves — taste it: it should be sweet-salty-forward with pear perfume behind, assertive enough that you'd worry it's too strong. It isn't; the meat and the grill will mute it. Checkpoint: the marinade coats the back of a spoon and smells of pear and soy, with no raw garlic harshness on the nose (the ginger covers it).

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Marry. Add the beef and the sliced onion rings; toss with your hands (the Korean word for this hand-mix, jumulleok, is its own record #M06) until every shaving is coated. Press flat, cover, refrigerate 2–8 hours. Checkpoint: at grilling time the beef has turned deeper red-brown at the edges and the onion has gone slack. No pooling liquid at the bottom beyond the marinade itself — pooling means the pear was over-squeezed or the slice too thick.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Grill hot and fast, in batches. Charcoal or a ripping cast-iron pan (a domed Korean bulgogi pan if you have one, 200 °C-plus at the surface — water should dance and vanish). Spread a single loose layer — piled meat steams in its own juice, and this dish's whole identity is browning plus juice, not steam. The shavings cook in 60–90 seconds a side. Flip when the edges weep and color, not on a clock: beads of pink juice at the rim and the first mahogany edge mean the grill boss turns the batch, then pulls it 20 seconds later when the raw red is just gone. Rest each batch on a warm plate; the moat juice goes to a small pot or the pan's rim to simmer with the mushrooms and carrot. Checkpoint: the eating test: a shaving straight off the grill should be caramel-sweet at the edge, juicy and soft in the middle, with no chewy gray band. Into a lettuce ssam with ssamjang (#SA01) it should taste like the genre's ceiling — but note honestly that the ssam is borrowed ceremony here; this dish's native table is rice, juice over rice, kimchi beside.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 4
recipeInstructions.text: Serve the rice-thief properly. The accumulated moat juice, simmered 2 minutes with any vegetables and poured over rice, is half the point of the lane. Don't discard it into the grill. Checkpoint: the bowl: rice, a ladle of juice, meat over, sesame and scallion. The juice should be sweet-savory and just glossy, not syrup; if it ran syrup, your pan was too cool and the batch steamed.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: restaurant — the Seoul postwar lane. This is the bulgogi the world met after the Korean War: thin beef shavings in a sweet pear-onion-soy slurry, grilled until the edges caramelize, with the juice collecting in the pan's moat to be poured over rice. It is not court food, and on this site we do not pretend it is — the scored soy-sesame sheet of neobiani (#M08) is the heritage cousin, and the two are different dishes that share an ancestor. What this version is, unapologetically, is the best of its own lane: real Asian pear in the marinade, beef sliced properly thin, and a tabletop plan so the last batch off the grill is as good as the first. Who cooks what: one grill boss works the grate while the table builds rice bowls. The moat juice is the shared treasure — protect it.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Slice first, everything else second. The marinade's job is to soak a thin sheet, not a steak — at 1–2 mm the pear's enzymes and the soy reach the center in two hours. Freeze the block firm (about 40 minutes) and slice against the grain with your longest knife, one long stroke per slice.
  • Grate, don't chop, the aromatics. Grated pear, onion, garlic, and ginger become a slurry that coats every shaving; chopped pieces sit on top and burn on the grill. Squeeze the grated pear lightly so the marinade is thick, not watery — a wet marinade steams instead of caramelizing.
  • Marinate 2 hours minimum, 8 maximum. Two hours for weeknight dinner is honest; overnight the pear starts breaking the meat down to mush. This lane wants hours in the fridge — that is the law of the Seoul moat, and it is the opposite of the Gwangyang ticket-toss clock (#M06).
  • Pull the meat from the fridge 20 minutes before grilling. Cold meat on a hot grate equals gray meat.

blocks.html:
Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The slice: 1–2 mm, against the grain, marinated 2–8 hours — never mushy.
  • The grill: single loose layer, flip at the weeping edge, pull when the raw red is just gone.
  • The moat: juice simmered and served over rice, glossy, not syrup.

blocks.name: finish-plate
blocks.html:
Finish & Plate

Pile the batches on a warm platter at the table's center, sesame and scallion over. Rice bowls with the juice ladled first, meat over, kimchi (#B01) and pajeori (#F02) within reach of every hand. Ssam leaves and ssamjang (#SA01) for anyone who wants the wrap; the honest Seoul way is the spoon.

blocks.html:
Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Marinated raw beef keeps 24 hours refrigerated (the clock is already running). Cooked bulgogi keeps 3 days and makes a superb kimchi fried rice or onigirazu filling; reheat hard and fast, never a slow simmer.
  • Variations: mushroom-soy umami build (#M02); the dry heritage fork (#M08); the gochujang lane is a different dish — spicy dwaeji bulgogi (#M13) — and pork, not this record.

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations- Marinated raw beef keeps 24 hours refrigerated (the clock is already running). Cooked bulgogi keeps 3 days and makes a superb kimchi fried rice or onigirazu filling; reheat hard and fast, never a slow simmer.
- Variations: mushroom-soy umami build (#M02); the dry heritage fork (#M08); the gochujang lane is a different dish — spicy dwaeji bulgogi (#M13) — and pork, not this record.

originalInstructions: **Build the slurry.** Combine grated pear, the grated half-onion, garlic, ginger, soy, rice wine, honey, sesame oil, and pepper in a bowl large enough for the beef. Stir until the honey dissolves — taste it: it should be sweet-salty-forward with pear perfume behind, assertive enough that you'd worry it's too strong. It isn't; the meat and the grill will mute it. Checkpoint — the marinade coats the back of a spoon and smells of pear and soy, with no raw garlic harshness on the nose (the ginger covers it).

**Marry.** Add the beef and the sliced onion rings; toss with your hands (the Korean word for this hand-mix, jumulleok, is its own record #M06) until every shaving is coated. Press flat, cover, refrigerate 2–8 hours. Checkpoint — at grilling time the beef has turned deeper red-brown at the edges and the onion has gone slack. No pooling liquid at the bottom beyond the marinade itself — pooling means the pear was over-squeezed or the slice too thick.

**Grill hot and fast, in batches.** Charcoal or a ripping cast-iron pan (a domed Korean bulgogi pan if you have one, 200 °C-plus at the surface — water should dance and vanish). Spread a single loose layer — piled meat steams in its own juice, and this dish's whole identity is browning plus juice, not steam. The shavings cook in 60–90 seconds a side. **Flip when the edges weep and color**, not on a clock: beads of pink juice at the rim and the first mahogany edge mean the grill boss turns the batch, then pulls it 20 seconds later when the raw red is just gone. Rest each batch on a warm plate; the moat juice goes to a small pot or the pan's rim to simmer with the mushrooms and carrot. Checkpoint — the eating test: a shaving straight off the grill should be caramel-sweet at the edge, juicy and soft in the middle, with no chewy gray band. Into a lettuce ssam with ssamjang (#SA01) it should taste like the genre's ceiling — but note honestly that the ssam is borrowed ceremony here; this dish's native table is rice, juice over rice, kimchi beside.

**Serve the rice-thief properly.** The accumulated moat juice, simmered 2 minutes with any vegetables and poured over rice, is half the point of the lane. Don't discard it into the grill. Checkpoint — the bowl: rice, a ladle of juice, meat over, sesame and scallion. The juice should be sweet-savory and just glossy, not syrup; if it ran syrup, your pan was too cool and the batch steamed.

title: Classic Samgyeopsal with Sesame-Salt Seasoning
times: Prep: 15 minutes · Cook: 25 minutes at the table · Total: About 40 minutes at the table · Serves 4

schema.name: Classic Samgyeopsal with Sesame-Salt Seasoning
recipeIngredient: 1.2 kg fresh pork belly, skin off, cut into slabs 1.5 cm thick and 5 cm wide (order "samgyeopsal cut" at a Korean market; the even ribbon shape is part of the dish)
1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds (about 8 g), lightly crushed
Gireumjang (#SA02): 3 tbsp toasted sesame oil (45 ml), 1 tsp coarse salt (about 5 g), a grind of pepper — the classic samgyeopsal dip
Ssamjang (#SA01): about 120 g from its record
1 head lettuce and 20 perilla leaves, washed and bone-dry
8 cloves garlic (about 32 g), sliced thick coins
1 bundle scallions or 100 g onion, thick-cut rings (the traditional grate-mates, grilled beside the pork in its fat)
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), kimchi (#B01), and a bottle of soju's worth of ceremony

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Lay the slabs flat, one layer, at the pan's center. They will not brown in the first minutes — they will render. Turn them every 2 minutes as the fat liquefies and the pan develops a shallow gloss of it. Salt faces lightly on the second turn; sesame seeds and pepper on the third. Checkpoint: the sound changes from a hiss to a steady sputter and the edges go translucent-gold: rendering is doing the cooking. If the pan smokes hard, lower the flame — burnt pork fat is bitter and it flavors the whole batch.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Grill the grate-mates in the fat. Push the scallion or onion rings into the pooling fat at the pan's edge and let them soften and brown. Garlic coins 30 seconds a side in the same fat until blond at the edges — the sweetest version of raw garlic, and half the table will eat these like chips. Checkpoint: the vegetables should be fat-glossed and softened, not crisped; they are condiments in progress, pulled to a side plate as each batch finishes.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: The scissors are the clock. At 12–15 minutes the slabs are deeply golden. Cut each slab crosswise with kitchen scissors directly on the pan into bite pieces (2–3 cm), toss the pieces once in the hot fat for a final 60–90 seconds to crisp the cut faces, and pull to the platter. The cut-and-toss is not a shortcut — the fresh faces take the crisping that makes classic samgyeopsal. Checkpoint: a test piece straight from the pan, dunked in gireumjang: shatter-crisp edge, yielding fat layer, tender meat layer, then the dip's sesame-salt. The three-layer bite is the doneness signal — if the fat layer is still bouncy and translucent, the slab needed more rendering; there is no such thing as "too long" here short of burning.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 4
recipeInstructions.text: The ssam sequence, the whole point. Leaf in the palm, a thin swipe of ssamjang (#SA01), a piece of hot pork, a grilled garlic coin, a chili slice or a strand of grilled scallion, fold, one bite. Between ssam: rice, kimchi, the gireumjang for the plain pieces. The table's rhythm belongs to the pan — as one batch leaves, the next slabs go on, and the tongs rotate. Checkpoint: the assembly test: the fold closes without tearing and delivers everything in one bite. A ssam that needs two bites was overloaded, and the guilty party does the next batch's tongs duty.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: restaurant — the pork commons. Samgyeopsal is the people's steak: thick slabs of pork belly, unmarinated, seasoned with nothing at the start but salt and sesame, grilled in the middle of the table until the fat renders and the edges crisp, then folded into lettuce with ssamjang, raw garlic, and green chili. The dish as a national institution is young — dedicated shops cluster in the late 1970s, and portable butane burners in the 1980s took the grill into every walk-up apartment — but the logic is old: a shared pan in the middle of the table, cooked by whoever's turn it is, so labor and talk share the fire. This record is the classic salt-and-sesame build. The gochujang-dressed cousin (#M11) is one lane over. Who cooks what: the tongs rotate around the table by convention, one flip per person. The grill boss of the evening only manages the fire itself.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Nothing marinates. That is the recipe's first instruction. The pork belly's job is to taste like pork and fire; every other flavor arrives at the ssam stage. Salt lightly just before the meat hits the grate, not before — salted-ahead belly weeps, and weeping meat steams.
  • Set the full table before the fire starts. Once the pork is grilling, nobody leaves their seat: both dips made, garlic and chili sliced, lettuce spun bone-dry, rice hot. The dips sit on the table's turntable with the meat platter.
  • Fire for steady medium, not searing. A tabletop gas burner on medium under a ridged pan or dome (a pan surface in the 180 °C range — water skitters, oil shimmer-strips), or charcoal at a gentle hand-count of 5 seconds. Pork belly renders its own fat for the cooking; the fire's only job is patience. Have a folded paper towel and tongs ready to manage flare-ups.

blocks.name: doneness
blocks.html:
Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The slabs: 1.5 cm, unmarinated, salted only at the second turn.
  • The render: translucent-gold edges, steady sputter, no hard smoke.
  • The scissors: cut at deep golden, tossed 60–90 seconds for crisp faces.
  • The bite: three layers — crisp, yielding fat, tender meat — in one closed ssam.

blocks.name: finish-plate
blocks.html:
Finish & Plate

The pan itself is the platter, refilled slab by slab at the table's center on its trivet. Both dip bowls flanking, the ssam leaves in a basket, grilled garlic and scallions on the side plate, rice and kimchi in reach. The bones-free ledger here is a plate of empties: how many ssam, how many bites — the count is the conversation.

blocks.html:
Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Samgyeopsal is a buy-and-grill record; the belly keeps 2 days refrigerated. Leftover cooked pieces keep 3 days and are the canonical kimchi fried rice meat — dice, fry hard in a spoon of their own reserved fat, kimchi and day-old rice in, sesame over.

title: Classic Ssamjang
metadata: Korean · Easy · Makes about 250 g (a table's bowl)
times: Prep: 10 minutes · Cook: 0 minutes (raw blend) or 5 (cooked build) · Total: 10 minutes · Makes about 250 g (a table's bowl)

schema.name: Classic Ssamjang
recipeIngredient: 1 tbsp honey or corn syrup (about 20 g)
1 tsp sesame seeds (about 4 g), lightly crushed
3 cloves garlic (about 12 g), grated or minced to a near-paste
1/2 Asian pear or apple (about 75 g), grated — the traditional sweetener and the bowl's secret freshness
A splash of mirin or water (about 15 ml), to loosen

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Blend the base: doenjang, gochujang, honey, sesame oil, worked to one uniform rust color. Checkpoint: no light-brown streaks; one paste.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: The pear in with its juice, the splash of mirin, then garlic, scallions, sesame. Fold to a spreadable paste — looser than jam, thicker than a dressing; it must cling to a lettuce leaf without pooling. Checkpoint: the raw-build taste test on the leaf: salty-fermented depth, pear's lift, garlic's bite, the scallion still crisp. This is the bowl.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: The cooked build (optional, for a mellower bowl): the blended paste simmered in a lightly oiled pan 3–4 minutes with a splash of water — the garlic rounds, the gochujang's raw edge cooks off, and the sauce keeps a day longer. The raw bowl is brighter; the cooked bowl is deeper; both are classic, and the choice is the table's. Checkpoint: the cooked build darkens a shade and smells toasted rather than sharp — pull it before the sugars catch (medium-low, stirring, no crisping).

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the table's oldest assembly. Ssamjang — literally "wrap sauce" — is the bowl that makes a grill table a ssam table: doenjang and gochujang in one paste, sweetened, studded with aromatics, sitting between the meat and the lettuce with an authority no bottled sauce matches. It is less a recipe than a ratio with every household's thumbprint on it; this record is the classic center from which the variations swing. Every meat record on this site points here, and the bowl takes ten minutes.

Work the doenjang and gochujang together first with the honey and sesame oil until the two pastes are one color (a minute of real stirring; lumps of pure doenjang in the bowl are the amateur tell), then the pear and its juice, then garlic, scallion, and seeds last so they stay bright.
  • Taste on a lettuce leaf, not a spoon: the leaf's water and bitterness are part of the sauce's final context. On the leaf it should read deep-savory first, sweet second, a slow warm hum behind.

Checkpoint — the raw-build taste test on the leaf: salty-fermented depth, pear's lift, garlic's bite, the scallion still crisp. This is the bowl.

**The cooked build (optional, for a mellower bowl):** the blended paste simmered in a lightly oiled pan 3–4 minutes with a splash of water — the garlic rounds, the gochujang's raw edge cooks off, and the sauce keeps a day longer. The raw bowl is brighter; the cooked bowl is deeper; both are classic, and the choice is the table's. Checkpoint — the cooked build darkens a shade and smells toasted rather than sharp — pull it before the sugars catch (medium-low, stirring, no crisping).

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: contemporary. Lamb is the newest voice at this grill — absent from the old lists, fully at home in the modern pantry — and it asks for the two pastes at once: doenjang for the savory floor, gochujang for the red heat, honey to hold them together against lamb's big flavor. This is a butterflied shoulder steak record: marinated long, grilled hot in thick slices, served ssam-style with the sharp fresh salads that lamb and the Korean table both love. No lineage claimed — this one is written for the cook who wants the Korean grill's flavors on the meat their butcher is proudest of this week.

blocks.html:

title: Contemporary Sesame Broccoli and Bell Pepper Salad
times: Prep: 12 minutes · Cook: 3 minutes · Total: About 20 minutes · Serves 4 as banchan

schema.name: Contemporary Sesame Broccoli and Bell Pepper Salad
recipeIngredient: 400 g broccoli, cut into flat-topped florets (the flat cut sears/blanches evenly)
1 red or yellow bell pepper (about 150 g), cut into batons
A pinch of gochugaru (about 1 g), optional

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The blanched, dried broccoli and the raw pepper in the serving bowl, the dressing poured over — sesame oil, soy, honey, garlic — and tossed with spoons for thirty seconds. Checkpoint: every floret glossed, the sesame seeds caught in the florets' crowns (the flat-top cut's doing), the pepper's raw crunch intact beside the broccoli's blanched-firm.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Scallion and gochugaru over, one more turn, and the bowl either serves now or lides and chills. Checkpoint: the eating test: sesame-forward, the broccoli's green sweetness, the pepper's bright crunch — a bowl that tastes like the modern Korean lunch café's cold-case, which is precisely its lineage and its honest seat at this grill table.

title: Doenjang-Butter Grilled Scallops
times: Prep: 10 minutes · Cook: 8 minutes · Total: About 20 minutes · Serves 3–4 (makes 12)

schema.name: Doenjang-Butter Grilled Scallops
schema.description: **Stream: contemporary — the fusion seat, labeled honestly.
recipeIngredient: 12 large sea scallops (about 500 g), dry-packed (no phosphate solution — see Note), patted bone-dry
Flaky salt (about 2 g), sliced scallion (about 10 g), toasted sesame seeds (about 4 g)
Thinly sliced cucumber or perilla, rice for the table

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Sear dry scallops, undisturbed, 90 seconds — no baste yet, because butter burns where the paste would scorch. The sear happens in plain fat and the flavor comes after. Checkpoint: lift one: a deep golden-brown crust on the bottom face. No crust, back down — and if the pan was smoking hard, it ran a notch hot for butter's tolerance.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Flip, and baste the seared faces now — brush or spoon the doenjang-butter over each scallop, 60–90 seconds more, off the fire while the centers still carry the faintest translucence at the very core (carryover finishes them on the platter). Checkpoint: the basted tops should sit glossy and foamy-gold. A test scallop cut in half: opaque to within a few millimeters of the center, buttery, just springy. Fully opaque-through at the pan means slightly over — edible, but the next batch pulls 15 seconds sooner.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Flaky salt, scallion, sesame; serve immediately, off the shared platter, one or two per diner with rice beside. Checkpoint: eating test: crust, then the sweet scallop burst, then doenjang's savory depth arriving on the butter — the three arriving in that order is the build working. Salty-only means the baste ran heavy on paste; a teaspoon, not a tablespoon, is the ratio.

Thinly sliced cucumber or perilla, rice for the table

blocks.html: Stream: contemporary — the fusion seat, labeled honestly. Doenjang and butter is the modern Korean bistro's signature move, and scallops are its best argument: the paste's fermented depth against sweet shellfish richness, with butter carrying both. Nothing about this record claims a lineage — it is exactly what its label says, a contemporary build using the pantry's oldest paste — and it is on the site because it is delicious and because it teaches the doenjang-and-fat principle better than any stew does.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Buy dry-packed scallops and dry them further. Wet scallops (soaked in phosphate solution) never sear — they leach white liquid into the pan and steam in it. Dry-packed, patted down, and left air-drying on paper towel for 10 minutes while the grill heats: that is the sear's whole foundation.
  • Whisk the baste warm: butter melted, doenjang worked in until smooth (a small bowl and a fork, one minute), honey, garlic, sesame oil. It should taste intensely savory-salty-buttery — it is a glaze in search of sweetness, which is what the scallop supplies.
  • Fire at medium-high with a flat cast-iron surface or grate bars wiped with oil — scallops need full contact, not grates with gaps.

title: Doenjang-Garlic Moksal Gui
times: Prep: 15 minutes, plus 2–4 hours marinating · Cook: 12 minutes at the table · Total: About 30 minutes at the table (marinate ahead) · Serves 4

schema.name: Doenjang-Garlic Moksal Gui
schema.description: **Stream: restaurant.** Moksal — pork collar, the shoulder's marble — is the connoisseur's cut of the tabletop: tender-firm with a fine fat weave that stands up to the grill better than loin ever will.
recipeIngredient: 900 g pork collar (moksal) or shoulder, sliced 7 mm thick
1 tbsp mirin or honey (15 ml / about 20 g)
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), lettuce ssam, ssamjang (#SA01), kimchi (#B01), musaengchae spicy radish (#B08) — the cold, crisp counter this rich cut wants

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Charcoal or cast-iron at medium-high. The slices go on in a single layer; with almost no sugar in the marinade, the grill boss is building crust, not managing lacquer. First side undisturbed 2–3 minutes. Checkpoint: the smell is roasted soybean and garlic over browning pork — deeper and darker than any other record at this grill. The underside should be crusty brown and release cleanly.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Flip once, 2 minutes more, pull when the meat's juices bead at the surface and the slice is just firm to a fingertip press. Rest the batch 1 minute; moksal carries a little and finishes gently. Checkpoint: test piece: crusty edge, juicy interior with a firm-but-tender chew that loin never gives, and the doenjang's savory depth arriving right behind the pork. No sweetness ahead of the meat — if there is, the honey ran heavy.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: restaurant. Moksal — pork collar, the shoulder's marble — is the connoisseur's cut of the tabletop: tender-firm with a fine fat weave that stands up to the grill better than loin ever will. Its natural partner is doenjang, the fermented soybean paste most Western kitchens only meet in jjigae. As a marinade base, doenjang gives pork what gochujang cannot: deep savory funk with almost no sugar, nothing to burn, and a crust that browns like a steak's instead of lacquering. This is the quiet record of the pork list — the one the regulars order.

title: Doenjang-Glazed Grilled Black Cod
times: Prep: 20 minutes, plus 24–48 hours curing · Cook: 12 minutes · Total: About 25 minutes on the day (cure ahead) · Serves 4

schema.name: Doenjang-Glazed Grilled Black Cod
schema.description: **Stream: contemporary — the Korean answer to the miso cod.
recipeIngredient: 4 black cod (sablefish) fillets (about 700 g), skin on or off (see Method), pin bones pulled
2 tbsp honey (about 40 g), 1 tbsp mirin (15 ml), 1 tsp soy sauce (5 ml)
1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds (about 8 g), thin-sliced scallion (about 10 g)
Steamed rice (about 500 g cooked), pickled perilla (#B24) or quick-pickled cucumber, and a plain lettuce salad — the rich lacquer wants sharp, simple things

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Slow face first: skin-on goes skin-down, skin-off goes presentation-face-down, on the moderate zone. Six to eight minutes — the surface caramelizes slowly from paste-pale to tea-brown, and the fillet's underside sets. Checkpoint: the surface color reads deep tea with darker edges; the flesh at the sides has turned opaque a third of the way up. No black — black means the zone is running hot; offset further from the coals.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Flip with a full spatula's support — black cod is soft as custard when raw and nearly as soft when cooked. Brush the caramelized first face with the finishing glaze, two minutes on the second side, glaze the second face, and pull at the flake stage: the flesh at the thickest point parts along the grain with a fork's weight and no force, still translucent-glossy at the very center (black cod's fat keeps it silky well past where other fish dry — around 55 °C internal at the center if you measure). Checkpoint: the test flake: sweet-savory lacquer outside, butter-fat silk inside, the doenjang's depth all the way through rather than sitting on the surface — that all-the-way-through is the 48-hour cure's signature, and no glaze trick can fake it.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Sesame and scallion over, and serve in wide spoons or on rice — the fillet barely holds a shape. The sharp pickle beside every plate; the lacquer's sweetness and the pickle's acid are the plate's argument. Checkpoint: eating test: the first bite should be lacquer, silk, then the pickle's cut — the three-beat finish. If the pickle is an afterthought on the plate it will be an afterthought on the palate; this fish makes its own case for why Korean tables always set a sharp thing beside the rich one.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: contemporary — the Korean answer to the miso cod. The famous miso-marinated black cod and this record share a fish and a technique family: a fermented bean paste cure, a long rest, and a slow sweet glaze under heat. The Korean version runs doenjang where the Japanese-American restaurant version runs miso — deeper, funkier, a shade less sweet — and the result is the same miracle from the other direction: buttery fish under a caramelized lacquer. Labeled honestly: this is a contemporary build, the pantry's oldest paste on a premium fish, and it is the site's special-occasion seafood record.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• The cure, 24–48 hours ahead, is the recipe. Whisk the cure's ingredients smooth and paint the fillets thickly on all faces; stack them in a dish, cover, refrigerate, turning once at the halfway mark. The paste's salt and enzymes work slowly into the flesh — at 24 hours the fish is seasoned; at 48 it is transformed, firm-silky and deeply savory. This is the one record on the site where "marinate longer" is always the right answer, and it is why the day-of work is fifteen minutes.
  • Decide the skin question before cooking: skin-on gives the crisp base and the fat's protection but shields the cure's contact; skin-off (this record's default for the full lacquer experience) wants a gentle touch and a moderate oven-or-grill path. Choose lacquer over crisp, or crisp over lacquer — both are correct, name the choice at the table.
  • Rinse or not: scrape the excess cure off the surface (leave the thin film that clings), but do not rinse the fillet — the rinse takes the cure's first two millimeters with it.
  • Fire for moderate and indirect-leaning: charcoal at medium with the fish offset, or a 200 °C oven finished under a hot broiler. The sugars caramelize over ten minutes; direct high heat takes them past caramel in two.

blocks.html:
Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The cure: 24–48 hours, turned once, excess scraped not rinsed.
  • The fire: moderate and offset; tea-brown caramel, never black.
  • The pull: parts at a fork's weight, translucent-glossy center — custard-soft, fully safe at the flake stage.
  • The plate: sharp pickle beside every serving; the richness is the foil, not the point.

Finish & Plate

One fillet per person on warm rice or a wide spoon, sesame and scallion over the lacquered face, the pickle plate passing. This is the seafood record that behaves like a main course — set it at the table's center and let the lacquer make the argument.

title: Doraji Muchim Spicy Bellflower Root
times: Prep: 25 minutes (plus 30 minutes salting) · Cook: 5 minutes · Total: About 1 hour, mostly waiting · Serves 4 as banchan

schema.name: Doraji Muchim Spicy Bellflower Root
recipeIngredient: 300 g fresh doraji (bellflower root), or 150 g dried, soaked 3 hours
1 tbsp coarse salt (about 15 g), for the 30-minute cure
1 tsp fish sauce or soy sauce (about 5 ml)
A few drops of rice vinegar (about 2 ml), optional

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Blanch the cured, squeezed ribbons 3–4 minutes in unsalted boiling water — they should turn from opaque white to translucent-edged, still crunchy. Checkpoint: a test ribbon bends into a U without breaking and keeps an audible crunch at the tooth. Overcooked doraji loses the crunch that is its whole identity; pull it while it still seems slightly too firm.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Cold rinse, drain, squeeze once more (gently this time — it has given enough), and cut into shorter lengths if it came in ribbons longer than 8 cm. Checkpoint: the ribbons are dry to the touch and springy.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: The seasoning bowl: gochugaru, fish sauce, garlic, sugar, sesame oil worked to a paste; the warm-not-hot ribbons tossed through with the full-minute hand massage the namul family demands (#B16's law), scallions and sesame last. Checkpoint: the eating test: crunch first, the mild-bitter vegetal note under it, the dressing's savory-heat arriving second, and the slight bitterness lingering as the finish — that finish is doraji's signature, the reason it has kept its seat at the table beside sweeter vegetables that try harder to please.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the medicinally minded banchan. Doraji — bellflower root, the white twisted ribbons of the doraji plant — is the banchan that tastes like the mountain apothecary: faintly bitter, deeply vegetal, crunchier than any root has a right to be after cooking. Dressed with gochugaru, garlic, and sesame, it becomes the traditional partner for oily fish (#SF07's table) and the bowl Korean grandmothers cite for throat health while everyone eats seconds. The technique is salt-cure and squeeze — the bitter compound leaves with the water.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Split and salt the fresh roots. Fresh doraji needs a violent rub with coarse salt (the classic treatment: salt between the palms, scrubbing the ribbons hard for two full minutes — the traditional method bruises the fibers and drives the bitter out), then a 30-minute rest, then a rinse and a hard squeeze by the fistful. The water that leaves carries most of the bitterness; the squeeze is the recipe.
  • Dried doraji skips the rub (it was treated in processing) but needs its long soak and a shorter squeeze.

Overcooked doraji loses the crunch that is its whole identity; pull it while it still seems slightly too firm.

Cold rinse, drain, squeeze once more (gently this time — it has given enough), and cut into shorter lengths if it came in ribbons longer than 8 cm. Checkpoint — the ribbons are dry to the touch and springy.

The seasoning bowl: gochugaru, fish sauce, garlic, sugar, sesame oil worked to a paste; the warm-not-hot ribbons tossed through with the full-minute hand massage the namul family demands (#B16's law), scallions and sesame last. Checkpoint — the eating test: crunch first, the mild-bitter vegetal note under it, the dressing's savory-heat arriving second, and the slight bitterness lingering as the finish — that finish is doraji's signature, the reason it has kept its seat at the table beside sweeter vegetables that try harder to please.

title: Dubu Jorim Braised Tofu
times: Prep: 10 minutes · Cook: 15 minutes · Total: About 25 minutes · Serves 4 as banchan

schema.name: Dubu Jorim Braised Tofu
schema.description: **Stream: heritage — the pan that makes tofu a banchan.
recipeIngredient: 400 g firm tofu, cut into 1 cm slabs, patted dry, salted lightly (about 2 g) and rested 10 minutes
1 tsp toasted sesame oil (5 ml), off heat
1 tsp toasted sesame seeds (about 4 g); a pinch of gochugaru (about 1 g), optional
1/2 Korean radish, sliced into thin half-moons (about 100 g), the traditional bed — optional but excellent

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The sear: oil at medium-high, slabs in without touching, 3–4 minutes to deep gold (they release when ready — nudged early, they tear), flip once, 2–3 minutes more, out to a plate. Checkpoint: both faces evenly golden-brown with a firming surface — the crust is the sponge that will drink the braise; a pale slab stays bland no matter how good the sauce.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Pour off the oil, braise liquids into the pan (water, soy, honey, garlic), radish bed if using, seared slabs back over. Simmer 4–5 minutes at medium-low, spooning the liquid over the slabs twice. Checkpoint: the liquid has reduced to a glossy shallow pool and the slabs' faces have gone from dry-gold to lacquered amber; the tofu, pressed thin before, has visibly drunk.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Sesame oil off the heat, sesame and scallion over. Checkpoint: the eating test: a slab on rice — savory-sweet glaze, the crust's chew, the soft interior, and the radish (if used) sweet enough to surprise. It should taste like the banchan board's quiet centerpiece, which at a table full of grilled meat is exactly what it is.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the pan that makes tofu a banchan. Dubu jorim takes the blandest protein on earth and makes it the bowl that disappears first from the vegetarian corner of the table: firm tofu, pan-seared into golden plates, then braised briefly in soy-garlic-sesame until every plate wears the glaze. The technique is the two-stage logic the potato record (#B09) runs in reverse — sear first for structure, braise second for flavor — and it converts tofu skeptics more reliably than any deep fry.

title: Eomuk Bokkeum Stir-Fried Fish Cake
times: Prep: 10 minutes · Cook: 8 minutes · Total: About 18 minutes · Serves 4 as banchan

schema.name: Eomuk Bokkeum Stir-Fried Fish Cake
schema.description: **Stream: restaurant — the market stall's home life.
recipeIngredient: 300 g Korean fish cake (eomuk), any mix of sheets and tubes, sliced into bite pieces
1 tbsp corn syrup or honey (about 20 g)
1 tsp toasted sesame oil (5 ml), 1 tsp sesame seeds (about 4 g), 2 scallions (about 30 g) cut into batons, a pinch of ground pepper

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Oil and garlic at medium-high until the garlic barely blonds, onion and carrot in, 90 seconds of high-heat softening — the vegetables should stay crisp-shouldered, not slack. Checkpoint: the pan smells of toasted garlic and sweet onion; the edges of the onion go translucent while its core stays white.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Fish cake in, stirred 2 minutes — it will soften a touch, flex, and its cut edges will sear lightly where they touch the pan. Checkpoint: the fish cake's surface changes from glossy-oily to matte and it bends without breaking — it is ready to take the sauce.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Soy, corn syrup, gochugaru, and the splash of water in, tossed every 30 seconds for 2–3 minutes as the liquid reduces and glosses everything. Checkpoint: the pan is nearly dry with a glossy film on every piece, the fish cake's edges caramelized in spots, the gochugaru's color even across the bowl. Off the heat: sesame oil, scallions, sesame. The eating test — a piece straight from the pan — should be sweet-savory with the fish cake's distinctive bounce and the scallion still raw-bright.

groups.title: The stir-fry

1 tsp toasted sesame oil (5 ml), 1 tsp sesame seeds (about 4 g), 2 scallions (about 30 g) cut into batons, a pinch of ground pepper

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: restaurant — the market stall's home life. Eomuk — Korean fish cake, the pressed sheets and tubes sold at every market's fish-cake stall — is famous for its soup, but the stir-fried banchan is the home table's quieter use: sheets sliced and tossed in a hot pan with soy, sugar, garlic, and gochugaru until the edges catch and glaze. It is five ingredients, eight minutes, and the bowl that tastes like a Korean market's afternoon.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Rinse the fish cake once under running water — a quick pass, ten seconds. It lifts the surface oil from the packaging (fish cake is pre-fried) and lets the seasonings reach the fish cake instead of sliding on its film. Pat roughly dry.
  • Slice everything first; the stir-fry itself is eight minutes start to finish with no pauses.

title: Galchi Gui Grilled Hairtail
times: Prep: 15 minutes, plus 30 minutes salting · Cook: 10 minutes · Total: About 55 minutes · Serves 3–4

schema.name: Galchi Gui Grilled Hairtail
recipeIngredient: 700 g hairtail (about 2 fish), cut into 10 cm fingers, or whole if your grill is long enough
Neutral oil for the grate (about 10 ml)
1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds (about 8 g), sliced scallion (about 10 g), lemon wedge or splash of vinegar (about 10 ml)
Steamed rice (about 500 g cooked), kimchi (#B01), and a light soy-vinegar dip (#SA05)

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Fingers skin-down on the oiled moderate grate, 3–4 minutes undisturbed. The skin will tighten, silver going pewter, then blister gold at the edges. Checkpoint: the skin lifts clean where it crisped and stays put where it has not — work from the done end with the spatula, not all at once. The flesh at the cut ends turns opaque upward from the skin.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: One gentle flip, 2–3 minutes more, off the fire when the flesh at the thickest finger's center is opaque and flakes at a fork's nudge. Checkpoint: a test finger pulled apart: opaque through, sweet and firm-juicy, the spine releasing from the meat with no resistance. Hairtail's flesh is dense but delicate — it will not forgive much past this point, but it does not need to; the clock is short.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Platter, sesame and scallion over, lemon beside, and the eating is handwork: lift the spine free of each finger, the meat in one or two pieces. Checkpoint: eating test: crisp skin and sweet white meat in the same bite, the soy-vinegar dip for the pieces that want brightening. If the skin is leathery instead of crisp, the finger went on wet — the drying law is the record.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: restaurant — the Jeju island classic. Hairtail — galchi, the silver ribbon fish — is the fish Jeju islanders grill more than any other: a meter of solid meat and no bones but the spine, salted and grilled until the silver skin blisters gold. It is the mackerel record's (#SF07) leaner sibling: where mackerel runs fat and needs the fermented cut beside it, hairtail runs clean and sweet, and its record runs the same cure-and-grill law at a shorter clock. The skin, gone crisp, is the delicacy — protect it with the grate discipline you learned on the mackerel.

title: Gamja Jorim Soy-Braised Potatoes
times: Prep: 10 minutes · Cook: 20 minutes · Total: About 30 minutes · Serves 4–6 as banchan

schema.name: Gamja Jorim Soy-Braised Potatoes
recipeIngredient: 700 g small yellow or red potatoes, cut into 3 cm chunks (skin on — the skin holds the chunk together through the braise)
1.5 tbsp corn syrup or honey (about 30 g)
1 tsp toasted sesame oil (5 ml), off heat
1 tsp toasted sesame seeds (about 4 g); 1 scallion (about 15 g), sliced; a pinch of gochugaru or sliced chili (about 1 g), optional

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Oil and garlic in a wide pan over medium until the garlic just turns blond (30 seconds — blond, not brown; browned garlic runs bitter through a sweet braise), potatoes in, stirred to coat, 2 minutes of sizzling together. Checkpoint: the potato edges turn translucent-gold and the pan smells of toasted garlic — the braise's flavor floor just got laid.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Water, soy, corn syrup, and sugar in; stir, lid on, medium-low. Ten minutes at a gentle bubble, stirring once at the halfway mark. Checkpoint: a paring knife into the largest chunk slides in with no resistance — the potato is cooked, and everything from here is reduction, not cooking. If the knife catches, three more minutes, lid on.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Lid off, and the reduction — the technique. High-medium now, stirring and turning every 60–90 seconds as the liquid boils down. The braise goes from soupy to syrupy to glaze: the pan's liquids thicken, the sugars caramelize on the turned potato faces, and the potatoes bounce in a slow thick sizzle instead of a boil. Five to six minutes, off the heat the moment the glaze coats and the pan is nearly dry. Checkpoint: a test chunk: glazed dark at two or three faces, glossy, and it holds its shape but yields to the tooth — the braise has painted it, not dissolved it. Burnt-sugar smell is the one-second warning: off the heat now, not next stir. Sesame oil, seeds, scallion over, off the heat.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the caramelized braise. Gamja jorim is the banchan that converts potato people on first bite: small chunks braised in soy, sugar, and garlic until the edges caramelize and glaze and the interiors drink the braise. It sits beside the grill's meats doing carbohydrate duty with a fork-sweetness that rice never attempts — the children's champion and the adults' quiet favorite of the banchan board. The whole technique is a reduced braise with corn syrup's gloss, finished fast.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 1. Oil and garlic in a wide pan over medium until the garlic just turns blond (30 seconds — blond, not brown; browned garlic runs bitter through a sweet braise), potatoes in, stirred to coat, 2 minutes of sizzling together. Checkpoint — the potato edges turn translucent-gold and the pan smells of toasted garlic — the braise's flavor floor just got laid.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 2. Water, soy, corn syrup, and sugar in; stir, lid on, medium-low. Ten minutes at a gentle bubble, stirring once at the halfway mark. Checkpoint — a paring knife into the largest chunk slides in with no resistance — the potato is cooked, and everything from here is reduction, not cooking. If the knife catches, three more minutes, lid on.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 3. Lid off, and the reduction — the technique. High-medium now, stirring and turning every 60–90 seconds as the liquid boils down. The braise goes from soupy to syrupy to glaze: the pan's liquids thicken, the sugars caramelize on the turned potato faces, and the potatoes bounce in a slow thick sizzle instead of a boil. Five to six minutes, off the heat the moment the glaze coats and the pan is nearly dry. Checkpoint — a test chunk: glazed dark at two or three faces, glossy, and it holds its shape but yields to the tooth — the braise has painted it, not dissolved it. Burnt-sugar smell is the one-second warning: off the heat now, not next stir. Sesame oil, seeds, scallion over, off the heat. Chef’s Note — corn syrup versus honey is this record's honest fork: corn syrup (the Korean home default) gives the glassy, no-flavor glaze that lets soy and garlic lead; honey gives flavor and browns faster and runs a shade softer. Either works — the clock in step 3 shortens by a minute with honey. What does not work is sugar alone: it crystallizes grainy instead of glossing, and the glaze is half the dish.

title: Ganjang Pork Bulgogi
times: Prep: 15 minutes, plus 2–4 hours marinating · Cook: 10 minutes at the table · Total: About 25 minutes at the table (marinate ahead) · Serves 4

schema.name: Ganjang Pork Bulgogi
schema.description: **Stream: restaurant.** The soy fork of pork bulgogi: same thin slices, same fast tabletop grill, no gochujang in sight.
recipeIngredient: 900 g pork shoulder or collar, sliced 4 mm against the grain
2 tbsp honey or brown sugar (about 40 g)
1/2 Asian pear (about 150 g), grated, juice included here — this lane wants the juice
1/2 tsp black pepper (about 2 g); 1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds (about 8 g)
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), lettuce ssam, ssamjang (#SA01), kimchi (#B01), gyeran mari rolled omelet (#B11) for the kids' plate

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Medium-high fire, single loose layer, sixty to ninety seconds undisturbed. The wet marinade wants a hiss, not a roar — if it boils gray in its own liquid, the pan is crowded; lift half the batch off and do two rounds. Checkpoint: the slices take color at the edges while the marinade caramelizes on the pan behind them — the smell is sweet soy and pork fat, and the pan should be building a glossy brown film, not a watery boil.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Flip at the beading edge, 60–90 seconds more, pull while the centers still shine. Scrape the pan's caramelized juice into a small bowl as you go — over rice is where it lands. Checkpoint: test piece: sweet-savory edge, juicy interior, no heat anywhere — the register should be round and gentle, with the pear as a perfume rather than a flavor.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Platter, sesame over; the bowl route (rice, juice, slices) and the ssam route both open. Checkpoint: the rice bowl test: the juice should be glossy brown and spoonable, milder than the marinade tasted raw — if it is syrupy-sweet, pull the honey back a tablespoon next batch.

blocks.html: Stream: restaurant. The soy fork of pork bulgogi: same thin slices, same fast tabletop grill, no gochujang in sight. Ganjang bulgogi is the version for the table that wants the sweet-savory register without the heat — kids' approval guaranteed, adults' silence guaranteed, because it disappears first at every mixed grill. It is also the best introduction to the genre: everything you learn here (the thin slice, the single layer, the flip at the weep) transfers directly to the spicy cousin (#M13).

title: Garlic-Scallion Chicken Skewers
times: Prep: 25 minutes, plus 1–3 hours marinating · Cook: 10 minutes · Total: About 40 minutes (marinate ahead) · Serves 4 (makes 12 skewers)

schema.name: Garlic-Scallion Chicken Skewers
recipeIngredient: 800 g boneless, skinless chicken thighs, cut into 3 cm cubes
2 bundles scallions (about 120 g), whites and pale greens cut into 3 cm segments
6 cloves garlic (about 24 g), grated — the garlic leads here
2 tbsp of the reserved marinade + 1 tbsp melted butter or extra sesame oil (15 ml)
Steamed rice (about 500 g cooked), cho-gochujang (#SA03) on the side as the dip, kimchi (#B01)

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Medium-hot fire, skewers laid across with a finger's width between them. First side undisturbed 3 minutes — the cubes need to release, and the scallion wants one face charred softly. Checkpoint: turn a test skewer: the chicken's underside should be browned with grill lines and release cleanly; the scallion's face should be charred at the tips and glossy in the middle. If the scallion is incinerated, the fire is a notch hot for its tolerance — slide the scallion ends toward the fire's cooler edge on the next round.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Turn every 2 minutes through three more faces, brushing with the sauce on the second turn — 8–10 minutes total. The corners of the cubes will take little char-kisses; the centers stay juicy. Checkpoint: pull when a test cube's cut face is opaque to the center with clear juices — no pink, chicken's absolute rule — and the scallion has gone sweet-soft with char at the edges.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Off the skewer at the table or straight off the stick; sesame over; cho-gochujang (#SA03) as the dip. Checkpoint: eating test: chicken and scallion from the same bite, garlic-soy glaze behind them, then the dip's sweet-heat on the finish. The stick is the portion — two skewers and rice is the honest serving.

2 bundles scallions (about 120 g), whites and pale greens cut into 3 cm segments

items: 6 cloves garlic (about 24 g), grated — the garlic leads here

groups.title: The brush sauce

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: restaurant. Skewers are the grill's oldest form on the peninsula — the jeok that sat at the center of the ceremonial table — and this record is the tabletop's weeknight version of that idea: chicken thigh cubes and scallion segments on a stick, in a garlic-soy-sesame marinade light enough that the scallion survives the fire. The skewer is not decoration here; alternating meat and scallion means every bite carries the allium's sweetness against the chicken fat.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Thread tight but not compressed: chicken cube, scallion segment, chicken, scallion, chicken — five pieces to a skewer, the scallion segments nestled flat between the cubes so the fat shields them from direct flame. Compressed cubes cook unevenly; a finger's kiss of contact is enough.
  • Marinate 1–3 hours, skewered or loose. Chicken cubes take flavor fast; past three hours the soy's salt starts winning.
  • Reserve two tablespoons of marinade before the chicken goes in — the brush sauce is built from the clean portion, never the used bowl.

title: Garlic-Scallion Grilled Mussels
times: Prep: 10 minutes · Cook: 8 minutes · Total: About 20 minutes · Serves 4

schema.name: Garlic-Scallion Grilled Mussels
recipeIngredient: 1 kg fresh mussels, scrubbed, beards removed, closed (tap-test any gapers: a live one closes; an open non-closer is discarded)
4 cloves garlic (about 16 g), sliced thin, not grated — slices toast sweet
4 scallions (about 60 g), sliced, whites and greens separated
1 tbsp gochujang (about 20 g), optional but this record's signature
Crusty bread (about 300 g) or steamed rice (about 400 g cooked), lemon wedges, an empty bowl for shells at the table's center

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Mussels into the warm pan with the toasted base and a splash of mirin, lid on, high heat under now — they steam in their own liquor, 3–5 minutes, one hard shake at the halfway mark. Checkpoint: the shells spring open and the kitchen smells of garlic steam and ocean. Off the heat the moment the majority gape; a mussel that refused its colleagues gets one more minute in the residual steam and then, still shut, goes to the discard bowl — the unopened mussel is the one absolute no in shellfish.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Gochujang and sesame oil in, swirled through the liquor off the heat until the pot runs glossy orange-gold; scallion greens over. Checkpoint: the broth test with the eating spoon: briny, buttery, garlic-sweet, a warm gochujang hum behind — it should taste like the sea made a sauce. Flat? A squeeze of lemon and a pinch of salt; this pot is forgiving.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Pan to the table on its trivet, shells bowl beside, bread or rice armed. The eating: pull the mussels from the shells by hand or with an empty shell as tongs (the tradition's own tool), a mussel and a spoon of broth per bite, bread for the pot's floor. Checkpoint: the empty-pot test: no broth left, the bread has been torn to ragged edges, someone has asked what was in the sauce. That is the record finished properly.

Checkpoint — the shells spring open and the kitchen smells of garlic steam and ocean. Off the heat the moment the majority gape; a mussel that refused its colleagues gets one more minute in the residual steam and then, still shut, goes to the discard bowl — the unopened mussel is the one absolute no in shellfish.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 2. Gochujang and sesame oil in, swirled through the liquor off the heat until the pot runs glossy orange-gold; scallion greens over. Checkpoint — the broth test with the eating spoon: briny, buttery, garlic-sweet, a warm gochujang hum behind — it should taste like the sea made a sauce. Flat? A squeeze of lemon and a pinch of salt; this pot is forgiving.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 3. Pan to the table on its trivet, shells bowl beside, bread or rice armed. The eating: pull the mussels from the shells by hand or with an empty shell as tongs (the tradition's own tool), a mussel and a spoon of broth per bite, bread for the pot's floor. Checkpoint — the empty-pot test: no broth left, the bread has been torn to ragged edges, someone has asked what was in the sauce. That is the record finished properly. Chef’s Note — the empty-shell-as-tongs is worth teaching once at the table: a half shell held like a pincer picks meat from other shells better than any fork, and it is the oldest utensil logic at any fire. The gochujang thread is deliberately thin — a tablespoon against a kilo of mussels — because the liquor is the sauce's body and the paste is its undertow; doubling it makes a different, louder pot.

title: Garlic-Sesame Galbisal
times: Prep: 15 minutes, plus 2–4 hours marinating · Cook: 10 minutes · Total: About 25 minutes at the table (marinate ahead) · Serves 4

schema.name: Garlic-Sesame Galbisal
schema.description: **Stream: restaurant.** Galbisal is the boneless strip off the rib — all of the galbi flavor, none of the bone, and it grills faster than its flanken cousin (#M03).
recipeIngredient: 800 g boneless beef short rib (galbisal) or chuck flap, sliced 5 mm against the grain
1 tsp toasted sesame seeds, plus more to finish (about 8 g total)
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), lettuce ssam, ssamjang (#SA01), gireumjang (#SA02) as the purist dip, kimchi (#B01)

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Charcoal or cast-iron at medium-high. The slices go on in a single layer, and because there is almost no sugar, the grill boss's job is color, not lacquer-management: leave them until the edges weep and the underside is browned, about 2 minutes. Checkpoint: the smell should be sesame and garlic over browning beef — a quieter grill smell than the sweet marinades, and the honest one for this cut.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Flip once, 90 seconds more, pull when the raw red is just gone at the center of the slice. Rest the batch 1 minute on a warm plate — galbisal is thin enough that carryover is quick and real. Checkpoint: eating test straight off the grill: beef first, garlic second, sesame after. If you taste marinade before meat, the soy ran heavy — pull back a teaspoon next batch.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Scissors into bite pieces, warm platter, sesame over, ssam station open. The purist dip here is gireumjang (#SA02) — sesame oil, salt, pepper — because it seasons without competing; ssamjang (#SA01) for the bolder table. Checkpoint: the ssam test: leaf, gireumjang, galbisal, fold — and it should taste like the steakhouse version of Korean grill, clean enough that the beef's quality is the headline. Buy the good beef for this one; there is nowhere to hide.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: restaurant. Galbisal is the boneless strip off the rib — all of the galbi flavor, none of the bone, and it grills faster than its flanken cousin (#M03). The classic restaurant treatment keeps the marinade short and quiet: garlic, sesame oil, soy, a thread of sweetness, black pepper. The meat is the argument; the marinade is the microphone. This is the record for the table that wants galbi flavor on a weeknight clock, and for the grill boss who is tired of managing sugar on the fire — there is barely any here to burn.

title: Gim Muchim Seasoned Seaweed
times: Prep: 10 minutes · Cook: 3 minutes · Total: About 15 minutes · Serves 4–6 as banchan

schema.name: Gim Muchim Seasoned Seaweed
recipeIngredient: 8 sheets of dried roasted seaweed (gim, about 20 g), the plain unseasoned kind
1.5 tsp honey or corn syrup (about 10 g)
A pinch of gochugaru (about 1 g), optional

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The dressing whisked smooth — soy, water, honey, garlic — in the bowl that will hold the finished banchan. Checkpoint: the dressing tastes like a strong dip: salty, sweet, sharp — the seaweed's mineral dryness will demand exactly this strength.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: The ribbons in, tossed gently with your hands (tongs shred; hands coat) until every ribbon goes from dry-crisp to glossy-supple, then sesame oil and seeds worked through. Checkpoint: the transformation is the checkpoint: the ribbons soften and darken into glistening strands that hold together on a spoon, no crispness left. Work fast and stop at uniformly glossy — over-tossed seaweed breaks down to flakes.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Scallion and gochugaru over, and the bowl is served within the hour. Checkpoint: the eating test with rice: a soft, savory, mineral-deep tangle — the sea's version of the spinach bowl (#B06), and the same reset-the-palate job. If it tastes only of the dressing, the seaweed was weak or old (seaweed that has lost its sea-smell has lost its reason).

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the sea's quick bowl. Gim muchim takes the same roasted seaweed sheets that wrap gimbap and turns them into a banchan in fifteen minutes: the sheets toasted, scissored into ribbons, and tossed in the sesame-soy dressing until they turn glossy and supple — the ocean's mineral depth carried in a soft, slippery-firm tangle. It is the fastest bowl on this list and the one that most needs to be eaten the day it is made, which the tradition handles by never making much of it.

title: Gireumjang Sesame-Oil Salt Dip
metadata: Korean · Easy · Makes about 80 ml (a table's bowl)
times: Prep: 5 minutes · Cook: 0 minutes · Total: 5 minutes · Makes about 80 ml (a table's bowl)

schema.name: Gireumjang Sesame-Oil Salt Dip
schema.description: **Stream: heritage — the purist's bowl.** Gireumjang is three ingredients and a warning that it looks like nothing: toasted sesame oil, coarse salt, and black pepper.
recipeIngredient: 1 tsp coarse salt (about 5 g) — flaky or kosher, not fine table salt
1/2 tsp coarsely ground black pepper (about 2 g)
1 scallion (about 15 g), finely sliced, folded in
1 tsp sesame seeds (about 4 g), lightly crushed

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Oil in the bowl, salt and pepper over, a stir — the salt suspends, swirls, settles. That is the dish. Checkpoint: the visual: visible salt grains suspended in amber oil, pepper flecking it. Taste on a piece of the plainest grilled pork: a spark of salt, the oil's roast-nut roundness, pepper's warmth — and the meat louder for it, not quieter. That inversion is the bowl's whole argument.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Serve in a shallow bowl (deep oil is a dunk hazard — a shallow pool is a touch-dip) beside the unmarinated meats, and say nothing; the table finds it. Checkpoint: by the second round of samgyeopsal, the ssamjang bowl (#SA01) and this bowl are both half-empty and the table has chosen its camps — or splits by mood, which is the usual result and the reason both bowls are set.

1/2 tsp coarsely ground black pepper (about 2 g)

groups.title: The optional build-outs (tradition allows either, never both loudly)

1 tsp sesame seeds (about 4 g), lightly crushed

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the purist's bowl. Gireumjang is three ingredients and a warning that it looks like nothing: toasted sesame oil, coarse salt, and black pepper. It is the dip that the unmarinated records — the classic samgyeopsal (#M10), the galbisal (#M05), the neobiani (#M08) — actually want, because it seasons without competing: the meat tastes like meat, the oil carries the salt, the pepper warms the finish. The neobiani record calls it the period-honest companion for exactly this reason. Five minutes, and the table's quietest bowl is its most important.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• The only technique is the salt's grain. Coarse salt sits in the oil and clings to the dipped meat in discrete sparks of salinity; fine salt dissolves into an oily brine that reads as one flat saltiness and over-salts fast. The dip's whole personality is the coarse grain.
  • Use genuinely toasted sesame oil (the amber, fragrant one — the same bottle the marinades run on). Cold-pressed pale sesame oil is a different ingredient entirely.
