blocks.originalText: Step 1. Oil in the bowl, salt and pepper over, a stir — the salt suspends, swirls, settles. That is the dish. Checkpoint — the visual: visible salt grains suspended in amber oil, pepper flecking it. Taste on a piece of the plainest grilled pork: a spark of salt, the oil's roast-nut roundness, pepper's warmth — and the meat louder for it, not quieter. That inversion is the bowl's whole argument.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 2. Serve in a shallow bowl (deep oil is a dunk hazard — a shallow pool is a touch-dip) beside the unmarinated meats, and say nothing; the table finds it. Checkpoint — by the second round of samgyeopsal, the ssamjang bowl (#SA01) and this bowl are both half-empty and the table has chosen its camps — or splits by mood, which is the usual result and the reason both bowls are set. Chef’s Note — gireumjang is the anti-sauce, and understanding why it works explains the whole dip grammar on this site: a dip's job is either to add a new voice (ssamjang, cho-gochujang) or to amplify the meat's own (this bowl, and the scallion-soy #SA04 for the shavings). The records that refuse marinades — samgyeopsal, chadolbaegi, galbisal — refuse them because their fat is the seasoning, and gireumjang is the only dip that agrees with that sentence instead of arguing with it.

Taste on a piece of the plainest grilled pork: a spark of salt, the oil's roast-nut roundness, pepper's warmth — and the meat louder for it, not quieter. That inversion is the bowl's whole argument.

Serve in a shallow bowl (deep oil is a dunk hazard — a shallow pool is a touch-dip) beside the unmarinated meats, and say nothing; the table finds it. Checkpoint — by the second round of samgyeopsal, the ssamjang bowl (#SA01) and this bowl are both half-empty and the table has chosen its camps — or splits by mood, which is the usual result and the reason both bowls are set.

title: Gochujang-Glazed Grilled Salmon
times: Prep: 15 minutes, plus 30 minutes resting · Cook: 10 minutes · Total: About 55 minutes · Serves 4

schema.name: Gochujang-Glazed Grilled Salmon
schema.description: **Stream: contemporary — the fusion seat, labeled honestly.
recipeIngredient: 4 salmon fillets (about 700 g), skin on, pin bones pulled, room temperature
1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds (about 8 g), sliced scallion (about 10 g)
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), sesame-soy cucumber (#B10's lane — any quick cucumber banchan), perilla leaves

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Skin-down on the moderate zone, oiled grate, 5–6 minutes undisturbed — the skin crisps in its own rendered fat exactly the way the duck skin does in #M19, and the skin is the platform: pull the fillet early elsewhere but never on the skin. Checkpoint: the skin releases clean and crisp-gold at the edges; the flesh at the sides has turned opaque a third of the way up the fillet.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Flip once, 2 minutes on the flesh side, then the glaze: brush, 45 seconds, second thin brush-stroke, and pull at the table's preferred center — salmon's window is wide, from just-translucent at 50 °C to opaque-flaky at 58 °C, and this glaze suits the juicier end. Checkpoint: a test flake at the thick end: it parts along the grain with no force, still glossy inside, glaze set brick-tacky on the outside. If the glaze blackens, the hot zone ran past its sugar — the fish is fine underneath; notch the fire down for the second set.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Sesame and scallion over, platter with the cucumber banchan and perilla beside. Checkpoint: eating test: glaze edge, salmon's sweet fat, the cucumber's cold snap between bites — rich, spiced, reset. A piece of the crisp skin with the glaze is the record's best single bite, and the cook's by right.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: contemporary — the fusion seat, labeled honestly. Glazed salmon is not a traditional Korean grill record; it is the modern Korean pantry applied to the fish the modern table buys most, and it works because salmon's fat and gochujang's ferment want each other the way duck fat and the jang set want each other (#M19). The technique is the glaze law from the shrimp record (#SF01) adapted to a thick fillet: dry sear first, glaze in the final minutes, and the fat carries the paste.

title: Gochujang Grilled Shrimp
times: Prep: 15 minutes, plus 30 minutes marinating · Cook: 6 minutes · Total: About 25 minutes · Serves 3–4

schema.name: Gochujang Grilled Shrimp
schema.description: **Stream: contemporary — the yangnyeom lane on shellfish.
recipeIngredient: 700 g large shrimp (16–20 count), shell on, deveined, or shell-off if the table prefers peeling-free eating
1 tsp gochugaru (about 3 g), optional heat dial
1 tsp toasted sesame seeds (about 4 g), sliced scallion (about 10 g)
Steamed rice (about 400 g cooked), oi muchim (#B07), lettuce ssam

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Dry shrimp onto a hot grate or pan in a single layer, two minutes undisturbed. If shell-on, they will char lightly at the edges; that char is the flavor and the table peels it off later. Checkpoint: the shells blush pink-white and the undersides show grill marks through the shell; shell-off shrimp turn opaque at the bottom edge and roll loosely on the grate.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Flip once, one minute more — the shrimp are nearly done now. Brush the glaze on the up faces, wait 30 seconds, flip, brush the second faces, 30 seconds, off the fire. Checkpoint: the glaze sets glossy and brick-toned in that final minute. If it blackens, the fire was past the glaze's tolerance — the shrimp are still good; note the notch down for the next batch.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Sesame and scallion over, platter, straight to the table — shrimp wait for nobody. Checkpoint: eating test: sweet-heat glaze on the first chew, then the shrimp's own snap and sweetness — the glaze should coat, not bury. One test shrimp that tastes only of gochujang means the coating ran thick; a thin brush-stroke is the whole technique.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: contemporary — the yangnyeom lane on shellfish. Shrimp are the fastest protein at any grill, and the gochujang glaze is the loudest flavor on this site's seafood list; together they make the record that converts skeptics at a mixed grill. The law is one sentence: glaze at the end, never at the start. Shrimp cook in three minutes and the paste burns in two — the glaze goes on when the shrimp are already almost done.

title: Gochujang Samgyeopsal
times: Prep: 15 minutes, plus 30 minutes resting · Cook: 20 minutes at the table · Total: About 35 minutes at the table · Serves 4

schema.name: Gochujang Samgyeopsal
recipeIngredient: 1.2 kg pork belly, skin off, cut into slabs 1 cm thick (slightly thinner than the classic — the paste wants faster cooking)
1 tsp gochugaru (about 3 g), for the heat-forward table
Lettuce and perilla ssam, ssamjang (#SA01) thinned with a splash of water for dipping, kimchi (#B01), steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), garlic coins and green chili slices

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Slabs on the pan in a single layer, medium-low. The first minutes are quiet rendering again — the paste darkens one shade at the edges and the fat begins to gloss the pan. Turn every 90 seconds. Checkpoint: the paste should deepen toward brick and smell toasted-chile-sweet, not burnt. Any black edges on the first turn mean the flame is a notch high — lower it and the batch is fine.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: At 12–14 minutes, scissors into bite pieces directly on the pan, toss in the hot fat 60 seconds for the crisp lacquered faces, and pull to the platter. Checkpoint: test piece: crisp lacquered edge, the three-layer belly interior, then the paste's ferment-heat arriving after the fat. If the heat lands before the pork, the film was thick — thinner next batch.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Ssam sequence as the classic: leaf, thin ssamjang swipe, hot pork piece, garlic or chili, fold, one bite. Rice and kimchi between. Checkpoint: the ssam test should read as the classic's rich cousin — same crisp, same fat, a red edge on the flavor — not as a sweet-spicy pork candy. When in doubt, thin the paste further; the pork is the headline.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: restaurant, the dressed lane. Take the classic salt-and-sesame samgyeopsal (#M10), paint the belly with a gochujang paste before the fire, and the dish changes personality: the render still does the cooking, but now there is a lacquer on the crisp edge and a slow ferment-heat under the fat. The dressed belly is a fixture of every tabletop restaurant that discovered its regulars wanted the classic's texture with more on top. It asks one thing the classic does not — paste discipline. Too much and you are grilling sauce, not pork.

title: Godeungeo Gui Grilled Mackerel
times: Prep: 20 minutes, plus 30 minutes salting · Cook: 12 minutes · Total: About 1 hour 5 minutes · Serves 4

schema.name: Godeungeo Gui Grilled Mackerel
recipeIngredient: 2 whole mackerel (about 350 g each), gutted and cleaned, heads on or off (the Korean market's default is dressed; both are correct), or 4 thick cross-cut steaks (about 450 g)
2 tsp coarse salt (about 10 g) — more than seems right; see Method
Neutral oil for the grate (about 10 ml)
1 lemon or a splash of rice vinegar (about 15 ml), optional but traditional beside
1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds (about 8 g) and sliced scallion (about 10 g), for the platter
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), kimchi (#B01) — the fatty-fish law is a fermented cut beside it — mu sangchae (about 100 g), and a bowl of the soy-vinegar onion dip (#SA05)

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Oiled grate, skin down, over the moderate zone — and leave it alone. Whole fish need 5–6 minutes on the first side; steaks 3–4. The skin will stick and then release itself as it crisps — the earliest tongs attempt tears the skin off and the skin is half the dish. Checkpoint: the skin is done when it lifts cleanly and shows crisp gold-brown with darker grill stripes; at the thickest score, the flesh below is opaque halfway to the bone. Fat will drip and flare — move the fish to the cool zone for 20 seconds when it does, back to finish. This dance is the whole technique.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: The one flip, gently. Two spatulas or one wide fish spatula and a confident turn: flesh side (or second steak face) down for 4–5 minutes on the moderate zone. The second side takes less time than the first — the fish is half-cooked already. Checkpoint: the doneness read at the backbone, the record's core test: at the thickest score on the second side, the flesh at the bone has just turned opaque and pulls away from the bone with a fork's gentle sideways nudge. Opaque-at-the-bone is done; translucent-at-the-bone is 2 more minutes; falling-apart is past. Mackerel is fatty enough to stay moist a full minute past done — use that grace, do not fear it, but do not bank on it either.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: The plate is the filet lesson. Whole fish to a warm platter; the top fillet lifts off the bones in one piece with a spatula run along the backbone (peel from head-end to tail). The skeleton lifts clear in one motion, the second fillet lies beneath — the oldest two-fillets-one-fish service in the world. Sesame and scallion over, lemon or vinegar beside. Checkpoint: eating test: a flake of the thick loin with a strand of kimchi — crisp skin in the same bite, rich sweet fat, the fermented cut answering it. If the flesh tastes under-seasoned, the cure ran shy (fix next fish: the full 2 teaspoons); the vinegar splash at the table is the patch, not the cure.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: restaurant — the whole-fish classic. Godeungeo gui — salted mackerel, grilled whole or in cross-cut steaks until the skin crisps and the fat renders — is the fish record of the Korean home table: cheap, abundant, rich enough to feed a family on one fish, and forgiving enough to cook in a toaster oven, a broiler, a grill basket, or over charcoal. It is also the site's master class in whole-fish grilling: the salt cure, the drying skin, the single flip, and the doneness read at the backbone. Master this fish and every record around it (#SF08, #SF09) is a variation.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Salt early, salt more than instinct says. Salt both fish's cavity and skin — 2 teaspoons feels like a lot, and it is the correct amount for this fat level: the cure seasons the flesh, firms it for the grill, and draws surface moisture to the skin where it will dry. A mackerel under-salted is the record's only unrecoverable failure; you can always add at the table, but you cannot cure after the fire.
  • Rest salted, refrigerated and uncovered, 30 minutes to 2 hours (longer is better — the classic home method salts the fish in the morning and grills at dinner). Before cooking, pat the skin bone-dry: wet skin steams, dry skin crisps.
  • Score the thickest part — three diagonal cuts to the bone on each side of whole fish. The scores are doneness windows (you watch the flesh at the bone) and they keep the skin from splitting as it shrinks.
  • Fire for moderate, indirect-adjacent: charcoal at medium with a cooler zone (roughly 180–200 °C over the cooking side — a hand held at the grate counts 3–4 seconds before flinching), or a broiler/grill basket arrangement where flare-ups can be dodged. Mackerel's fat drips and catches; the plan is to manage that, not prevent it.

blocks.name: doneness
blocks.html:
Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The fish: cured with the full salt measure, dried uncovered, skin patted bone-dry, thickest part scored to the bone.
  • The fire: moderate with a cool zone; the skin releases itself — never forced.
  • The pull: flesh opaque at the backbone at the thickest score, pulling from the bone with a nudge.
  • The plate: two fillets off one skeleton, skin crisp, fermented cut beside every plate.

title: Gosari Namul Seasoned Fernbrake
times: Prep: 15 minutes (dried fernbrake rehydrates overnight) · Cook: 15 minutes · Total: Overnight soak, then about 30 minutes · Serves 4–6 as banchan

schema.name: Gosari Namul Seasoned Fernbrake
recipeIngredient: 50 g dried gosari (fernbrake fiddleheads) — a Korean market staple
Water for soaking and simmering; 1 tsp salt (about 5 g) in the simmer
A pinch of gochugaru (about 1 g), optional

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The drained, cut gosari and all the seasonings into a bowl, tossed by hand for a full minute — the fernbrake's fibrous surface needs the massage to take the oil and garlic, more than any leafy namul does. Checkpoint: every strand glossed and fragrant; taste one — it should be tender-chewy with a deep green bitterness the sesame rounds.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: The optional finish that deepens it: 2 minutes in a warm pan with a drop of oil, just to warm through and wake the garlic — the braised register — or served as-is, the tossed register. Both are traditional; the tossed is brighter, the pan is deeper. Checkpoint: the eating test with rice and any of this site's grilled meats: a wild, earthy chew against the rich plate — gosari is the banchan that tastes like it came from somewhere further than a farm.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the mountain table's vegetable. Gosari — fernbrake, the curled fiddleheads of the bracken fern — is the banchan that connects the Korean table to its mountains: dried fiddleheads, rehydrated overnight, braised tender, and dressed in the garlic-sesame namul that the whole #B06 family shares. It is the vegetable of bibimbap's traditional spread and of the spring mountain harvest, and its deep, green, faintly wild flavor is unlike any domestic vegetable. The record is short; the clock is long — the overnight soak is the recipe.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• The overnight soak, then the honest simmer. Cover the dried gosari with warm water and leave overnight (8–12 hours); it swells to about four times and turns from woody-brown to pliable green. Then simmer in salted water 15–20 minutes, until a stem bends without snapping — the same bend law as the kimchi cabbage (#B01), one ridge further along. Drain, rinse, and cut into 5 cm lengths. (Sold "pre-cooked" in the refrigerated section? The soak is done for you; start at the cut.)
  • Reserve a handful extra — the traditional bibimbap vegetable keeps, and tomorrow's rice bowl will want it.

title: Gyeran Jjim Steamed Eggs
times: Prep: 5 minutes · Cook: 12 minutes · Total: About 17 minutes · Serves 2–3 (one pot)

schema.name: Gyeran Jjim Steamed Eggs
recipeIngredient: 160 ml warm water (or light anchovy-kelp stock, the deeper traditional build)
A drop of toasted sesame oil (about 2 ml), 1 scallion (about 15 g) sliced, 1 tsp sesame seeds (about 4 g), optional red chili thread
A small heatproof pot, ceramic ttukbaegi, or ramekins (the traditional single-serve); a lid or foil

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The egg mixture poured into the vessel, any additions (a single anchovy, a piece of fish cake) hidden at the bottom — the treasure custom. Lid on, vessel set over the lowest heat your stove holds (or into a steamer over gentle steam). recipeInstructions.name: Step 2

title: Gyeran Mari Rolled Omelet
times: Prep: 10 minutes · Cook: 10 minutes · Total: About 20 minutes · Serves 4 (makes 1 roll)

schema.name: Gyeran Mari Rolled Omelet
recipeIngredient: 6 large eggs (about 300 g), at room temperature
1 tsp toasted sesame seeds (about 4 g), to finish
1 small carrot (about 40 g), cut into fine matchsticks (optional, for the color spiral)
1 strip of fish cake or a few leaves of baby spinach or perilla, shredded (optional fillings — pick one, not all)
1 tsp neutral oil for wiping (about 4 g), plus a paper towel

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The first layer and the first roll. Wipe the pan with the oiled towel, pour a thin layer of egg (about a quarter of the bowl) to coat the pan's floor, and let it set from the bottom — the surface should stay barely wet. Scatter a pinch of scallion (and carrot, if using) across. When the bottom is set and the top just barely not, roll the layer away from you: spatula lifts the far edge, and three folds bring a tight log to the pan's far side. Checkpoint: the first roll is the hardest and the least pretty, and that is fine — it becomes the log's core. The egg sheet should be tender-gold, not browned; browning means the pan crossed out of the medium-low zone, and the next layer tears at the roll.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: The pour-roll rhythm, layer by layer. Pull the pan off the heat (this is the secret beat — the pour onto a slightly cooled pan keeps the next layer from instantly scrambling), re-oil with the towel, pour the next quarter of egg to coat the floor in front of the log, and let it flow slightly under the log's base. Back on the heat until the new sheet's top is barely wet, then roll the log forward over it — one fold, then another, the new layer wrapping the log. Checkpoint: each new layer should bond to the log (the wet-under pour does the welding) and the log grows visibly with each wrap. If a layer detaches, the sheet set too dry before the roll — wetter topside, earlier roll.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Finish and shape. After the last layer (about four pours), roll the finished log to its seam-side down and press gently on all four faces with the spatula in the warm pan — 30 seconds of shaping that turns a rough cylinder into a squared log that slices cleanly. Checkpoint: the finished log is evenly golden, firm but springy at a press, and the spiral is already visible at the ends. Cut test at the pan: a clean cross-section of tight layers with the scallion (and carrot) threading the spiral — no gaps, no torn sheets.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 4
recipeInstructions.text: Rest 3 minutes, then slice thick — 2 cm coins, a serrated or very sharp knife, one draw-stroke per coin (pressing saw-hand through a hot roll crushes the layers it took ten minutes to build). Checkpoint: the eating test: the coin holds its spiral to the last bite, each layer tender and just-bound, scallion's hum through it — and at the grill table it is the banchan that kids and elders reach for simultaneously, which is the dish's honest social job.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the pan-roll craft. Gyeran mari — the Korean rolled omelet — is one of those dishes whose whole difficulty hides in one repeated motion: pour a thin layer of egg, roll it to one side, pour the next, roll again, until a golden log of a dozen layers sits in the pan. The banchan it becomes needs nothing else — salt, scallion, maybe a strip of carrot — because the layering IS the texture and the flavor: tender sheets of egg, rolled tight, sliced into spirals that disappear at the grill table faster than anything but the meat. This is the site's egg-craft record, the one that teaches pan temperature and the roll in one lesson.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The eggs: gently beaten to uniform, additions fine and dry.
  • The pan: medium-low and cycled — off-heat at every pour, tender-gold never browned.
  • The roll: each layer welded under the log, four or five pours to the finish, seam pressed.
  • The slice: 2 cm coins, one draw-stroke, the spiral intact.

blocks.html:
Finish & Plate

The coins go to the table arranged cut-face up in one overlapping line — the spirals are the plating, no garnish needed, though a dot of ketchup at the kids' end of the plate is a tradition the record declines to fight.

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • The whole log keeps 2 days refrigerated and slices cold into lunchboxes — gyeran mari is the packed-lunch banchan by long tradition. Reheat slices 20 seconds in a pan, never a long microwave (it weeps and toughens).

title: Hobak Bokkeum Stir-Fried Zucchini
times: Prep: 8 minutes · Cook: 7 minutes · Total: About 15 minutes · Serves 4 as banchan

schema.name: Hobak Bokkeum Stir-Fried Zucchini
recipeIngredient: 500 g zucchini (2 medium), cut into 1 cm half-moons
1 tsp coarse salt (about 5 g), for the 10-minute draw
A pinch of salt (about 1 g) and ground pepper
1 scallion (about 15 g), sliced; a pinch of gochugaru (about 1 g), optional

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Oil at medium-high, garlic in for 30 seconds of blonding, then the pressed zucchini in one layer as much as the pan allows — 2 minutes undisturbed for the first side. Checkpoint: the cut faces gold against the green skin, and the pan sizzles steadily rather than hissing out steam — the draw did its work. If the pan floods with liquid, the press was skipped; pour it off, accept a softer bowl, salt earlier next time.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Toss or turn, 2–3 minutes more — the zucchini should stay crisp-shouldered with gilded edges, not collapse. Checkpoint: the bend test: a half-moon bends with a spine of resistance. Fully limp zucchini is over; this bowl's identity is the last of the crunch.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Off the heat: soy, pepper, sesame oil, seeds, scallion, gochugaru if using — the residual heat blooms them without cooking them away. Checkpoint: the eating test with rice: sesame-garlic first, the zucchini's sweet green core, a clean finish. It should taste like the vegetable decided to dress up, not like dressing looking for a vegetable.

originalInstructions: Oil at medium-high, garlic in for 30 seconds of blonding, then the pressed zucchini in one layer as much as the pan allows — 2 minutes undisturbed for the first side. Checkpoint — the cut faces gold against the green skin, and the pan sizzles steadily rather than hissing out steam — the draw did its work. If the pan floods with liquid, the press was skipped; pour it off, accept a softer bowl, salt earlier next time.

Toss or turn, 2–3 minutes more — the zucchini should stay crisp-shouldered with gilded edges, not collapse. Checkpoint — the bend test: a half-moon bends with a spine of resistance. Fully limp zucchini is over; this bowl's identity is the last of the crunch.

Off the heat: soy, pepper, sesame oil, seeds, scallion, gochugaru if using — the residual heat blooms them without cooking them away. Checkpoint — the eating test with rice: sesame-garlic first, the zucchini's sweet green core, a clean finish. It should taste like the vegetable decided to dress up, not like dressing looking for a vegetable.

title: Hotteok Brown-Sugar Seed Pancakes
times: Prep: 20 minutes, plus 1 hour rising · Cook: 20 minutes · Total: About 1 hour 40 minutes · Makes 8 pancakes (serves 4)

schema.name: Hotteok Brown-Sugar Seed Pancakes
recipeIngredient: 50 g sweet rice flour (chapssalgaru — the chew; substitute fine glutinous rice flour)
250 ml warm milk or water (about 40 °C — warm to the wrist, not hot)
1 tbsp neutral oil (about 12 g), worked into the dough
2 tbsp sunflower or pine nuts, coarsely chopped (about 20 g)
Neutral oil for the pan (about 3 tbsp / 40 g total across the batch)

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Shape the pockets with oiled hands, not floured ones. With wet or oiled palms, tear off a ball of dough (about 80 g), and flatten it in your hand into a 10 cm disc — the dough is too soft to roll; the palm is the rolling pin. A spoonful of filling (about 20 g) into the center, then the disc's edges gathered up and pinched closed like a drawstring purse, seam down on the plate. Eight of them. Checkpoint: each purse is fully sealed with no sugar showing (an open seam leaks molten sugar straight into the oil — the batch's one real hazard, both for the fry and for the sugar lost from the pancake) and the dough around the filling is even, without a thin blowout side.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Fry low and slow, flatten once. A generously oiled pan at medium-low — the oil at a lazy shimmer, not a sizzle (around 160 °C if the pan could speak). Two or three purses in seam-side-down, 60–90 seconds to set the bottom, then flip and press each one flat with the spatula — one confident press into a 1.5 cm disc — and another 2–3 minutes on that side, flipping once more briefly to re-crisp the first face. Checkpoint: the crust goes deep golden and lacy-crisp at the pressed edges while the interior stays thick and pale-soft; press one at the center — it should give like a cushion. A dark crust at 90 seconds means the heat is running high and the filling inside is still grainy — the low-slow fry exists precisely so the sugar melts in the time the crust browns.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Rest one minute — the safety minute — and serve. Off the pan to a rack or plate, and a full minute before the first bite: the filling is molten syrup at 120 °C-plus straight from the pan, the street cart's small legend of burned mouths and burned fingers. Checkpoint: the eating test: the first bite tears the crisp crust and the syrup runs — dark brown sugar, cinnamon, the seeds' crunch, the chewy-soft interior catching it all. It should be slightly too hot, slightly messy, and completely worth both. That is the street cart's exact register, reproduced.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the street cart's sweet. Hotteok is the winter street cart's calling card: a soft yeasted dough, flattened in the palm, filled with a pocket of brown sugar, cinnamon, and seeds, then pan-fried until the crust crisps and the filling melts into molten syrup that stays dangerously hot inside. It is the grill meal's traditional walk-away dessert — the cart at the market's mouth after the table clears — and the one that ends this site's record list because it ends the meal in real life. The craft is a working dough, a sealed pocket, and the low-slow fry that melts the sugar without burning the crust.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Mix the dough wet and let it rise covered, 1 hour. Hotteok dough is stickier than bread dough — that wetness is the soft interior's promise. Flour, sweet rice flour, sugar, salt, and yeast whisked dry; the warm milk in, mixed to a shaggy paste, the oil worked in, then covered in the bowl until doubled, puffy, and bubbling at the surface. Checkpoint — the doubled dough jiggles when the bowl is tapped and smells of yeast and sweetness. Punch it down and it re-inflates slowly — a working dough, not an exhausted one.
  • Mix the filling in a dry bowl and set it beside the stove with a small bowl of cold water for your hands and a plate for the shaped dough: the assembly is a production line and the fry waits for no one. The brown sugar's clumps broken fully — a hard clump in the pocket melts to a lava pocket that stays molten five minutes longer than the rest.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The serve: the one-minute rest, then straight from the rack — hotteok has no second act.

Finish & Plate

Two pancakes per person on a small plate with a napkin — the street cart's service, unchanged. Coffee or the sikhye (#D05) beside, and the table eats them leaning forward, which is the posture the dish has always demanded.

title: Injeolmi Toast with Ice Cream
times: Prep: 10 minutes · Cook: 8 minutes · Total: About 20 minutes · Serves 4 (8 toasts)

schema.name: Injeolmi Toast with Ice Cream
recipeIngredient: 8 small rectangle injeolmi rice cakes (about 240 g), or fresh mochi cut to size — the refrigerated Korean-market kind, not frozen
4 thick slices milk bread or brioche (about 200 g)
4 tbsp roasted soybean powder (injeolmi powder / konggaru, about 30 g)
3 tbsp honey or condensed milk (about 60 g)
4 small scoops vanilla or milk-flavored ice cream (about 200 g)
A pinch of fine salt (about 1 g), over the toast

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Toast the bread golden in half the butter — pan or grill grate, the grill's last heat is the tradition's own trick — and hold it warm. Checkpoint: deep golden and butter-crisp at the face, still soft at the center — thick bread's job is to be a warm, crisp platform.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: The rice cakes into the remaining butter at medium heat, pressed flat with the spatula (each pressed to half its height), 90 seconds a side to a blistered, crisped, lightly golden skin with the interior gone stretchy-soft. Checkpoint: the pressed cake's surface is blistered and toasted, and a test pull stretches — crisp outside, mochi inside, the dessert's central texture in one piece.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: The build, per plate: toast, a drizzle of honey, two pressed rice cakes over, a heavy dust of the soybean powder (the flavor that names the dessert — nutty, roasted, faintly sweet), another honey drizzle, the ice cream scoop crowning, a final dust over the whole plate. Checkpoint: the eating test, immediately, while the temperatures still oppose: the ice cream melting into the powder's dust, the rice cake's stretch, the toast's butter-crisp, and the soybean-honey flavor running through all three layers. Ninety seconds of contrast is the dessert's whole window — serve at the pan, not from the kitchen.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: contemporary — the café's grill-adjacent dessert. Injeolmi toast is the modern Korean café's signature sweet: mochi rice cakes pressed crisp in a buttered pan, stacked on toast, dusted with roasted soybean powder and honey, and — the full build — crowned with a scoop of ice cream that melts down through the warm layers. It is the sweet that tastes like Seoul's dessert cafés, born decades after every other record on this dessert list, and it is here because the grill meal's table deserves one hot-cold showpiece that takes twenty minutes.

title: Jangjorim Soy-Braised Beef
metadata: Korean · Medium · Makes one jar (a month of tables)
times: Prep: 15 minutes · Cook: 1 hour 15 minutes · Total: About 1 hour 30 minutes, mostly untended · Makes one jar (a month of tables)

schema.name: Jangjorim Soy-Braised Beef
schema.description: **Stream: heritage — the jar that owns the month.
schema.recipeYield: Makes one jar (a month of tables)
recipeIngredient: 600 g lean beef (eye of round, brisket point's lean half, or shank), one piece, tied if it wants to fall apart
6 cloves garlic (about 24 g), crushed, and a thumb of ginger (about 15 g), sliced — the poaching aromatics
1 tsp salt (about 5 g), in the poach
3 tbsp corn syrup or 2 tbsp honey (about 50 g)
4–6 bird's eye chilies (about 8 g), whole, stems on
1 tsp toasted sesame oil (5 ml), off heat

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The poach (40 minutes). The beef in cold water with the aromatics, brought to the barest simmer — a bubble every few seconds, 90 °C-plus but never a rolling boil (a hard boil tightens the fibers this recipe is trying to shred) — skimmed once at the come-up, lid ajar, 40 minutes to just-tender. Checkpoint: a chopstick slides into the meat with firm resistance — cooked through, not yet falling. Lift the beef to a board (save the liquid — it is stage two's base), rest it 10 minutes, and slice across the grain into 5 mm strips, then tear the strips by hand into shreds along the fibers. The hand-tearing (not knife-cutting) is what gives jangjorim its signature fibrous pull.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: The braise (25–30 minutes). The shredded beef, soy, 150 ml of the poaching liquid, syrup, mirin, the ten garlic cloves, and the chilies into the wide pan — at a steady simmer now, lid off, stirring every 5 minutes as the liquid reduces. Checkpoint: at 20 minutes the liquid has dropped below the beef's level and the pan's sounds deepen from bubbling to a slow sizzle; the shreds are turning glossy mahogany and the garlic has gone amber at its edges. The target is a wet-not-soupy mass — spoonable with liquid just filling the gaps, not a dry stir-fry and not a stew.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: The jar and the month. Off the heat, sesame oil and seeds through, and pack into a clean glass jar while hot — the residual heat and the salt content are the keeping. Cool uncovered, then lid and refrigerate. Checkpoint: the eating test, warm from the pan and again cold from the fridge on day three: the shreds should pull into long savory-sweet strands, the garlic crushes into them like a paste, the chili sits whole for the brave — and over hot rice, one spoonful should make the bowl disappear faster than anything else on the table. That is the rice-thief standard, and this jar meets it.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the jar that owns the month. Jangjorim is the banchan that behaves like a preserve: a lean cut of beef braised in soy until the fibers pull apart into strands, packed into a jar with its braising liquid, whole garlic cloves gone amber, and bird's eye chilies — and then it serves the table for weeks, a spoonful of shreds over rice at every meal until the jar runs dry. It is salty-sweet, intensely savory, the "rice thief" category's champion, and at the grill table it is the bowl that outlasts every other banchan on the board. One afternoon of mostly-untended braising buys a month of meals.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• The two-stage liquid is the architecture. Stage one poaches the beef in plain aromatized water (the fibres relax, the beef's own flavor builds the broth); stage two reduces a soy-sweet braise with that broth as its base. Skipping stage one and boiling the beef in soy from the start makes over-salty, tight-fibered shreds — the common shortcut and the common disappointment.
  • Count the garlic: the ten whole cloves of stage two are not a typo. They braise to spreading-soft, amber-sweet, and the jar's second treasure — regulars fish for them first.

- The two-stage liquid is the architecture. Stage one poaches the beef in plain aromatized water (the fibres relax, the beef's own flavor builds the broth); stage two reduces a soy-sweet braise with that broth as its base. blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 1. The poach (40 minutes). The beef in cold water with the aromatics, brought to the barest simmer — a bubble every few seconds, 90 °C-plus but never a rolling boil (a hard boil tightens the fibers this recipe is trying to shred) — skimmed once at the come-up, lid ajar, 40 minutes to just-tender. Checkpoint — a chopstick slides into the meat with firm resistance — cooked through, not yet falling. Lift the beef to a board (save the liquid — it is stage two's base), rest it 10 minutes, and slice across the grain into 5 mm strips, then tear the strips by hand into shreds along the fibers. The hand-tearing (not knife-cutting) is what gives jangjorim its signature fibrous pull.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 2. The braise (25–30 minutes). The shredded beef, soy, 150 ml of the poaching liquid, syrup, mirin, the ten garlic cloves, and the chilies into the wide pan — at a steady simmer now, lid off, stirring every 5 minutes as the liquid reduces. Checkpoint — at 20 minutes the liquid has dropped below the beef's level and the pan's sounds deepen from bubbling to a slow sizzle; the shreds are turning glossy mahogany and the garlic has gone amber at its edges. The target is a wet-not-soupy mass — spoonable with liquid just filling the gaps, not a dry stir-fry and not a stew.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 3. The jar and the month. Off the heat, sesame oil and seeds through, and pack into a clean glass jar while hot — the residual heat and the salt content are the keeping. Cool uncovered, then lid and refrigerate. Checkpoint — the eating test, warm from the pan and again cold from the fridge on day three: the shreds should pull into long savory-sweet strands, the garlic crushes into them like a paste, the chili sits whole for the brave — and over hot rice, one spoonful should make the bowl disappear faster than anything else on the table. That is the rice-thief standard, and this jar meets it. Chef’s Note — jangjorim is the banchan that explains why "banchan" resists translation: it is not a "side dish," it is an infrastructure — a preserved, salty, long-shelf flavor base that makes rice and porridge meals work between the shopping trips. The grill table's fresh bowls (#B06, #B07) last a day; this jar quietly underwrites the whole month, and the tradition's rhythm — a big braise, portioned across weeks — is meal-prep three centuries before the term.

title: Jeonbok Gui Grilled Abalone
times: Prep: 20 minutes · Cook: 6 minutes · Total: About 30 minutes · Serves 4 (makes 8)

schema.name: Jeonbok Gui Grilled Abalone
schema.description: **Stream: restaurant — the coastal luxury.** Abalone is the coastal grill's ceremony dish — the shell itself the vessel, the meat cooked in minutes with nothing but butter, garlic, and the abalone's own juices.
recipeIngredient: 8 live abalone in the shell (about 80–100 g each), or 8 cleaned abalone meats with shells reserved
1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds (about 8 g), finely sliced scallion (about 10 g)
Steamed rice (about 300 g cooked), a light lettuce salad, and the table's best drinks — this is a celebration record

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: A spoon of butter into each shell's hollow, the scored abalone over it, shells to the moderate fire in their cradle. Four minutes, no touching. Checkpoint: the butter bubbles around the meat's edge, the scores open pale, and the surface turns from glassy to matte. The smell is butter and sweet ocean.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Baste each meat with the garlicky butter from its own shell, one more minute, off the fire while the foot still has spring at a fingertip press. Checkpoint: the pull test is the record: pressed, the meat springs back slowly (tender-window) — a fast hard snap-back means it tightened past the window; if it never firmed at all, thirty seconds more. The test piece cut thick: resistant-tender, buttery, ocean-sweet — abalone's texture is the dish, and "just right" is a real, findable 60 seconds.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Sesame and scallion over each, the shells straight to the table in the cradle, drinks already poured. Checkpoint: eating test: the whole meat in two or three thick bites off a small fork or the tip of a chopstick's handle, rice after — and the shell's butter-juice pooled beneath is the cook's sip, the oldest gratuity at the coast.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Clean them (if live): slide a short spoon between meat and shell at the narrow end, work around, and pop the meat free. Cut away the dark viscera and the mouth disc; scrub the foot's edge. The green-gray trim and the liver are delicacies to some tables and discards to others — ask yours; both answers are correct. Return each meat to its shell, fatty foot-side up.
  • Score the foot lightly — a shallow crosshatch, five or six cuts: the scores help the heat in and the baste down, and they telegraph the cooking on the surface.
  • Fire moderate, pan or grate, with the shells set in a foil cradle or bed of coarse salt so they sit level.

title: Jjukkumi Gui Grilled Baby Octopus
times: Prep: 20 minutes, plus 30 minutes marinating · Cook: 10 minutes at the table · Total: About 1 hour 10 minutes, mostly resting · Serves 3–4

schema.name: Jjukkumi Gui Grilled Baby Octopus
recipeIngredient: 800 g baby octopus (jjukkumi), cleaned — beaks and innards removed, bodies left whole; thawed fully and patted dry if frozen
2 tbsp honey or corn syrup (about 40 g)
2 tsp gochugaru (about 6 g) — the heat dial for the drinking table
2 scallions (about 30 g), cut into 5 cm lengths
100 g cabbage or perilla leaves, rough-torn (optional but traditional)
Steamed rice (about 500 g cooked), mu sangchae (about 100 g) or cucumber banchan (#B07), soju's ceremony

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Onion down first, octopus over. Lay the onion arcs across the hot oiled pan as a bed, and spread the marinated jjukkumi over and around them in a single layer — the bodies will curl and the tentacles tighten into little crowns as they hit. Checkpoint: a hard sizzle and steam rising off the marinade's water, sweet chile in the air within a minute. If the pan is quiet and pooling liquid, it was not hot enough — pull the batch, reheat, restart; jjukkumi boiled in marinade is rubber in glaze.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Turn with the tongs, two minutes at a time, glaze as it reduces. The marinade's water cooks off and what remains on the pan thickens to a glaze that lacquers each octopus as you turn them through it — four to six minutes total. Scallions in for the last two. The bodies are done when they are firm-plump, glossy red-brown, and a body cut at the pan reads opaque to its center. Checkpoint: the pan should be nearly dry, everything coated brick-glossy, onion edges char-sweet and translucent. One test octopus whole: snap-tender (they are small — this is the tender side of octopus's law), sweet-heat lacquer, the ocean's sweetness under it. If any bite is rubbery, that piece needed one more minute in the reducing glaze — small octopus tenderizes briefly under heat before it tightens, unlike squid's instant law.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Pan to the table on its trivet, sesame over, straight off the pan. Jjukkumi's window is while the glaze still sizzles; rice in one hand, tongs in the other, the cabbage or perilla to wrap the sweetest, hottest ones. Checkpoint: the table test: a whole octopus over rice in one bite-set — glaze edge, snap, chew, heat blooming late — with the cold radish between rounds. The platter should be empty before the pan stops sizzling; that is not a metaphor, it is the recipe's honest clock.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: restaurant — the tent's signature. Jjukkumi are baby octopus the length of a hand, and their grill record is the drinking table's favorite version of the octopus idea: whole little octopus tossed in a sweet-spicy gochujang marinade, seared fast on a hot pan or tabletop dome until the sauce caramelizes into glaze, and eaten entire — head, tentacles, everything — with rice or straight off the pan with soju. Where the nakji record (#SF05) pre-simmers a bigger octopus, jjukkumi are small enough to grill from raw, which is the entire reason they own the lane: no simmer, no pounding, just the marinade clock and a hot pan. Who cooks what: the pan belongs to whoever loses the first round of drinks-buying. Tongs rotate with the batches.

  • Marinated jjukkumi hold 24 hours refrigerated. Cooked, 2 days — chopped into fried rice or bibim-guksu (cold spicy noodles), where the leftover glaze seasons the whole bowl.
  • Variations: the big-octopus fork with the pre-simmer (#SF05); squid takes this same marinade and the #SF04 clock; a handful of rice cakes tossed onto the pan in the last three minutes is the tent's carb course and entirely correct.

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations- Marinated jjukkumi hold 24 hours refrigerated. Cooked, 2 days — chopped into fried rice or bibim-guksu (cold spicy noodles), where the leftover glaze seasons the whole bowl.
- Variations: the big-octopus fork with the pre-simmer (#SF05); squid takes this same marinade and the #SF04 clock; a handful of rice cakes tossed onto the pan in the last three minutes is the tent's carb course and entirely correct.

originalInstructions: **Onion down first, octopus over.** Lay the onion arcs across the hot oiled pan as a bed, and spread the marinated jjukkumi over and around them in a single layer — the bodies will curl and the tentacles tighten into little crowns as they hit. Checkpoint — a hard sizzle and steam rising off the marinade's water, sweet chile in the air within a minute. If the pan is quiet and pooling liquid, it was not hot enough — pull the batch, reheat, restart; jjukkumi boiled in marinade is rubber in glaze.

**Turn with the tongs, two minutes at a time, glaze as it reduces.** The marinade's water cooks off and what remains on the pan thickens to a glaze that lacquers each octopus as you turn them through it — four to six minutes total. Scallions in for the last two. The bodies are done when they are firm-plump, glossy red-brown, and a body cut at the pan reads opaque to its center. Checkpoint — the pan should be nearly dry, everything coated brick-glossy, onion edges char-sweet and translucent. One test octopus whole: snap-tender (they are small — this is the tender side of octopus's law), sweet-heat lacquer, the ocean's sweetness under it. If any bite is rubbery, that piece needed one more minute in the reducing glaze — small octopus tenderizes briefly under heat before it tightens, unlike squid's instant law.

**Pan to the table on its trivet, sesame over, straight off the pan.** Jjukkumi's window is while the glaze still sizzles; rice in one hand, tongs in the other, the cabbage or perilla to wrap the sweetest, hottest ones. Checkpoint — the table test: a whole octopus over rice in one bite-set — glaze edge, snap, chew, heat blooming late — with the cold radish between rounds. The platter should be empty before the pan stops sizzling; that is not a metaphor, it is the recipe's honest clock.

title: Jogae Gui Grilled Clams

schema.name: Jogae Gui Grilled Clams
recipeIngredient: 1.2 kg small hard-shell clams (littleneck, manila, or vongole), mixed sizes welcome
Cold salted water (about 3 tbsp salt per liter, close to seawater), 30 minutes
1 tsp gochugaru (about 3 g), 1 tsp sesame seeds (about 4 g)
1 tsp toasted sesame oil (5 ml), a pinch of garlic (about 2 g), grated
Steamed rice (about 400 g cooked) or noodles later — see Note — and the shell bowl

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Clams onto the moderate grate in a single layer, hollow-side up where the shells allow. Nothing happens for 2–3 minutes — then they begin to pop open one by one, unevenly, each on its own clock. Checkpoint: an opened clam shows the meat just firmed at the edges and its liquor steaming — that one comes off now, not when its neighbors open. The grill boss works by eye, tongs ready, pulling gapers continuously.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: The discard law at the fire: a clam that stays fully shut after its batch-mates have opened (a full 2-minute grace) does not get forced or knifed — it goes to the discard bowl. Same law as the mussels (#SF13) and oysters (#SF12): the unopened shell is the sea's own warning label. recipeInstructions.name: Step 3

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• The purge is the recipe's first half: clams spend 30 minutes in cold salted water in a single loose layer, breathing out their sand, then are lifted (not poured — the sand sits in the bottom) and scrubbed.   • Mix the dip and set the table: the clams' pace at the fire leaves no hands free.
  • Fire moderate, grate oiled, or a grill basket that lets the shells sit level; a foil tray with a few knife slits works on a gas grill.

title: Jogi Gui Grilled Yellow Croaker
times: Prep: 10 minutes, plus 1–2 hours salting · Cook: 12 minutes · Total: About 1 hour 25 minutes, mostly salting · Serves 3–4

schema.name: Jogi Gui Grilled Yellow Croaker
schema.description: **Stream: restaurant — the dried-fish tradition's fresh cousin.
recipeIngredient: 4 whole yellow croaker (about 200 g each), gutted, cleaned, scored twice on each side
2 tsp coarse salt (about 10 g), worked into the scores and the cavity
Neutral oil for the grate (about 10 ml)
1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds (about 8 g), sliced scallion (about 10 g)
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), kimchi (#B01), mu sangchae (about 100 g) — jogi runs salty-savory and wants the cold crunch

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Oiled moderate grate, scored side down, 5 minutes undisturbed. The skin is thinner than mackerel's — it goes golden faster and wants a notch less heat. Checkpoint: golden skin at the scores, the flesh at the cuts turning opaque; the release is clean where the skin crisped.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: One flip, 4–5 minutes more, and jogi's doneness read is the same backbone test as the mackerel's (#SF07): at the deepest score, opaque at the bone and pulling away with a nudge. Checkpoint: a test flake from the thick shoulder: salty-savory, concentrated, firm but juicy — the flavor should sit somewhere between fresh fish and its dried cousin, which is exactly the record's register.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Platter with sesame and scallion; the filet service runs the same two-fillets-one-skeleton as the mackerel record. Checkpoint: eating test: flake, rice, a strand of kimchi, and — the jogi-specific bite — a piece of mu sangchae's cold crunch with the salty fish. The table should reach for the rice bowl more often than the dip; this fish seasons itself.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: restaurant — the dried-fish tradition's fresh cousin. Jogi — yellow croaker — is the fish of the Korean salted-and-dried tradition (the gulbi hung in rows at any market), and its fresh-grilled record runs that same idea on a home clock: a stronger salt cure than the other fish here, a longer rest, and a grill that concentrates rather than merely cooks. The gulbi tradition is the honest ancestor — this record is the fresh fish borrowing the dried fish's seasoning logic, and the table will recognize the flavor immediately.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• The long cure is the recipe: salted, uncovered, refrigerated 1–2 hours. The salt goes past seasoning into concentrating — the flesh tightens and its flavor deepens toward its dried gulbi cousin. Pat dry after; do not rinse.

  • While the fish cures: everything else — rice, table, banchan — the record has no other work.

title: Jumulleok Sesame-Garlic Steak Bites
times: Prep: 10 minutes · Cook: 8 minutes · Total: About 20 minutes · Serves 3–4

schema.name: Jumulleok Sesame-Garlic Steak Bites
schema.description: **Stream: restaurant, the instant-toss clock.** Jumulleok means "hand-mixed" — cubed steak tossed in seasoning minutes before it hits the fire, not hours.
recipeIngredient: 700 g sirloin or tenderloin, cut into 3 cm cubes (refrigerated until the toss — food safety is the one place this record is strict)
Steamed rice (about 500 g cooked), gireumjang (#SA02) for extra dipping, kimchi (#B01), lettuce ssam

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Toss the first batch: meat into the bowl, hands or tongs, thirty seconds of turning until every cube wears the mix. Onto the hot grate with a finger's width between cubes — crowded cubes steam gray. Checkpoint: the cubes should hit with an aggressive sizzle and the sesame-garlic smell should rise immediately. No sizzle, no sear — pull the batch back and let the grate recover.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Grill 90 seconds undisturbed, turn each cube to a new face, another 90 seconds, then roll to the last faces for 30–60 seconds. Total cook: about 4 minutes for medium at 3 cm. Pull when the faces are browned and the cube feels softly springy at a finger press. Checkpoint: cut one open at the grill station: a thin browned crust and a rosy interior. Gray to the center means the grate was too cool or the cubes too big — 3 cm is the ceiling.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Sesame seeds over, warm platter, straight to the table. Toss the next batch while the table eats this one — the rhythm of the record is toss, grill, eat, repeat, and the meat is at its best in the first minute off the fire. Checkpoint: eating test: crust, juice, sesame. The center should taste of beef and black pepper more than soy — if it reads salty, the soy ran a teaspoon heavy; the toss is measured in grams for a reason.

Of everything on this site, this is the fastest route from the butcher to the table — ten minutes of prep, a hot grate, and the seasoning bowl right at the grill so the next batch can be tossed while the first one cooks. Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • This is a cook-and-eat record; the toss doesn't hold. Leftover cooked cubes keep 2 days and make the best fried rice in this whole category — the sesame-garlic crust re-toasts beautifully in a hot pan.

originalInstructions: Toss the first batch: meat into the bowl, hands or tongs, thirty seconds of turning until every cube wears the mix. Onto the hot grate with a finger's width between cubes — crowded cubes steam gray. Checkpoint — the cubes should hit with an aggressive sizzle and the sesame-garlic smell should rise immediately. No sizzle, no sear — pull the batch back and let the grate recover.

Grill 90 seconds undisturbed, turn each cube to a new face, another 90 seconds, then roll to the last faces for 30–60 seconds. Total cook: about 4 minutes for medium at 3 cm. Pull when the faces are browned and the cube feels softly springy at a finger press. Checkpoint — cut one open at the grill station: a thin browned crust and a rosy interior. Gray to the center means the grate was too cool or the cubes too big — 3 cm is the ceiling.

Sesame seeds over, warm platter, straight to the table. Toss the next batch while the table eats this one — the rhythm of the record is toss, grill, eat, repeat, and the meat is at its best in the first minute off the fire. Checkpoint — eating test: crust, juice, sesame. The center should taste of beef and black pepper more than soy — if it reads salty, the soy ran a teaspoon heavy; the toss is measured in grams for a reason.

title: Kkaennip Jangajji Pickled Perilla Leaves
metadata: Korean · Easy · Makes 1 jar (a month's table)
times: Prep: 30 minutes · Cook: 5 minutes · Total: 35 minutes, ready in 1–2 days · Makes 1 jar (a month's table)

schema.name: Kkaennip Jangajji Pickled Perilla Leaves
recipeIngredient: 40–50 fresh perilla leaves (kkaennip, about 60 g), stemmed, washed, spun thoroughly dry
1.5 tbsp honey or corn syrup (about 30 g)

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The paint-and-stack, leaf by leaf. One leaf on the board, paste painted across its face with a brush or the back of a spoon, the next leaf laid over, painted, the next — the stack becomes the pickle's structure, every layer's seasoning facing the next leaf's face. Ten leaves to a stack, a stack pressed gently, and the stacks stood or laid into the clean jar, pressed down. Checkpoint: the stack holds together when lifted, and cut at the edge, shows its cross-section: leaf, dark line of seasoning, leaf — the jar's architecture, built.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Any remaining paste and a splash of water over the stack in the jar, pressed once more, and the brine that weeps out over the first hours becomes the jar's own liquid. Lid on, refrigerate. Checkpoint: by the next morning, the leaves have darkened to deep olive-bronze and the jar holds a shallow soy-amber liquid — the pickle has set. Taste one leaf at 24 hours.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: The 48-hour readiness. Day one is good; day two is the jar's true voice — the leaf's anise-mint tamed to an herb depth, the brine's soy-sweet in every fold, the texture silky-supple. Checkpoint: the eating test, one leaf over hot rice: fold, bite — a complex savory-herbal chew that no other pickle on any table resembles. And the ssam use — one leaf wrapping a hot piece of samgyeopsal with a grain of rice — is this site's best single bite between the meat rounds.

• Dry the leaves completely — the jar's one rule. Washed perilla carries surface water that dilutes the seasoning layers and shortens the jar's life; a salad spinner and then an hour on towels does it. Any soft or torn leaves are eaten today, not jarred.

title: Kkakdugi Radish Kimchi
times: Prep: 45 minutes, hands-on · Cook: 0 minutes · Total: 45 minutes, then 1–2 days fermenting, then the fridge · Makes about 1.5 kg

schema.name: Kkakdugi Radish Kimchi
schema.description: **Stream: heritage — the kimchi that matches the stew pots.
recipeIngredient: 1.5 kg Korean radish (mu) or daikon, peeled, cut into 2.5 cm cubes
2 tbsp water (30 ml), or the drained brine

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The drained cubes and the paste folded together with your hands until every cube wears a coat and the bowl runs deep red-orange. Checkpoint: taste a pasted cube raw: salty, savory-hot, the radish's sweet pepper under it. This is day zero — the flavor that ferments into the bowl.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Pack into a clean jar with 3 cm of headspace, pressed to squeeze out air, weight on top, loose lid — B01's entire packing law, unchanged. Checkpoint: brine rises over the cubes within a day (top up with the saved brine or salted water if it lags — under-liquid is the safety architecture, same as the cabbage).

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Ferment at cool room temperature 1–2 days (radish runs faster than cabbage — its sugars are more available) until the brine fizzes faintly and the sourness arrives, then refrigerate. Checkpoint: day-two taste: the cube snaps audibly, the paste's heat has rounded, a clean sour line on the finish. Kkakdugi's window from young-crunchy to complex-sour is weeks in the fridge, and its snap outlives cabbage's by a wide margin.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the kimchi that matches the stew pots. Kkakdugi is baechu kimchi's (#B01) radish sibling: the same paste, cubed Korean radish instead of cabbage, a faster ferment, and a crunch that survives weeks longer. At the grill table it is the bowl that loves the braised and stewed records — the jangjorim (#B20), the oily fish (#SF07) — because radish's clean, peppery snap cuts richness the way cabbage's leaves cannot. If you have made B01, you have already made this paste; this record is the cube law and the radish clock.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Cube evenly — the cube is the recipe's clock. 2.5 cm cubes salt and ferment at the same rate; a batch mixed with half-cubes and whole chunks ferments unevenly (the small cubes go sour while the large ones stay raw). Weigh your knife discipline here, not your ingredients.
  • Salt the cubes 30 minutes, loose in a bowl, turning once. The radish weeps a brine and its corners soften a half-step. Save 2 tablespoons of the wept brine for the paste; drain the rest.
  • Make the paste while the cubes drain: everything above whisked to a rust slurry, scallions last.

title: Kongnamul Muchim Seasoned Soybean Sprouts
times: Prep: 5 minutes · Cook: 6 minutes · Total: About 15 minutes · Serves 4–6 as banchan

schema.name: Kongnamul Muchim Seasoned Soybean Sprouts
schema.description: **Stream: heritage — the everyday namul.** Soybean sprouts are the banchan that appears at nearly every Korean meal, including the grill table's — crunchy, nutty, cheap, and ready in fifteen minutes.
recipeIngredient: 500 g soybean sprouts (kongnamul, the yellow-beaned ones — mung sprouts are a different, softer thing), rinsed, loose hulls and sad stragglers picked out
Water to barely cover (about 1 liter), 1 tsp salt (about 5 g)
A pinch of gochugaru (about 1 g), optional color
1 tsp fish sauce or soy sauce (about 5 ml), optional depth

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Salted water at a full boil, sprouts in, uncovered — the law of this record. Six minutes at a steady boil, stirred once. Checkpoint: a test sprout: the tail is fully tender (no string) and the bean is just soft with the faintest bite, and the raw-grassy smell from the pot's first minute has cooked off entirely — that smell leaving is exactly what the uncovered boil lets happen.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Drain well — really well, a full minute in the colander, shaking — and turn the hot sprouts into the seasoning bowl while they still steam. Checkpoint: the residual heat is doing the garlic's cooking: thirty seconds after tossing, the bowl smells nutty-savory, not sharp-raw.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Toss with everything, taste, adjust — the banchan should read sesame-first, salt behind, a clean crunch. Checkpoint: the eating test with rice and any grilled meat from this site's M-list: the sprouts reset the palate between rich bites. That is the banchan's job description, and this bowl does it as well as anything on the table.

Soybean sprouts are the banchan that appears at nearly every Korean meal, including the grill table's — crunchy, nutty, cheap, and ready in fifteen minutes. This is also the parent recipe for the whole muchim/namul family on this site (#B06, #B17): blanch, shock, season is the pattern.

title: Korean BBQ Onion Soy-Vinegar Dipping Sauce
times: Prep: 10 minutes · Cook: 0 minutes · Total: 10 minutes · Makes about 200 g

schema.name: Korean BBQ Onion Soy-Vinegar Dipping Sauce
recipeIngredient: 1 small sweet onion (about 150 g), halved and sliced paper-thin (thinness is the recipe — see Method)
A pinch of gochugaru (about 1 g), optional color and warmth

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: restaurant — the steakhouse bowl. The onion-soy dip is the tabletop steakhouse's bowl: sweet onion macerated in soy and vinegar until it turns translucent and half-pickled, served ice-cold beside the big beef cuts. Where the scallion build (#SA04) is sharp and green, this one is sweet-rounded — onion's sugars soften the soy's salt and the vinegar turns it all bright — and its cold temperature against a just-off-the-grill rib is the entire reason it exists. It is also the easiest make-ahead on the site: ten minutes, a night in the fridge, better for it.

title: Korean BBQ Restaurant-Style Macaroni Salad
times: Prep: 15 minutes · Cook: 10 minutes · Total: About 25 minutes · Serves 6–8 as banchan

schema.name: Korean BBQ Restaurant-Style Macaroni Salad
schema.description: **Stream: restaurant — the macaroni bowl of the grill halls.
recipeIngredient: 250 g small macaroni or small shells (about 2.5 cups dry)
1 tbsp condensed milk or sugar (about 20 g) — the grill-hall sweetness signature
1/2 cucumber (about 100 g), small-diced, salted 10 minutes and squeezed
1 small carrot (about 60 g), fine-diced or grated

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The dressing whisked smooth first — mayo, condensed milk, vinegar, salt — tasting distinctly sweeter than seems right at room temperature. It is: cold suppresses sweetness, and the chill will bring it to target. Checkpoint: the dressing tastes sweet-tangy, pourable, just shy of a sauce — it will be swallowed by the pasta, so run it loose.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: The drained, cooled, still-damp pasta and the dressing tossed while the pasta is cool but not fridge-cold (the dressing coats evenly at this temperature; fridge-cold pasta repels mayo), then the cucumber, carrot, egg, and scallion folded through. Checkpoint: every noodle glossed, the mix-ins distributed, the bowl holding together without a puddle at the bottom. If it pools, the cucumber's squeeze was skipped.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Chill 30 minutes minimum, taste, and adjust — cold macaroni salad always needs one more grain of salt and a few drops of vinegar at the finish. Checkpoint: the eating test between bites of bulgogi (#M01): cold, sweet, soft-with-crunch, mild — the palate's reset button, which is the entire reason the grill halls serve it and the reason this bowl rides alongside the richest plates.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: restaurant — the macaroni bowl of the grill halls. Every Korean barbecue restaurant that opened across America in the last forty years put a cold macaroni salad on the banchan tray, and every table ate it first: small pasta in a sweet mayo dressing with cucumber and carrot, cold and crunchy and mild — the cooling valve between rounds of galbi (#M03) and bulgogi (#M01). It has no deep lineage and needs none; it is a restaurant invention that earned its seat. This record is the style as the grill halls run it.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Boil the pasta one minute past the box's al dente. This is the anti-Italian rule of the genre: the cold salad firms as it chills, and pasta cooked properly hot turns stiff-cold; a minute extra holds the tender chew after the chill. Rinse under cold water to stop the cooking and cool it — the one pasta record where rinsing is correct.
  • Salt and squeeze the cucumber (#B07's law — it is the water law of every cold bowl on this site); boil the egg with the pasta's first minutes.

title: Korean Potato Salad
times: Prep: 20 minutes · Cook: 20 minutes · Total: About 40 minutes · Serves 6–8 as banchan

schema.name: Korean Potato Salad
recipeIngredient: 700 g russet or yukon gold potatoes, peeled, cut into 4 cm chunks
3 tbsp Kewpie-style Japanese mayonnaise (about 45 g) — the one non-negotiable brand-loyalty in this record
1/2 cucumber (about 75 g), small-diced and salted 10 minutes
1 scallion or 2 tbsp minced onion (about 10 g), optional

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Rice the potatoes or mash them coarse — deliberately coarse, with visible small chunks left in. Korean potato salad is not a smooth puree; the texture target is "mostly mashed, part smashed," with bits that keep the bowl interesting. Checkpoint: the mash holds a spoon's trail briefly and no water pools at the bowl's edge (if it does, the dry-steam was skipped — work quickly now, the mayo comes later).

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Fold while just-warm — this is the timing law: the sugar, salt, and about two-thirds of the mayo folded into warm potato (it melts in and seasons evenly), then the apple, squeezed cucumber, eggs, and scallion folded in as it cools. Checkpoint: the fold test at the end: the mix-ins distribute without mashing further, and every spoonful carries apple and egg — it should look generous, not potato-with-flecks.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Chill 30 minutes minimum — the bowl is served cold, and the flavors need the chill to marry. The remaining mayo over the top, a grind of pepper. Checkpoint: the eating test, cold: soft-sweet, the apple's crisp-sweet snap and the cucumber's cool, the egg's richness, mayo's tang behind everything — a children's champion with a grown-up following, and the perfect cooling counter at a heavy grill table.

groups.title: The bind and the mix-ins

1/2 cucumber (about 75 g), small-diced and salted 10 minutes

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: contemporary — the Western-contact bowl, claimed. Korean potato salad is what happened when Western salad met the Korean banchan table: mashed potato bound lightly with mayo and fruit — apple, sometimes raisins or cucumber — sweet, soft, and completely unbothered by anyone's definition of salad. It arrived in the twentieth century, stayed for the children, and every Korean grill restaurant now serves it (#B22's macaroni sibling beside it). Labeled honestly as the modern bowl it is; loved without reservation, because it works.

title: Korean-Style Gochujang Grilled Pork Ribs
times: Prep: 20 minutes, plus 8–24 hours marinating · Cook: 40 minutes · Total: About 1 hour 10 minutes (marinate ahead) · Serves 4

schema.name: Korean-Style Gochujang Grilled Pork Ribs
recipeIngredient: 1.5 kg country-style pork ribs (boneless shoulder-cut, about 6 pieces), or bone-in pork ribs cut into individual ribs
1/2 Asian pear (about 150 g), grated and squeezed nearly dry
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), kimchi (#B01), musaengchae (#B08), lettuce ssam

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Stage one — roast gentle. Thick-side down on the cool zone, lid down, turning every 8–10 minutes, 25–30 minutes total. The fat renders slowly and the interior cooks through without the sugars involved yet. No glaze in this stage — glaze on raw heat is the burned-sugar trap. Checkpoint: at stage one's end the meat is firm-poached looking, opaque to the center at a test cut edge (pork's rule: no pink for the cautious table, a faint blush acceptable at exactly 70 °C internal if you measure), and the surface is dry-ish and ready to take glaze.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Stage two — glaze hot. Move the ribs to the hot zone. Brush the reserved marinade on both faces, turning every 90 seconds, building two or three thin coats — 6–8 minutes total. Each thin coat sets glossy; one thick coat burns. Checkpoint: the surface should go brick-red and tacky-glossy, charred only at the fat edges. If any face blackens, it has had enough fire — back to the cool zone to rest.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Rest 5 minutes, cut between the bones (or into thick slices for boneless), sesame over, platter. Checkpoint: eating test: the glaze's sweet-heat edge, then rendered-soft shoulder meat that pulls tender under the tooth — this should eat like the best version of backyard ribs that a Korean pantry makes, and the honest note at the table is that it is a modern hybrid, not an old recipe wearing a new one.

groups.title: The marinade-glaze
items: 1/2 Asian pear (about 150 g), grated and squeezed nearly dry

groups.title: The table
items: Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), kimchi (#B01), musaengchae (#B08), lettuce ssam

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: contemporary. This is the grill-country bridge record: country-style pork ribs — those thick, meaty shoulder chops sold as ribs — wearing a gochujang marinade built for low-and-slow-ish grilling rather than the tabletop's speed rounds. It is not a traditional recipe with a lineage to defend; it is the yangnyeom lane's flavor set applied to a cut that loves it, written honestly as a modern build. The technique worth keeping is the two-stage fire: gentle roasting first to render and cook through, then a hot finish to set the glaze.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Marinate long — this cut earns it. Country ribs are thick; the 8–24-hour soak is the difference between glazed meat and spiced meat. Reserve a third of the marinade in a separate container before the ribs go in — that clean portion becomes the finishing glaze.
  • Plan a two-zone fire (or a two-stage oven-and-grill path): one side medium-low for the roast stage, one side hot for the glaze finish. If the tabletop burner is all you have, this record moves to the oven for stage one (160 °C, 25 minutes) and the pan for stage two.
  • Pull the ribs from the fridge 30 minutes ahead.

Checkpoint — at stage one's end the meat is firm-poached looking, opaque to the center at a test cut edge (pork's rule: no pink for the cautious table, a faint blush acceptable at exactly 70 °C internal if you measure), and the surface is dry-ish and ready to take glaze.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 2. Stage two — glaze hot. Move the ribs to the hot zone. Brush the reserved marinade on both faces, turning every 90 seconds, building two or three thin coats — 6–8 minutes total. Each thin coat sets glossy; one thick coat burns. Checkpoint — the surface should go brick-red and tacky-glossy, charred only at the fat edges. If any face blackens, it has had enough fire — back to the cool zone to rest.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 3. Rest 5 minutes, cut between the bones (or into thick slices for boneless), sesame over, platter. Checkpoint — eating test: the glaze's sweet-heat edge, then rendered-soft shoulder meat that pulls tender under the tooth — this should eat like the best version of backyard ribs that a Korean pantry makes, and the honest note at the table is that it is a modern hybrid, not an old recipe wearing a new one. Chef’s Note — the reserved-glaze habit is the transferable trick: never glaze from the bowl the raw meat marinated in, and never glaze a piece whose sugars have not yet been diluted by rendered juice. Thin coats, many turns — the same law the yangnyeom fried chicken kitchens run at the toss.

title: Korean-Style Grilled Duck Breast
times: Prep: 15 minutes, plus 30 minutes salting · Cook: 15 minutes · Total: About 1 hour including rest · Serves 3–4

schema.name: Korean-Style Grilled Duck Breast
recipeIngredient: 2 duck breasts, skin on, about 350 g each, room temperature
1 tsp coarse salt (about 6 g) and black pepper, for the skin
2 cloves garlic (about 8 g), grated; 1 thumb ginger (about 10 g), grated
1 tsp toasted sesame seeds (about 4 g), 2 scallions (about 30 g) finely sliced
Steamed rice (about 400 g cooked), sangchu geotjeori (#F03) or minari muchim (#F04) — the sharp fresh salad is not optional here, kimchi (#B01) beside

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Cold pan, skin down. The one instruction that sounds wrong and is right: the breast goes into a cold pan or onto a grill grate set at its lowest, skin down, and the heat comes up under it. Render 8–10 minutes at gentle heat, pouring off the fat as it pools (keep it — duck fat is this record's second product). Checkpoint: the skin should go from pale to deep gold slowly, the crosshatch opening as the fat renders out of it. No spitting violence: if the pan roars, the heat is too high and the skin browns before the fat has left — lower it and pour off the fat.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Flip to the flesh side, 2–3 minutes only, brushing the cooked flesh face with the sauce as it comes off the heat. Duck breast's doneness is medium — the center rosy at 54–56 °C on a thermometer, or the feel of the base of your thumb when your thumb touches your ring finger. Checkpoint: the flesh face should be just colored and glazed, not crusted. Overcooked duck is the record's only real failure; a rosy center is correct here in a way it never is for chicken (#M16, #M17) — duck is served medium at every table that knows it.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Rest 8 minutes — the full eight. Duck carries hard, and a breast cut at the pan bleeds its juice onto the board; a breast cut at eight keeps it. Then slice across the breast, on the bias, into thick coins, skin up. Sesame and scallion over, the rest of the brush sauce spooned around. Checkpoint: eating test, with the sharp salad in the same bite: crisp, fully rendered skin; rosy, silky-fatty flesh; soy-ginger glaze; then the geotjeori's vinegar cutting clean. Rich, then reset — that rhythm is the whole plate.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: contemporary. Duck is the guest at this table, not a native — you will not find it on the old grill lists — but the Korean pantry fits it like it was invited: duck's rich fat wants sesame, soy, garlic, and ginger, and the sharp fresh banchan cut it exactly where it needs cutting. This record runs a skin-on breast the French way, cross-hatched and rendered slow, then finished in the Korean register with a soy-ginger brush and a scallion-sesame finish. Written honestly: a modern bridge, and a good one.
