title: LA-Style Galbi
times: Prep: 25 minutes, plus 6–24 hours marinating · Cook: 12 minutes · Total: About 40 minutes at the table (marinate ahead) · Serves 4

schema.name: LA-Style Galbi
recipeIngredient: 1.6 kg beef short ribs, flanken-cut across the bone, 8–10 mm thick (6–8 pieces; order "LA galbi cut" at a Korean market)
1 Asian pear (about 300 g), grated with juice
2 scallions (about 30 g), sliced; 1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds (about 8 g)
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), lettuce and perilla leaves for ssam, ssamjang (#SA01), pajeori (#F02), kimchi (#B01), garlic cloves sliced thick

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Set the fire for medium-hot, two-zone if you can. Charcoal burned down to gray-edged coals, or a grill you can hold your hand over for 3–4 seconds at the cooking height (around 200 °C). Galbi's sugar wants to blacken; a cooler zone gives you an escape hatch when a strip lacquers before the meat at the bone is done. Lay the strips in one layer, bone side down first. Checkpoint: the first minute tells you if the fire is right: steady sizzle, light smoke, the smell of caramelizing soy. Violent flare-ups mean drip fat found the coals — move the strip, don't lose it.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Grill 3–4 minutes a side, flipping once or twice. The grill boss's law: leave the strips alone until the edges weep and the underside goes mahogany, then flip with tongs — never a fork; the juice is the point. The second side takes a minute less. If a strip's sugars run ahead of the meat, shift it to the cool zone and close the lid for 90 seconds; steam finishes the center while the lacquer rests. Checkpoint: the pull test: the meat between the bones has firmed, the surface is glossy mahogany with char in the crosshatch scores, and the cut edge at a bone shows no raw red — a sliver of pink at the bone is right, raw is not. One test piece eaten at the grill boss's station is traditional and non-negotiable.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Scissors, platter, ssam. Pull the strips and cut them with kitchen scissors into single-bone pieces, straight onto a warm platter at the table's center. Sesame and scallion over; the pieces go straight into waiting ssam: leaf, a thin swipe of ssamjang (#SA01), a piece of galbi while it is still hot, a strand of pajeori or a slice of raw garlic, fold, one bite. The bone gets gnawed at the table; that is what bones are for. Checkpoint: the ssam test: one bite, everything at once — sweet lacquer edge, juicy beef, ssamjang's fermented depth, the leaf's snap. If the galbi overpowers the ssamjang, the marinade ran sweet; trim the sugar next batch by a fifth. If the ssam falls apart, less is in the leaf than you think is enough.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: diaspora. LA galbi is the Korean-American chapter of the galbi story: beef short ribs cut flanken-style, across the bone, into thin strips about a centimeter thick — a cut immigrant butchers in 1970s and 80s Southern California turned into the backyard and restaurant grill's finest hour. The name honors where the cut became standard, not where the dish was invented; the soy-pear-sugar marinade it wears is the sweet register of the postwar era, dialled further for American palates. Cooked right it is one of the best things that ever happened to a charcoal grill: lacquered edges, juicy meat, and a strip of bone the table fights over. This record is the honest diaspora master — sweeter than the Seoul classic, unmistakably galbi. Who cooks what: one grill boss with tongs and scissors, a designated bone-counter keeping the pieces fair, everyone else on ssam duty.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Blend the marinade. Unlike bulgogi, where the aromatics are grated for a slurry, galbi's marinade is better blitzed smooth in a blender — pear, onion, garlic, ginger with the soy, sugar, mirin, sesame oil, and pepper. Thirty seconds, completely smooth. The sugar dissolves fully and every millimeter of the flanken strip takes the bath evenly.
  • Trim and score. Look at each strip: pull off the membrane on the bone side if the butcher left it, and score the meat between the bones in a shallow crosshatch — two or three light cuts each way. The scores let the marinade reach the center and stop the strips from cupping on the grill.
  • Marinate 6 hours minimum, 24 maximum, refrigerated, in a flat dish so the strips lie in one layer. Flip once halfway.
  • Pull the ribs out 30 minutes before grilling; cold galbi on hot charcoal steams gray at the bone before the surface lacquers.

blocks.html:
Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The cut: flanken, 8–10 mm, crosshatch scored, membrane off.
  • The marinade: blended smooth, 6–24 hours, flat single layer.
  • The grill: mahogany lacquer, char in the scores, no raw red at the bone, a sliver of pink allowed.
  • The table: scissors to single bones, ssam while hot, bones gnawed.

blocks.html:
Finish & Plate

Warm platter at center, scissors left in the pile — the table cuts as it eats. Ssam leaves, ssamjang (#SA01), pajeori (#F02), sliced garlic, and rice within every reach. The gnawed bones stack on a side plate, and the count at the end is the meal's honest ledger.

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Marinated strips keep 24 hours (freeze in the marinade up to a month, thaw overnight — the pear keeps working, so freeze flat and early). Cooked galbi keeps 3 days; chop and fry into kimchi fried rice with the bones for stock.

One test piece eaten at the grill boss's station is traditional and non-negotiable.

**Scissors, platter, ssam.** Pull the strips and cut them with kitchen scissors into single-bone pieces, straight onto a warm platter at the table's center. Sesame and scallion over; the pieces go straight into waiting ssam: leaf, a thin swipe of ssamjang (#SA01), a piece of galbi while it is still hot, a strand of pajeori or a slice of raw garlic, fold, one bite. The bone gets gnawed at the table; that is what bones are for. Checkpoint — the ssam test: one bite, everything at once — sweet lacquer edge, juicy beef, ssamjang's fermented depth, the leaf's snap. If the galbi overpowers the ssamjang, the marinade ran sweet; trim the sugar next batch by a fifth. If the ssam falls apart, less is in the leaf than you think is enough.

title: Mechurial Jangjorim Soy-Braised Quail Eggs
metadata: Korean · Easy · Serves 4–6 as banchan (makes about 24 eggs)
times: Prep: 10 minutes · Cook: 25 minutes · Total: About 35 minutes · Serves 4–6 as banchan (makes about 24 eggs)

schema.name: Mechurial Jangjorim Soy-Braised Quail Eggs
recipeIngredient: Water to cover; 1 tsp salt (about 5 g); a splash of vinegar (about 5 ml) in the boil
1 tbsp corn syrup or honey (about 20 g)
A few slices of jalapeño or a dried chili (optional, the spicy fork)
1/2 tsp toasted sesame oil (about 2 ml), off heat; sesame seeds to finish (about 2 g)

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The peeled eggs into the simmering braise, 10 minutes at the barest bubble — this first simmer drives the soy in through the warm shell-less whites. Checkpoint: the whites have gone from white to café-au-lait at the surface; the braise smells of soy and sweet garlic.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Off the heat, and the marinating is the recipe: the eggs sit in the braise 1 hour at room temperature, then refrigerate in their liquid overnight. The color deepens to walnut, the soy reaches the yolk's border, the flavor rounds. Checkpoint: the next day's taste test: cut one — a marbled tan white, a bright yolk with a savory halo at its edge. The egg should taste seasoned-through, not dipped.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Serve drained, lightly wet with the braise, sesame over — and the braise itself goes back to work: it is now an egg-fragrant half-batch of jangjorim soy, ready to braise the beef (#B20) or a second round of eggs (top the liquid up with a splash of water and soy). Checkpoint: the eating test at the drinking table or in the lunchbox: one bite, the savory-sweet white snapping against the rich yolk — the bowl empties two eggs at a time per person, and that ratio is the recipe's only scaling law.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the lunchbox jewels. Quail eggs, hard-boiled and peeled, braised in the jangjorim soy (#B20's braise) until the whites marble tan and the eggs turn savory through to the yolk's edge: these are the lunchbox's jewels and the drinking table's best one-bite. They run the same braise as the beef record with a shorter clock and one technique of their own — peeling quail eggs without losing half the white.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Boil 4 minutes, shock, peel wet. Quail eggs boil fast — 4 minutes from the drop for just-set yolks — and the peel works only under water: the shell's membrane releases in the cold shock, and peeling under a thin stream or in a bowl of water saves the whites. Older eggs (a week in the fridge) peel more kindly than fresh; the opposite of the fry-up's law, worth knowing once.
  • Bring the braise liquids to a simmer while you peel — the eggs should go into hot braise, never cold, to start the marbling at once.

title: Minari Muchim Water Parsley Salad
times: Prep: 15 minutes · Cook: 2 minutes · Total: About 20 minutes · Serves 4 as banchan

schema.name: Minari Muchim Water Parsley Salad
recipeIngredient: 300 g fresh minari (Korean water parsley) or watercress, roots trimmed, washed twice
A pinch of gochugaru (about 1 g), optional
1 tsp rice vinegar (5 ml) and 1 tsp gochugaru (about 3 g), swapped in for the warm seasoning

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: A pot of boiling water and the minari in for a count of ten — stems first, leaves under at the last three seconds — then straight to ice water. Checkpoint: the stems bright green and just-barely bent, the leaves vivid and untouched by cooking time. Ten seconds is not shorthand; minari's whole character is its snap, and thirty ruins it.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Squeeze by the fistful — the #B06 law, the water out so the seasoning in — and cut the squeezed bundles once across, into 7 cm lengths. Checkpoint: dry, springy bundles that hold shape in the hand.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Warm the seasoning in the bowl, minari in while the greens are still faintly warm, the full-minute hand toss (the massage is the recipe's only labor), sesame over. Checkpoint: the eating test: the stem's clean, peppery snap with sesame and garlic riding it — a green that tastes like it grew in moving water, which is exactly what it did. Beside samgyeopsal (#M10) it does the work a whole pickle plate attempts.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the spring water green. Minari — water parsley, Korean watercress's sharper cousin — is the green that arrived with spring floods and got its own seat at the table: blanched for seconds, dressed warm in the namul set (#B06's family) or served as a cold, punchy salad beside rich grilled meat. Its flavor is celery, parsley, and pepper in one stem, and it is the most distinctive green on this site's fresh list. This record runs the blanched-dressed build, the more traditional of its two lives.

title: Musaengchae Spicy Radish Salad
times: Prep: 15 minutes · Cook: 0 minutes · Total: 15 minutes, best within a few hours · Serves 4–6 as banchan

schema.name: Musaengchae Spicy Radish Salad
recipeIngredient: 500 g Korean radish (mu) or daikon, peeled, cut into matchsticks 5 cm long and 5 mm thick (a mandoline earns its drawer here)
1 tsp fish sauce (about 5 ml) or soy sauce

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The dressing whisked in the big bowl while the radish weeps — gochugaru, fish sauce, honey, garlic, ginger, vinegar worked to a loose paste. Checkpoint: taste on a radish off-cut: savory-sweet with a warm edge and a clean acid finish, a shade stronger than target.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: The squeezed radish and scallions tossed through the dressing, sesame last, and a 10-minute rest before serving — the rest is when the gochugaru's color blooms into the sticks. Checkpoint: the eating test: snap, the radish's pepper-sweet, the dressing's warm-sweet-acid in one bite — and beside a piece of grilled mackerel (#SF07) the fish tastes lighter for it. That is musaengchae's entire job, performed.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the fresh-cut radish bowl. Musaengchae is the fresh, unfermented sibling of kkakdugi (#B02): the same radish and the same red seasonings, but matchsticks instead of cubes and a twenty-minute clock instead of a two-day ferment. It is the traditional partner of the oily fish records — the mackerel (#SF07) and croaker (#SF09) tables almost always carry it — because radish's clean pepper-sweet snap and the dressing's light acid cut fish fat better than anything fermented.

• Matchstick, don't grate — the texture is the bowl. Grated radish gives up all its water instantly and the musaengchae goes from salad to sauce before dinner; matchsticks hold their snap for hours.
  • Salt the matchsticks 10 minutes, then squeeze them gently by the handful: the same weep-and-press law as the cucumber (#B07), at a gentler squeeze because the radish is firmer.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 1. The dressing whisked in the big bowl while the radish weeps — gochugaru, fish sauce, honey, garlic, ginger, vinegar worked to a loose paste. Checkpoint — taste on a radish off-cut: savory-sweet with a warm edge and a clean acid finish, a shade stronger than target.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 2. The squeezed radish and scallions tossed through the dressing, sesame last, and a 10-minute rest before serving — the rest is when the gochugaru's color blooms into the sticks. Checkpoint — the eating test: snap, the radish's pepper-sweet, the dressing's warm-sweet-acid in one bite — and beside a piece of grilled mackerel (#SF07) the fish tastes lighter for it. That is musaengchae's entire job, performed. Chef’s Note — this bowl and kkakdugi (#B02) split the radish year between them: the fermented cubes carry winter's depth and the stew pots, the fresh matchsticks carry summer's fish and the grill — same vegetable, same paste family, opposite clocks. If your kkakdugi jar runs empty mid-season, this twenty-minute bowl is the honest bridge until the next batch fizzes.

title: Mushroom-Soy Beef Bulgogi
times: Prep: 15 minutes, plus 2 hours marinating · Cook: 10 minutes · Total: About 25 minutes at the table (marinate ahead) · Serves 4

schema.name: Mushroom-Soy Beef Bulgogi
recipeIngredient: 700 g sirloin or chuck eye, sliced 1–2 mm against the grain (bulgogi-slice)
1 tbsp honey or brown sugar (about 20 g)
1 tbsp rice wine or mirin (15 ml)
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), sliced king oyster or fresh shiitake (100 g) for the moat, kimchi (#B01), sesame seeds (about 4 g) and sliced scallion (about 15 g)

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Whisk the marinade: strained soaking water (about 60 ml), soy, honey, rice wine, garlic, ginger, grated onion, sesame oil, pepper, and the mushroom paste. Add the beef and toss by hand until every shaving is coated. Press flat, cover, refrigerate 2 hours. Checkpoint: taste the marinade on a fingertip before the beef goes in: salty first, savory-mushroom second, sweetness clearly behind both. If it tastes as sweet as #M01's slurry, the balance drifted — this lane keeps the sugar in the back seat.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Grill hot and in batches — charcoal or a smoking cast-iron pan. Single loose layer; the shavings take 60–90 seconds a side. Flip when the edges weep and color, pull when the raw red is just gone. Toss the sliced fresh and rehydrated mushrooms at the pan's edge in the rendering juice; they drink the marinade the meat leaves behind. Checkpoint: eating test off the grill: the edge should be savory-brown, the middle juicy, and the aftertaste should be mushroom and soy, not sugar. The mushrooms should be glossy and nearly meaty.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Serve over rice with the pan juice, scallion and sesame over everything. Checkpoint: the bowl test: juice over rice first, meat and mushrooms over, and the whole bowl should read as a deeper, more savory version of the classic — unmistakably the same family, unmistakably not the same dish.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: contemporary. Same Seoul-lane architecture as the pear classic (#M01) — thin shavings, sweet-soy marinade, fast hot grill — but the sweetness is trimmed back and the savory dial is cranked with dried mushrooms. It is the bulgogi for the person who loves the genre but wants less sugar and more depth: shiitake powder and a splash of its soaking water turn plain soy into something that tastes like it simmered all day. Twenty minutes of that marinate does real work.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Soak the shiitake first — it makes two ingredients. Twenty minutes in the hot water rehydrates the caps (slice them for the moat) and leaves behind the soaking liquid that carries most of the umami. Strain it; grit sits at the bottom.
  • Grind two of the rehydrated caps to a paste and whisk them into the marinade directly. Mushroom in the soak plus mushroom in the paste is what separates this from soy bulgogi with mushrooms nearby.
  • While the beef marinates (2 hours, refrigerator), cook the rice and set the table — the same tabletop plan as #M01: one grill boss, everyone else on bowls.

blocks.name: storage-variations
blocks.html:
Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Marinated beef keeps 24 hours refrigerated. Cooked, it keeps 3 days and makes an excellent bibimbap topping or mushroom-fried-rice base — the savoriness survives reheating better than the pear version.
  • Variations: add a teaspoon of gochujang for a faint spice line toward #M13; swap beef for chicken thighs (#M16 architecture); fold the leftover soaking water into doenjang jjigae instead of water.

title: Myeolchi Bokkeum Stir-Fried Anchovies
times: Prep: 5 minutes · Cook: 10 minutes · Total: About 15 minutes · Serves 4–6 as banchan

schema.name: Myeolchi Bokkeum Stir-Fried Anchovies
recipeIngredient: 150 g dried baby anchovies (myeolchi, the tiny 2–3 cm grade — not the large ones, which want a different dish)
2 tbsp crushed roasted peanuts or walnuts (about 20 g), optional but the classic drinking build
1.5 tbsp corn syrup or honey (about 30 g)

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The dry toast first — the technique. Dry pan, medium heat, anchovies tossed for 4–5 minutes until they smell toasted-nutty and turn matte and snap-crisp (break one: it should crack, not bend). Checkpoint: the smell shift is unmistakable: from the fish-market jar smell to warm, toasty, almost nut-like. This pre-toast is the difference between crisp-chewy perfection and the tough, faintly damp disappointing version.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Push the anchovies to the pan's side, oil into the empty half, garlic in until it sizzles blond (30 seconds), then the soy, syrup, and gochugaru stirred into the oil — a bubbling glaze — anchovies and nuts tossed through, 1–2 minutes of constant motion as the glaze tightens and coats. Checkpoint: every anchovy wears gloss, the pan is nearly dry, and a test piece has the target texture: crisp shell, faint chew at the core, sweet-salty-heat. The 60-second window between glazed and tough is the only clock in the recipe — off the heat when they still seem slightly soft, because they crisp further as they cool.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Off the heat: sesame oil and seeds, a final toss, spread on a plate to cool in a single layer (piled hot, they steam each other soft). Checkpoint: fully cooled, an anchovy snaps cleanly. The bowl is ready — and it keeps, in a sealed jar, for two to three weeks, which makes it the banchan board's only long-shelf member.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the drinking table's crunch. Dried baby anchovies, toasted in a pan with garlic, soy, and sweetness until they turn from stiff to crisp-chewy, glazed and sesame-dusted: myeolchi bokkeum is the banchan that doubles as the anju — the snack that appears beside beer and soju at every drinking table in the country. At the grill it is the bowl between the meat rounds, salty-sweet crunch that the whole table picks at like it owes them money. Fifteen minutes, keeps for weeks.

title: Neobiani Royal-Style Grilled Beef
times: Prep: 25 minutes, plus 30–60 minutes resting · Cook: 10 minutes · Total: About 1 hour 15 minutes, mostly resting · Serves 4

schema.name: Neobiani Royal-Style Grilled Beef
recipeIngredient: 700 g beef tenderloin or sirloin, cut against the grain into wide sheets, 4–5 mm thick (about 8 sheets, palm-sized)
3 tbsp good soy sauce or soup soy (45 ml) — the closest modern shelf equivalent to the old jinjang
2 tbsp toasted sesame seeds, half ground to a coarse salt (about 16 g total — this is kkaesogeum, sesame salt)
4 cloves garlic (about 16 g), very finely minced
Optional, and dated if used: 1 tsp sugar (about 4 g) — sugar enters the written court line in the 1957 write-down, not earlier; include it as the mid-century layer and say so at the table
Oak or lump charcoal (about 1 kg), or a ripping cast-iron pan as the honest indoor bridge
Sesame salt and a few whole toasted sesame seeds, for the finish
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), lettuce and perilla ssam, gireumjang (#SA02) — the sesame-oil salt dip is the period-honest companion; pajeori (#F02) and kimchi (#B01) beside

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Grill the sheets one at a time, or two if the grate is wide. Lay the sheet flat, single layer, and let it sit undisturbed 60–90 seconds — the soy film sets and takes color, and the smell should be sesame and browning beef, not burning sugar. The grill boss's clock here is the edge: when the rim of the sheet pales and beads a little juice, it is time. Checkpoint: the underside, peeked at with tongs, is browned in a dry grid from the grate with no black — a sheet past mahogany into black has crossed from the sesame-soy register into bitterness, and the coals are too eager. Raise the grate a hand-width.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Flip once, finish fast. The second side takes 45–60 seconds. Pull the sheet when the raw red is just gone; the scoring has already guaranteed tenderness, so the only variable left is juice, and juice leaves with every extra second. Straight to the board. Checkpoint: press the sheet's center with a fingertip: it should give and spring, not resist. A test piece eaten standing at the grill should taste sesame, soy, smoke, beef — in that order of arrival, with sweetness absent unless the 1957 sugar layer is in, in which case it arrives last and faint.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Cut after the fire, in squares. The 1917 witness is specific and it is good practice: the whole sheet comes off the grate, rests half a minute, then is cut into neat squares — two or three cuts each way — for the platter. The square is the old table's portion logic, and it gives every diner an edge piece and a center piece. Sesame salt and a few whole seeds over the cut faces. Checkpoint: the squares on the platter should show the crosshatch scoring crisped at the intersections, browned faces, and an interior still faintly rosy at 4–5 mm. Squares that bleed red went too short; squares gray through went too long — and gray-through is the more common failure, because cooks trained on thin bulgogi shavings underestimate how fast a scored sheet's center arrives.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 4
recipeInstructions.text: Serve hot, in the moment, with the pan-truth stated. This dish dies holding: the 1957 line is "grill at the meal," and every minute on a warm platter trades sesame perfume for steam. The ssam build for this record is the quiet one: leaf, a bare finger-swipe of gireumjang (#SA02), one or two squares while they are still hot, fold, one bite. Heavy ssamjang buries the sheet's register; save it for the pork records (#M10). Checkpoint: the eating test at the table's first ssam: the wide, scored-but-intact bite — tender to the tooth with a structure thin bulgogi never has, smoke in the crosshatch, sesame on the finish. If the first taste is sweetness, the wrong cousin is on the plate.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the household-book line. Neobiani is the old beef sheet: tender loin cut wide and thin, its faces worked with the knife tip until the meat yields, coated in a soy-sesame seasoning set, and grilled fast over charcoal. The method enters print in the late 1800s household compilation Siuijeonseo under the heading 너븨안이, is witnessed again in 1917 as a sirloin or tenderloin sheet finished with sesame salt on a charcoal grate and cut into squares after the fire, and is written down once more in 1957 from palace-kitchen memory with sugar and the serve-hot-at-the-meal rule added. That is the lineage this record cooks. It is not "the original bulgogi" — the sweet pear-slurry dish (#M01) is a postwar Seoul development that shares an ancestor but not a kitchen — and the fastest way to ruin neobiani is to import that cousin's habits: no pear here, no gochujang, no overnight soak, and never a grind.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• The knife is the technique. Jankaljil — fine scoring with the knife tip, both faces, on the bias in a crosshatch, rows about 5 mm apart. You are cutting surface fibers, not hacking: each stroke is shallow, a few millimeters, and the sheet should relax and widen visibly as you work it. This mechanical tenderizing is what lets a 4–5 mm sheet eat tender at the table without fruit, enzymes, or hours of soak. A sheet that gets ground or minced has left this recipe entirely — that is the yaksanjeok and tteokgalbi road (#M09).
  • Build the paste. Stir the soy, sesame oil, ground sesame salt, garlic, scallion, and pepper into a thick paste. It should be assertive and smell of sesame first, soy second. Sugar only if you are cooking the 1957 layer — and if a guest asks why it's there, the honest answer is that the palace memory added it, the 1800s sheet did not carry it.
  • The rest is short. Coat each sheet lightly on both sides, stack them in a dish, and let them rest 30–60 minutes at cool room temperature — a coat, not a bath. The 1957 witness is explicit about the clock: rest, then grill at the meal, serve hot, do not hold. This is the opposite of the Seoul lane's overnight slurry, and the difference is the point.
  • Build a charcoal fire burned to gray-edged coals — hot but not flaming, a grate surface in the 230 °C range where a drop of water vanishes on contact. Neobiani's paste wants fast dry heat; a flame-up will take the sesame oil's perfume away in smoke.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 1. Grill the sheets one at a time, or two if the grate is wide. Lay the sheet flat, single layer, and let it sit undisturbed 60–90 seconds — the soy film sets and takes color, and the smell should be sesame and browning beef, not burning sugar. The grill boss's clock here is the edge: when the rim of the sheet pales and beads a little juice, it is time. Checkpoint — the underside, peeked at with tongs, is browned in a dry grid from the grate with no black — a sheet past mahogany into black has crossed from the sesame-soy register into bitterness, and the coals are too eager. Raise the grate a hand-width.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 2. Flip once, finish fast. The second side takes 45–60 seconds. Pull the sheet when the raw red is just gone; the scoring has already guaranteed tenderness, so the only variable left is juice, and juice leaves with every extra second. Straight to the board. Checkpoint — press the sheet's center with a fingertip: it should give and spring, not resist. A test piece eaten standing at the grill should taste sesame, soy, smoke, beef — in that order of arrival, with sweetness absent unless the 1957 sugar layer is in, in which case it arrives last and faint.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 3. Cut after the fire, in squares. The 1917 witness is specific and it is good practice: the whole sheet comes off the grate, rests half a minute, then is cut into neat squares — two or three cuts each way — for the platter. The square is the old table's portion logic, and it gives every diner an edge piece and a center piece. Sesame salt and a few whole seeds over the cut faces. Checkpoint — the squares on the platter should show the crosshatch scoring crisped at the intersections, browned faces, and an interior still faintly rosy at 4–5 mm. Squares that bleed red went too short; squares gray through went too long — and gray-through is the more common failure, because cooks trained on thin bulgogi shavings underestimate how fast a scored sheet's center arrives.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 4. Serve hot, in the moment, with the pan-truth stated. This dish dies holding: the 1957 line is "grill at the meal," and every minute on a warm platter trades sesame perfume for steam. The ssam build for this record is the quiet one: leaf, a bare finger-swipe of gireumjang (#SA02), one or two squares while they are still hot, fold, one bite. Heavy ssamjang buries the sheet's register; save it for the pork records (#M10). Checkpoint — the eating test at the table's first ssam: the wide, scored-but-intact bite — tender to the tooth with a structure thin bulgogi never has, smoke in the crosshatch, sesame on the finish. If the first taste is sweetness, the wrong cousin is on the plate. Chef’s Note — the modern-cut bridge: tenderloin at 4–5 mm with jankaljil scoring is the technique; the Gwangyang grill houses run the same idea one step thinner (3–3.5 mm) with a last-second toss, which is why their sheets taste like cousins of this one. If your fire is strong and your sheets are cut slightly thin, borrow their clock — season at the table, grill immediately — and you will still be inside the tradition. What no clock fixes is a soaked sheet: thirty minutes is already pulling juice into the dish, and overnight is a different recipe wearing this one's name.

blocks.name: doneness
blocks.html:
Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The sheet: 4–5 mm, against the grain, crosshatch-scored both faces, paste-coated 30–60 minutes — never ground, never soaked.
  • The fire: gray-edged charcoal, dry grid marks, mahogany not black, flipped once at the weeping edge.
  • The pull: raw red just gone, faintly rosy center, fingertip spring.
  • The finish: squares cut after the fire, sesame salt over, served hot with the pan-truth named.

blocks.name: finish-plate
blocks.html:
Finish & Plate

The squares go to the table's center while they still carry the grate's heat, on a warm platter with the sesame salt alongside. Rice, lettuce and perilla, the gireumjang (#SA02) bowl, and the honest quiet of a dish that needs no lacquer — the last sheet off the grate goes to whoever has been running the fire, by the table's oldest rule.

schema.name: Oi Muchim Spicy Cucumber Banchan

1 tsp fish sauce or soy sauce (about 5 ml)

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the instant cucumber bowl. Oi muchim is cucumber's same-hour answer to kimchi: sliced, salted ten minutes to draw the water, tossed in a gochugaru-garlic dressing and on the table before the rice cools. It is the cold-crunch bowl the spicy records keep calling for — the site's M-records reach for it the way rich tables reach for cold anything — and it is the easiest banchan on this list. No ferment, no cook, one law: salt first, dress second.

title: Oi Sobagi Cucumber Kimchi
metadata: Korean · Easy · Makes about 800 g (a small jar, eaten within the week)
times: Prep: 30 minutes · Cook: 0 minutes · Total: 30 minutes, best 6–24 hours later · Makes about 800 g (a small jar, eaten within the week)

schema.name: Oi Sobagi Cucumber Kimchi
schema.description: **Stream: heritage — the summer day's kimchi.** Oi sobagi is the kimchi of one afternoon: cucumbers stuffed with the kimchi paste, ready by dinner and gone by the weekend.
schema.recipeYield: Makes about 800 g (a small jar, eaten within the week)
recipeIngredient: 6 small Korean (pickling) cucumbers or kirby (about 900 g)
2 scallions (about 30 g) and a handful of Asian chives (about 20 g), cut small
100 g Korean radish or carrot, fine matchsticks

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Build the stuffing: gochugaru, fish sauce, garlic, ginger, sugar worked to a paste, then the scallion, chives, radish matchsticks and sesame folded through so it holds together as a coarse stuffing rather than a slurry. Checkpoint: taste a matchstick: full kimchi register, slightly stronger than you want to eat — the cucumber will dilute it over the hours.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Open each cucumber's fingers and press the stuffing into the pocket and between every finger, a generous teaspoon's worth; close, roll lightly in the bowl's remaining paste. Checkpoint: each cucumber is visibly stuffed, red in the seams, green at the shoulders.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Pack snugly in a container, lid on, refrigerate. Ready at 6 hours, best at 24. Checkpoint: the day-of taste: cold snap, the stuffing's salt-heat in the seams, a barely-started sourness. By day two the sourness is present; by day three the cucumbers are softening — the bowl's honest end.

blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the summer day's kimchi. Oi sobagi is the kimchi of one afternoon: cucumbers stuffed with the kimchi paste, ready by dinner and gone by the weekend. Where the cabbage jar (#B01) runs a month's arc, cucumber kimchi runs three days — it has no long-ferment ambition, because cucumber's water works fast in both directions. This is the bowl to make the morning of a summer grill, the cold crunch against the pork records' (#M10, #M11) richness.

title: Ojingeo Gui Spicy Grilled Squid
times: Prep: 25 minutes, plus 30 minutes marinating · Cook: 8 minutes · Total: About 1 hour 5 minutes · Serves 4

schema.name: Ojingeo Gui Spicy Grilled Squid
recipeIngredient: 4 whole squid (about 700 g cleaned weight), bodies 15–20 cm, cleaned, skins peeled, tentacles separated
1 tsp coarse salt (about 5 g) and a light grind of pepper
1.5 tbsp honey or corn syrup (about 30 g)

3 tbsp soy sauce (45 ml), 1 tbsp rice vinegar (15 ml), 1 tsp gochugaru (about 3 g), 1 tsp sesame seeds (about 4 g), 1 scallion (about 15 g) sliced, 1/2 Korean chili or jalapeño (about 8 g) sliced into rings
Steamed rice (about 500 g cooked), soju or beer's ceremony, mu sangchae (thin radish batons, about 100 g) to cut the heat

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Dry-grill first, glaze second. The scored bodies go on scored-face-down over the hot fire, tentacles beside them. Ninety seconds undisturbed — the bodies will curl and the scores will gape open, toasting in their grooves; the tentacle tips will char at their edges. Checkpoint: the scored face shows toasted brown in the grooves with light char at the curling edges; the smell is sweet-iodine ocean toast (this is correct — squid's smell on fire should be oceanic, never sulfurous; a sulfurous fish-market smell means the squid was past its day). blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: restaurant — the street-and-tavern grill. Ojingeo gui is whole grilled squid, Korea's pojangmacha (street tent) and drinking-table classic: one squid, scored, rushed over charcoal, brushed with a sweet-spicy gochujang glaze in the last minutes, cut into rings at the table, and eaten with the dipping sauce and cold beer or soju that the dish was engineered to sell. It looks like restaurant theater and cooks like a technique lesson — squid has exactly one doneness question (2 minutes or 2 hours, nothing between), and this record is a masterclass in the fast answer.

blocks.html:
• Score the bodies — inside faces. Lay each body open flat (it is a tube; cut along one side and open it like a book). Score the inner face in a diagonal crosshatch, 5 mm apart, shallow cuts only — the blade should never go through. Two things happen on the fire: the scored faces curl and open into blossoms, and the increased surface area catches glaze and char. Leave the outer face smooth.

  • Fire hot, with distance control: charcoal burned to gray-edge with the grate close (a palm's count of 2 seconds above the coals, roughly 250 °C at the surface), and the option to raise it.

blocks.name: doneness
blocks.html:
Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The squid: cleaned, skinned, inner-face crosshatch at 5 mm, bone-dry before the fire.
  • The grill: hot and close (about 250 °C at the surface), dry sear first, glaze after the flip only.
  • The pull: scored face toasted, glaze glossy, body springy-with-give before the four-minute mark.
  • The table: scissors to rings, dip ready before the fire, cold drinks standing by — the dish's whole grammar.

blocks.name: finish-plate
blocks.html:
Finish & Plate

The whole cut squid goes to the table's center on a warm board, rings and tentacles mixed, the dip bowl beside, radish batons and rice in reach. The last tentacle goes to whoever lost count of the soja glasses; the street-tent rule is the oldest rule.

blocks.name: storage-variations
blocks.html:
Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Raw squid keeps 1 day on ice; glaze and dip keep a week (the dip improves). Cooked rings keep 1 day and make a fierce stir-fried rice or noodle addition, reheated hard and fast — remember, this record is the 2-minute pole of squid's doneness law; the 2-hour pole is a different dish entirely (braised ojingeo-jjim, not this record).
  • Variations: the clean-lane fork skips the glaze for soy-garlic baste and the #SF02 register; baby octopus runs this same glaze on the jjukkumi record (#SF06); the dip doubles as the sauce for cold boiled eggs, a pojangmacha two-fer.

title: Pajeori Korean Scallion Salad
metadata: Korean · Easy · Serves 4 as the table's salad
times: Prep: 15 minutes · Cook: 0 minutes · Total: 15 minutes · Serves 4 as the table's salad

schema.name: Pajeori Korean Scallion Salad
recipeIngredient: 3 large bundles scallions (about 300 g), cut into 5 cm lengths, the whites halved lengthwise into thick ribbons
1 tsp rice vinegar (5 ml), optional but the table's brightness

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The cut scallions in the bowl; the dressing poured over — gochugaru, soy, honey, vinegar, sesame oil — and tossed with your hands for a full minute, squeezing the dressing gently through the ribbons as you turn them. Checkpoint: the scallions have just begun to glisten and bend — the salt starting its fast half-pickle — and every ribbon wears red-flecked gloss. It should taste sharp, savory, faintly sweet, with a slow gochugaru hum.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Sesame seeds over, one more toss, and the bowl goes to the table beside the meat. Checkpoint: the eating test: a pinch of pajeori and a piece of galbi (#M03) in the same bite — the scallion's snap and its clean heat cutting the marinated beef's sweetness. The bowl should empty at the pace of the meat; pajeori leftover at meal's end means the table missed its purpose.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the grill's counterweight. Pajeori is the scallion salad that lands beside the meat at every Korean grill table: big-cut scallions tossed in a bright gochugaru-soy-sesame dressing, slightly pickled by their own contact with salt, crunchy and sharp against the richest plates. It is the record the M-list cites more than any other fresh bowl — the galbi records (#M03, #M04) and the bulgogi (#M01) all reach for it — because scallion against beef fat is one of the cuisine's oldest and best pairings.

title: Patbingsu Red-Bean Shaved Ice
times: Prep: 20 minutes (plus freezing for home shavers) · Cook: 0 minutes · Total: About 30 minutes, assembled at the table · Serves 4 (one shared mountain)

schema.name: Patbingsu Red-Bean Shaved Ice
schema.description: **Stream: heritage — the summer grill's cold ending.
recipeIngredient: 200 g dried red beans (pat), 100 g sugar, a pinch of salt, water to cover — simmered 60–90 minutes to soft, then drained and half-mashed (the traditional sweet bean, best made a day ahead)
Or 400 g canned sweet red beans (pat in a can, the Korean market's), lightly crushed with a spoon
4 cups shaved ice (about 600 g): a shaved-ice machine, a food processor in pulses, or two trays of ice crushed in a towel with a rolling pin then pulsed — the target is snow, not cubes
1 banana, sliced (about 100 g); 100 g strawberries or kiwi; a handful of crispy rice cereal or crushed walnuts (about 20 g); 8 small mochi balls (about 60 g), optional
Injeolmi powder or roasted soybean powder (about 10 g), optional, the café's signature dust

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Shave the ice into a chilled wide bowl — a snow mound, higher at the center, worked quickly (shaved ice melts while you look at it). Checkpoint: the ice is snow-flaked, not granular — it should compress lightly under a spoon and hold the mound's shape. Coarse granita-textured ice is the difference between patbingsu and a snow cone, and the difference is the whole dessert.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: The toppings arranged in wedges on the snow — the bean in a fat stripe down the mountain, fruit wedges around, mochi and crunch scattered, the condensed milk zigzagged over everything, the injeolmi powder dusted last. Checkpoint: the visual is the recipe's second half: a striped, crowning mountain, every topping visible, assembled in under three minutes from the first shave (the clock is real — the mountain loses a millimeter a minute at room temperature).

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: To the table immediately, four long spoons, everyone digging from their own side. Checkpoint: the eating test: the first spoonful should carry ice, bean, condensed milk, and fruit together — cold, sweet, creamy, the bean's earthy depth under the milk's sweetness. The mountain collapses as you eat, the toppings avalanche into the melting snow, and the bowl's last puddle — bean, milk, meltwater — is drunk or fought over. That collapse is the dish's design, not its failure.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the summer grill's cold ending. Patbingsu is the shared mountain of shaved ice, sweetened red bean, condensed milk, and fruit that ends a summer grill meal the way the hotteok (#D01) ends a winter one: with the whole table around one bowl and four long spoons. The cafe-era versions run elaborate; the home version this record builds is the honest core — ice, pat, milk, a few good toppings — and the technique is entirely in the ice and the bean.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Make the pat ahead — the day before is ideal. Simmer the soaked beans to fully soft (a bean crushes to paste between fingers), drain, and stir in the sugar and salt off the heat; it thickens as it cools to a spoonable, spoon-stands-in-it spoonable paste.   • Freeze your ice in advance if you are making it: plain water frozen in a shallow tray shaves better than bagged cubes.
  • Chill the bowls — everything about this dish is temperature, and a warm bowl costs you five minutes of mountain.

- Variations: the injeolmi powder's café classic; green tea powder dusted with red bean; the fruit-swap of the season; a scoop of ice cream buried in the mountain center, the summer festival's extravagance.

originalInstructions: Shave the ice into a chilled wide bowl — a snow mound, higher at the center, worked quickly (shaved ice melts while you look at it). Checkpoint — the ice is snow-flaked, not granular — it should compress lightly under a spoon and hold the mound's shape. Coarse granita-textured ice is the difference between patbingsu and a snow cone, and the difference is the whole dessert.

The toppings arranged in wedges on the snow — the bean in a fat stripe down the mountain, fruit wedges around, mochi and crunch scattered, the condensed milk zigzagged over everything, the injeolmi powder dusted last. Checkpoint — the visual is the recipe's second half: a striped, crowning mountain, every topping visible, assembled in under three minutes from the first shave (the clock is real — the mountain loses a millimeter a minute at room temperature).

To the table immediately, four long spoons, everyone digging from their own side. Checkpoint — the eating test: the first spoonful should carry ice, bean, condensed milk, and fruit together — cold, sweet, creamy, the bean's earthy depth under the milk's sweetness. The mountain collapses as you eat, the toppings avalanche into the melting snow, and the bowl's last puddle — bean, milk, meltwater — is drunk or fought over. That collapse is the dish's design, not its failure.

schema.name: Sangchu Geotjeori Fresh Lettuce Salad
schema.description: **Stream: heritage — the lettuce bowl beyond the wrap.
recipeIngredient: 1/2 head green or red leaf lettuce (about 300 g), torn into bite pieces, washed and spun bone-dry
A splash of rice vinegar (about 3 ml), optional

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The dressing stirred together in the serving bowl — gochugaru, soy, honey, garlic — into a loose paste. Checkpoint: tastes a shade too strong on a fingertip; the lettuce's water will round it, same law as every fresh bowl in this family.

title: Scallion-Gochujang Grilled Oysters
times: Prep: 15 minutes · Cook: 8 minutes · Total: About 25 minutes · Serves 4 (makes 12)

schema.name: Scallion-Gochujang Grilled Oysters
recipeIngredient: 12 fresh oysters in the shell, scrubbed (medium size — large cups hold more sauce)
A folded towel or rock salt to steady the shells, lemon wedges, rice or just the platter and drinks

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Whole (no-shuck): cup-down on the moderate grate, lid or foil tent over, 5–8 minutes. They will hiss, gap, and sometimes snap audibly — each one that opens comes off immediately, knife-tip through the hinge, top shell off. Checkpoint: an opened oyster shows the liquor steaming and the meat just firmed at the ruffle's edge — poached, not dried. An oyster that stays shut after 8 minutes gets one more minute and then, still shut, goes to the discard pile — the raw-bar safety rule transplanted to the grill: a cooker that will not open is telling you something.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Sauce each cup: a spoon of the gochujang butter into the hot liquor — it foams and melds in the shell — scallion over, back on the grill (or under a broiler) for 60–90 seconds to set. Checkpoint: the sauce bubbles at the shell's edge and smells of butter, chile, and ocean. The meat should still be plump and just-set; over-sauced cups that boiled hard taste of butter alone.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Shucked-ahead path, for the confident: top shell off, a spoon of sauce in each cup, cup-down on the moderate grill 4–5 minutes until the edges frill and the sauce bubbles — same checkpoint, one step fewer at the fire. Checkpoint: eating test, the whole ceremony in one motion: tip the shell's contents into the mouth — liquor first, then the meat with the sauce's sweet-heat riding it, then the scallion's bite. The shells stack empty; the count is the scoreboard.

This is the easiest showpiece on the seafood list: shuck or no-shuck, ten minutes from grill to platter, and the table eats them like soup.

title: Sigeumchi Namul Seasoned Spinach
times: Prep: 5 minutes · Cook: 2 minutes · Total: About 12 minutes · Serves 4 as banchan

schema.name: Sigeumchi Namul Seasoned Spinach
schema.description: **Stream: heritage — the three-minute namul.** Spinach namul is the fastest bowl in the whole banchan tradition: blanch, squeeze, dress.
recipeIngredient: 500 g spinach, mature bunched (not baby), roots trimmed, washed twice (grit hides in the crown)
1 tsp toasted sesame seeds (about 4 g), lightly crushed

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Pot of unsalted water at a rolling boil, spinach in by the handful, stems first (hold the bunch tops-down, stems in the water twenty seconds, then plunge the leaves). Sixty to ninety seconds total — no more, the leaves cook in the time it takes to stir them under. Checkpoint: the leaves go vivid and just-wilted, stems bright and beginning to bend. Pull at vivid — the color at the pot is the color at the table, minus what overcooking steals.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Straight into cold water to shock, then — the technique — squeeze by the fistful, hard. The spinach must leave the colander as compressed, nearly dry bundles; a wet spinach bowl is a diluted one. Roughly chop the squeezed bundles once or twice. Checkpoint: a squeezed bundle holds its shape in the hand and drips not at all. This squeezing is the entire difference between restaurant namul and the sad watery version.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Season while the spinach is still faintly warm: sesame oil, salt, garlic, soy, sesame — tossed by hand, loosened to a bowl. Checkpoint: the taste: sesame-nut first, the green's mineral sweetness, garlic's hum, salt just behind. It should taste seasoned-through, not dressed-on-top — if the first bite is plain spinach and the second is garlic, the toss was short.

blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the three-minute namul. Spinach namul is the fastest bowl in the whole banchan tradition: blanch, squeeze, dress. It is the gateway recipe that teaches the Korean vegetable logic — greens seasoned with sesame, garlic, and salt until they are a dish rather than a side of greens — and at the grill table it is the bowl that keeps appearing alongside the rich meats because it weighs nothing on the palate. Master this and the pattern (#B05's blanch-dress law) is yours forever.

originalInstructions: Pot of unsalted water at a rolling boil, spinach in by the handful, stems first (hold the bunch tops-down, stems in the water twenty seconds, then plunge the leaves). Sixty to ninety seconds total — no more, the leaves cook in the time it takes to stir them under. Checkpoint — the leaves go vivid and just-wilted, stems bright and beginning to bend. Pull at vivid — the color at the pot is the color at the table, minus what overcooking steals.

Straight into cold water to shock, then — the technique — squeeze by the fistful, hard. The spinach must leave the colander as compressed, nearly dry bundles; a wet spinach bowl is a diluted one. Roughly chop the squeezed bundles once or twice. Checkpoint — a squeezed bundle holds its shape in the hand and drips not at all. This squeezing is the entire difference between restaurant namul and the sad watery version.

Season while the spinach is still faintly warm: sesame oil, salt, garlic, soy, sesame — tossed by hand, loosened to a bowl. Checkpoint — the taste: sesame-nut first, the green's mineral sweetness, garlic's hum, salt just behind. It should taste seasoned-through, not dressed-on-top — if the first bite is plain spinach and the second is garlic, the toss was short.

title: Sikhye Sweet Rice Punch
times: Prep: 15 minutes, plus 4–6 hours incubating · Cook: 1 hour · Total: About 6 hours, mostly untended · Makes about 1.5 liters (serves 6)

schema.name: Sikhye Sweet Rice Punch
recipeIngredient: 200 g short-grain rice (or sweet rice, the deeper traditional build), cooked soft with a little extra water (a loose pot, not a fluffy one)

200 g malt powder (yeotkireum, Korean barley malt — the enzyme source, from any Korean market), mixed with 1.5 liters warm water and rested 30 minutes, then strained through cloth or fine sieve, pressing the liquid out
A pinch of ginger (about 2 g), a few pine nuts (about 8 g) and 2 dried jujubes (about 10 g) for serving cups, optional

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The strained malt liquid poured over the cooked rice in a heavy pot, at a temperature your wrist reads as warm-not-hot (about 55 °C — the enzymes' working range; much above 65 °C they die), and held there: pot lid on, pot wrapped in a towel, in the warmest room or a 60 °C oven's residual heat, 4–6 hours. Checkpoint: at the hours' end, the evidence of conversion is unmistakable: the grains float to the top, hollowed and translucent, and a taste of the liquid is sweet — the starch became maltose while you were elsewhere. No floating, no sweetness: the hold ran too cool — reheat gently to warm and give it two more hours.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Boil briefly to stop the ferment: lift the floated grains out (rinse them, keep them — they are the drink's drifting rice), bring the liquid to a bare boil with the sugar, 5 minutes, skim, and chill thoroughly. Checkpoint: the cooled taste: lightly sweet, malty, faintly sparkling-fresh on the tongue, none of the raw-malt's edge. Sweetness dials up or down with sugar at this stage — sikhye runs gently sweet, a closing drink, not a soda.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Serve ice-cold in small cups, a spoon of the reserved rice grains in each, a pine nut and a jujube floating. Checkpoint: the drinking test: cold, malty-sweet, the grains eaten from the cup's bottom with the spoon after the liquid — the drink and its bite, the meal's last act. It should feel like the table exhaling.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the meal's closing cup. Sikhye — fermented rice punch, the faintly sparkling, gently sweet, malty-cold drink with rice grains drifting at the bottom of the cup — is how the traditional Korean table closed a heavy meal: not dessert's weight but a cold, alive, barely-sweet digestif that the holiday table poured after the meat and the fried everything. It closes this site's ledger the same way. The craft is a patient enzyme conversion: malt powder turns cooked rice's starch to sugar over a warm afternoon, and the cook's job is temperature patience.

blocks.html:
Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Keeps 4–5 days refrigerated (the boil and the cold hold it; the ferment's clock slows, never stops — drink it young). The grains keep separately in a little of the liquid. Cans of sikhye are the market's honest shortcut for the week the afternoon won't cooperate.
  • Variations: the yeot-sweetened winter build; a drop of yuja (#F09's jar) per cup for the citrus fork; the floating grains over shaved ice, sikhye-bingsu, the summer café's brilliant closing move.

title: Soy-Garlic Grilled Shrimp
times: Prep: 15 minutes, plus 20 minutes marinating · Cook: 6 minutes · Total: About 25 minutes · Serves 3–4

schema.name: Soy-Garlic Grilled Shrimp
schema.description: **Stream: restaurant — the clean lane.** The other grilled shrimp: no glaze, no heat, soy and garlic and sesame doing exactly what they do to good beef in the galbisal record (#M05).
recipeIngredient: 700 g large shrimp (16–20 count), shell on, deveined
1 tsp honey (about 4 g) — structure, not sweetness
Yangnyeom ganjang (#SA04), the scallion-soy dip, in a bowl the table shares
Steamed rice (about 400 g cooked), kimchi (#B01), lettuce ssam

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Hot grate or pan, single layer, two minutes undisturbed. The shells take light char at the tips; the smell is garlic and sesame over toasting shell. Checkpoint: the shells blush and the bottom edges char thinly; lift one — the meat below should be opaque more than halfway up.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Flip once, 60–90 seconds, off the fire the moment the last translucence at the center of a test shrimp is gone. Checkpoint: pull one and cut: opaque white through, still plump and springy. Shrimp's overcook line is 30 seconds past this point — the grill boss eats the test piece standing up, as is right.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Platter, and the dip is half the dish: yangnyeom ganjang (#SA04), scallions heavy, each shrimp dunked at the table. Checkpoint: eating test: snap, sweetness, soy-garlic roundness, the dip's scallion bite — shrimp first, seasoning behind, always. This lane exists to let the shrimp talk.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Marinate 20 minutes only. Soy and shrimp work fast; past half an hour the salt starts curing the flesh to a chalky edge. Twenty minutes is flavor; more is texture damage.
  • Pat the shrimp dry after the marinade drains, so the grate sears instead of steams.
  • Make the dip while the grill heats — everything at this record's speed happens at the end.

title: Soy-Pear Dak Bulgogi
times: Prep: 15 minutes, plus 2–6 hours marinating · Cook: 12 minutes at the table · Total: About 30 minutes at the table (marinate ahead) · Serves 4

schema.name: Soy-Pear Dak Bulgogi
schema.description: **Stream: restaurant.** Dak bulgogi is chicken's seat at the bulgogi table: thigh slices in the soy-pear marinade, grilled fast and hot like every other bulgogi lane record.
recipeIngredient: 900 g boneless, skinless chicken thighs, sliced 7 mm thick or left whole and butterflied
1/2 Asian pear (about 150 g), grated with juice
2 tbsp honey or brown sugar (about 40 g)
1 thumb ginger (about 10 g), grated — ginger works harder here than in the beef lanes
1/2 tsp black pepper (about 2 g); 1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds (about 8 g)
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), lettuce ssam, ssamjang (#SA01), kimchi (#B01), scallion threads

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Medium-high fire, single layer, slices not touching. Chicken's surface water steams before it browns if the pan is crowded — space is crust. Checkpoint: the first side is undisturbed until the edges turn opaque and the underside is browned, about 2 minutes for slices, 4 for butterflied whole thighs.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Flip once; the second side runs 1–2 minutes more for slices. Pull when the meat's juices run clear at a thick piece's cut edge and the surface is glossy brown — no pinkness anywhere, chicken's absolute rule. Checkpoint: test piece: glossy, tender, sweet-savory with ginger brightening the finish — chicken's mildness is the marinade's showcase, and every ingredient reads clearly here.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Scissors into bite pieces, sesame and scallion over, warm platter. Ssam or rice bowl, both lanes open. Checkpoint: the rice bowl test: juice over rice first — the pan will have a glossy glaze of rendered fat and marinade that spoons like a sauce, milder and rounder than the beef version. That spoon is the record's quiet prize.

title: Spicy Dwaeji Bulgogi
times: Prep: 20 minutes, plus 2–8 hours marinating · Cook: 12 minutes at the table · Total: About 35 minutes at the table (marinate ahead) · Serves 4

schema.name: Spicy Dwaeji Bulgogi
recipeIngredient: 900 g pork shoulder or collar (moksal), sliced 4 mm against the grain (ask for dwaeji bulgogi slice)
2 tbsp gochugaru (about 12 g) — the ceiling dial; 1 tbsp for a mild table
1.5 tbsp honey or brown sugar (about 30 g)

blocks.name: doneness
blocks.html:
Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The slice: 4 mm against the grain, shoulder or collar, marinated 2–8 hours in a smooth paste.
  • The grill: single loose layer, flip at the beading edge, brick-brown not black, under three minutes a batch.
  • The pull: juicy centers with a blush of juice, never gray-through.
  • The table: ssam or rice-bowl, cold banchan in reach, heat dialed for the end of the meal.

Finish & Plate

Platter at the center, sesame and scallion over the glistening red slices, and the pan's juice scraped into a small bowl for the rice. Ssam leaves, ssamjang (#SA01), garlic coins, and the cold cucumber (#B07) within every hand's reach — this record's table runs hot, and the cold crunch is not optional garnish.

blocks.name: storage-variations
blocks.html:
Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Marinated pork keeps 24 hours (freeze flat up to a month). Cooked, 3 days — and the leftovers are arguably the record's second life: kimchi fried rice with diced dwaeji bulgogi, or a melt-grade cheese-and-dwaeji quesadilla that the fusion lane would claim if it could.
  • Variations: the same paste on pork belly slabs (#M11's slower cousin); on chicken thighs (#M17); thinned with mirin into a glaze for the shrimp record (#SF01). The soy-pork fork without heat is ganjang pork bulgogi (#M14).

title: Spicy Gochujang Galbi
times: Prep: 20 minutes, plus 6–24 hours marinating · Cook: 12 minutes · Total: About 35 minutes at the table (marinate ahead) · Serves 4

schema.name: Spicy Gochujang Galbi
schema.description: **Stream: restaurant, the yangnyeom lane.** Plain language first, per this site's standing rule: gochujang-marinated beef is not "bulgogi with gochujang.
recipeIngredient: 1.6 kg beef short ribs, flanken-cut across the bone, 8–10 mm thick, lightly crosshatch scored
2 tbsp honey or brown sugar (about 40 g)
1/2 Asian pear (about 150 g), grated and squeezed nearly dry
2 tsp gochugaru (about 6 g), for the ceiling-chasers
1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds (about 8 g), to finish
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), lettuce ssam, cold oi muchim (#B07) and kimchi (#B01) — the fresh, cold banchan matters more here, the ribs run hot

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Charcoal or cast-iron at medium-hot — you can hold your hand over it 3–4 seconds. The gochujang sugars scorch faster than soy marinade, so build a cool zone or keep the grate a hand higher than for #M03. Bone side down first, single layer. Checkpoint: the paste should sizzle quietly and smell toasted-chile-sweet, not burnt. Any black smoke in the first minute means the fire is too close — raise the grate before the first flip, not after the first casualty.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Grill 3–4 minutes a side. The visual law changes in this lane: you are not waiting for mahogany, you are waiting for the red paste to darken one shade toward brick and go glossy at the edges. Flip once at the weep; pull the strip when the cut edge at the bone shows no raw red. Checkpoint: the pull test: brick-red lacquer, glossy, light char in the score marks, meat firm at the bone with a pink sliver allowed. Eat one piece at the grill station — the heat should land after the sweet, never before it.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Scissors to single-bone pieces, warm platter, sesame over, straight into ssam with rice and a piece of cold cucumber banchan in the same bite's orbit. Checkpoint: eating test: sweet, then warm heat, then beef — and the cold oi muchim resets the palate between ssam. If the heat erases the beef, the gochujang ran over 80 g; weigh it next time.

title: Spicy Gochujang Grilled Chicken Thighs
times: Prep: 15 minutes, plus 4–12 hours marinating · Cook: 14 minutes at the table · Total: About 30 minutes at the table (marinate ahead) · Serves 4

schema.name: Spicy Gochujang Grilled Chicken Thighs
schema.description: **Stream: restaurant, the yangnyeom chicken lane.** The spicy fork of dak bulgogi: boneless thighs in a gochujang marinade, grilled to a red-brown gloss.
recipeIngredient: 900 g boneless, skin-on chicken thighs, butterflied to an even 1.5 cm (skin on renders and crisps; skinless works, glaze harder)
1 tbsp gochugaru (about 6 g) — the heat dial
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), lettuce ssam, cold oi muchim (#B07), kimchi (#B01), pickled radish cubes

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Skin side down first on a medium fire — the skin renders slowly into its own fat bath and crisps while the paste on the meat side stays safe above it. Six to eight minutes, undisturbed, while the fat builds. Checkpoint: the skin releases on its own when it is deep golden and crisp; if it is still welded, it is not done. Never force the flip early.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Flip to the paste side, 4–5 minutes. The glaze sets in the rendered fat's heat; watch the edges, where it blackens first. Any flare-up: move the piece to the cool corner for 30 seconds, back to finish. Checkpoint: pull when the center of a test piece is opaque and its juices run clear — no pink, chicken's absolute rule — and the glaze is brick-glossy, charred only at the very fat edge.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Rest 3 minutes, scissors into strips across the thigh, sesame over, platter. Checkpoint: eating test: crisp skin snap, then the juicy paste-glazed meat, heat blooming after the sweet — and the cold cucumber between bites resetting the palate. That triangle is the record.

Six to eight minutes, undisturbed, while the fat builds. Checkpoint — the skin releases on its own when it is deep golden and crisp; if it is still welded, it is not done. Never force the flip early.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 2. Flip to the paste side, 4–5 minutes. The glaze sets in the rendered fat's heat; watch the edges, where it blackens first. Any flare-up: move the piece to the cool corner for 30 seconds, back to finish. Checkpoint — pull when the center of a test piece is opaque and its juices run clear — no pink, chicken's absolute rule — and the glaze is brick-glossy, charred only at the very fat edge.

blocks.name: step
blocks.originalText: Step 3. Rest 3 minutes, scissors into strips across the thigh, sesame over, platter. Checkpoint — eating test: crisp skin snap, then the juicy paste-glazed meat, heat blooming after the sweet — and the cold cucumber between bites resetting the palate. That triangle is the record. Chef’s Note — skin-on vs. skinless is the table's real choice here: skin gives the crisp face and self-bastes the glaze, but it also blunts the paste's contact with the meat. The regulars' compromise — skin on, and a thin extra brush of the reserved marinade on the meat side at the flip — gets both. Reserve a spoon of marinade before the chicken goes in; the bowl the raw meat sat in is done for the night.

  • Marinated thighs keep 24 hours. Cooked, 3 days — cold strips over hot rice, or chopped into a spicy chicken fried rice with the leftover glaze.
  • Variations: the soy-pear fork (#M16); the same marinade on wings, double-glazed in the last minutes, is the tabletop's snack lane; thinned and brushed on the shrimp record (#SF01) for the spicy table.

title: Spicy Grilled Nakji Octopus
times: Prep: 25 minutes, plus 1 hour tenderizing · Cook: 12 minutes · Total: About 1 hour 40 minutes, mostly resting · Serves 3–4

schema.name: Spicy Grilled Nakji Octopus
schema.description: **Stream: restaurant.** Nakji is the small octopus of the nakji-bokkeum tradition — the fierce stir-fried classic — and this record is that flavor set run over live fire instead of a screaming wok.
recipeIngredient: 2 small whole octopus (about 300 g each), cleaned — or 600 g octopus, tentacles and body separated
Water to cover, 1 tbsp salt (about 15 g), 3 slices ginger (about 10 g), 2 scallion whites (about 20 g)
Steamed rice (about 500 g cooked), bean sprouts or mu sangchae (about 100 g) for the cold crunch, sesame seeds (about 4 g)

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Dry slices onto the hot grate in a single layer, 90 seconds undisturbed — you are searing color onto already-cooked octopus, so every second is flavor, not doneness. Checkpoint: char marks on the faces and edges, the scored sheets curling open. The smell is toast over the ocean — clean and sweet.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Flip, brush the seared faces with glaze, 45–60 seconds, second brush-stroke, off the fire. Total grill time under 3 minutes — the simmer did the cooking and the glaze only needs to set. Checkpoint: glossy brick-red slices, char at the edges. The eating test at the grill station: tender-chewy with a snap that yields (nakji's correct texture — firmer than squid, never rubber), sweet-heat over octopus depth.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Platter, sesame over, and the table eats it over rice with the cold crunchy banchan beside. Checkpoint: the bowl test: glaze-slicked nakji over rice with bean sprouts in the same bite — heat, chew, crunch. If every bite is all glaze, the slices were too small; wide pieces carry the balance.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: restaurant. Nakji is the small octopus of the nakji-bokkeum tradition — the fierce stir-fried classic — and this record is that flavor set run over live fire instead of a screaming wok. The technique difference matters more than the flavor one: a whole small octopus (about 300 g each) is too thick to stay tender at grill speed, so it needs either the old-school pounding or a brief pre-simmer before the grill. This record runs the simmer-then-grill path — the home-kitchen-honest one — and the gochujang glaze lands in the final minute, same law as the squid record (#SF04).

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• The pre-simmer is the tenderizing — do not skip it for the fire's sake. Bring the salted, gingered water to a boil, drop in the octopus, and simmer exactly 4 minutes for small ones. Lift, cool under running water, and drain. The flesh is now tender-set and the grill's job is color and glaze only. Skipping this and grilling raw is how nakji becomes a rubber band.
  • Slice after the simmer: body into wide rings or opened flat into sheets (scored lightly in a crosshatch, the #SF04 law), tentacles in halves lengthwise. Pat thoroughly dry.
  • Whisk the glaze and park it at the grill station. Fire at medium-high.

It works, it is theatrical, and it takes a strong arm and ten honest minutes per octopus. The simmer is the calmer road to the same tenderness, with the small trade that the octopus loses a little of its juice to the pot — the glaze gives it back.

title: Ssam Lettuce and Herb Platter
times: Prep: 15 minutes · Cook: 0 minutes · Total: 15 minutes · Serves 4 (the table's foundation)

schema.name: Ssam Lettuce and Herb Platter
schema.description: **Stream: heritage — the table's other main dish.** The ssam platter is not a side.
recipeIngredient: 1 head green leaf lettuce (about 300 g) — the everyday wrap, mild cup
1 head red leaf or butter lettuce (about 250 g) — the tender alternative
20–30 perilla leaves (kkaennip, about 40 g) — the flavor wrap, anise-mint
1 bunch napa cabbage leaves, the tender inner ones (about 200 g), optional — the crisp snap wrap
1 small bunch watercress or minari (about 50 g)
Garlic cloves, sliced into thick coins (about 40 g), raw
Green chili or jalapeño, sliced (about 20 g)
Thinly sliced onion, soaked 10 minutes in cold water (about 100 g)
Ssamjang (#SA01), gireumjang (#SA02), the scallion-soy dip (#SA04), a bowl of rice, and the banchan board

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The platter's arrangement — bigger leaves under, herbs through. The lettuce cups fanned around the platter's rim as the chassis layer, perilla and cabbage tucked inside the ring, garlic coins, chili, and drained onion in small piles at the center where every hand reaches. Checkpoint: the geometry test: every diner, from any seat, can reach a cup, a perilla leaf, and a center pile without asking anyone to pass. The platter turns; build it round.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: The wrap build, the table's own method. The sequence this site's M-records keep citing: one leaf (or a lettuce cup lined with one perilla leaf — the double-bottom, the connoisseur's build), a thin swipe of ssamjang or a finger-dip of gireumjang, the meat while it is still hot, a garlic coin or chili slice or onion thread, a pinch of rice if the wrap runs meat-only, fold stem-side over, tuck the sides, one bite. Checkpoint: the fold closes without tearing and delivers everything in a single bite: that is the doneness of a ssam. Two bites means the leaf was overfilled; a torn wrap means the sauce ran to the fold — swipe thinner, higher.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: The pacing — the platter sets the meal's rhythm. Meat, wrap, rice, banchan, repeat. The leaves are the meal's brakes and its carriers; a table that runs out of leaves starts eating meat with chopsticks alone, and the meal quietly becomes a different, heavier thing. Checkpoint: the end-of-meal test: empty leaf platter, empty ssamjang bowl, and the grill's last pieces going into the last wraps — the platter planned to the end is the record's real success metric.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the table's other main dish. The ssam platter is not a side. On this site's grammar it is half the architecture of the meal: a basket of leaves and herbs, washed, dried, and built for wrapping, sitting beside the meat with the ssamjang (#SA01) and the dips. Every grilled-meat record from the bulgogi (#M01) to the lamb (#M20) points at this platter, and the meal's best bites happen inside it. This record is the assembly: what leaves, what each one does, and how the table builds the wrap.

blocks.name: before-you-cook
blocks.html:
• Wash everything, dry everything completely. Wet leaves tear at the fold and water down the ssamjang into a slick; a salad spinner and a towel hour is the whole prep. Cold water, then the fridge until serving — the chill is part of the contrast with hot meat off the fire.
  • Sort by leaf: the big lettuce cups stacked flat, the perilla in its own pile (it bruises under weight), the herbs in water and spun at the last minute.
  • Slice the garlic thick and soak the onion — the ten-minute cold soak takes its raw bite to the sweet-edged place the wrap wants.

title: Tomato-Onion Sesame Salad
times: Prep: 15 minutes · Cook: 0 minutes · Total: 15 minutes, best within 2 hours · Serves 4 as banchan

schema.name: Tomato-Onion Sesame Salad
schema.description: **Stream: heritage — the summer garden bowl.** The simplest bowl on the fresh list: ripe tomato and sweet onion in a soy-sesame dressing, the garden's summer answer to the pickle plate.
recipeIngredient: 3 ripe but firm tomatoes (about 450 g), cut into thick wedges
1/2 sweet onion (about 75 g), sliced paper-thin, soaked 10 minutes in cold water
Black pepper; 1 tsp toasted sesame seeds (about 4 g)
A pinch of gochugaru (about 1 g), optional
1 scallion or a few chives (about 10 g), sliced

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: The dressing whisked — soy, honey, vinegar, sesame oil — and tasted: it should run lighter than the cabbage family's dressings (#F05), soy present but polite. Checkpoint: the spoon test: bright, mild-savory, the sesame forward. The tomato brings its own acid and sugar; the dressing frames it.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Wedges and onion folded in with spoons — one gentle turn, the tomatoes bruise at the second — pepper, sesame, scallion over. Checkpoint: the eating test: the wedge's cold burst, the onion's sweet crunch, the dressing's savory line through it. Beside jumulleok (#M06) — plain seared beef — this bowl is the plate's entire garnish department, and it is enough.

blocks.name: intro
blocks.html: Stream: heritage — the summer garden bowl. The simplest bowl on the fresh list: ripe tomato and sweet onion in a soy-sesame dressing, the garden's summer answer to the pickle plate. title: Tteokgalbi Grilled Beef-and-Pork Patties
times: Prep: 30 minutes, plus 2 hours resting · Cook: 16 minutes · Total: About 1 hour at the table (rest the mix ahead) · Serves 4

schema.name: Tteokgalbi Grilled Beef-and-Pork Patties
schema.description: **Stream: restaurant — the ground road, honestly flagged.
recipeIngredient: 500 g beef chuck or short rib meat, ground coarse
300 g pork shoulder, ground coarse (the beef-pork split is the classic juiciness build)
1/2 Asian pear (about 150 g), grated and squeezed to a dry pulp
2 tbsp honey or brown sugar (about 40 g)
4 strips of bone or sturdy metal skewers (optional; see Method step 3)
2 tbsp soy sauce (30 ml), 1 tbsp honey (about 20 g), 1 tbsp mirin (15 ml), 1 tsp gochugaru (about 3 g, optional)
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), lettuce ssam, ssamjang (#SA01), kimchi (#B01), pickled raw onion or kkakdugi (#B02)

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Grill over medium, not rocket-hot. Charcoal at gray-edge with the grate a hand higher than for bulgogi shavings, or a pan at a solid medium (surface around 190 °C). The patty is thick and sweetened; a rocket fire blackens the glaze before the center cooks. Lay the patties with a finger's width between them, bone-end down if boned. Checkpoint: the first side is undisturbed for 5 minutes: the underside should be browned and release cleanly when lifted. A patty that sticks is a patty that isn't ready — the grate tells you when to flip, not the clock.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Flip once, then press. Turn the patties, and press each one flat with a spatula — 30 percent thinner, a deliberate smash. The press is tteokgalbi's signature move: it widens the patty onto the grate for a second seared face, squeezes the rendered fat into the fire for the smoke that flavors the batch, and sets the dense-chewy texture the name promises. Press once; re-pressing squeezes out juice. Checkpoint: the pressed face browns 4 minutes; the patty is done at 8 minutes a side total when the center is just past pink at a test cut (ground meat cooks to no-pink, full stop — this is the doneness rule for every ground record on this site).

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Glaze in the final 2 minutes, both faces. Brush the glaze on the top face, let it set 60 seconds, flip, brush the second face, 60 seconds more, off the fire. The glaze should arrive glossy and just tacky — lacquered, not candied. If it runs and burns, the fire is still too hot for the glaze stage; finish the batch higher above the coals. Checkpoint: the finished patty: glossy dark glaze, two seared faces, dense and springy to the press of a finger, and — cut one at the grill station — juicy inside with no pink, the pear's sweetness woven through the meat rather than sitting on it.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 4
recipeInstructions.text: Pull the bones at the table — the ceremony. For bone-in patties, the bone slides free with a twist and a pull, leaving a clean trough; the bones stack on a side plate and the trough fills with a little ssamjang (#SA01) from the table's bowl. That is the old restaurant move, and children of every age take the bone duty seriously. Checkpoint: eating test, in a ssam: leaf, ssamjang swipe, a chunk of patty torn or scissors-cut from the oval, fold, one bite. The texture should be the record's signature — softer and chewier than any burger, juicier than bulgogi, the glaze's edge against the ssamjang's depth. If the center is dense and dry, the press was repeated or the mix overworked at shaping; if it falls apart, the knead was short.
